title: 4 Month Sleep Regression: Signs, Duration & Help | Yorix
heading: 4 Month Sleep Regression: Signs, How Long It Lasts, and What Helps
description: The 4 month sleep regression is usually temporary. Learn typical signs, how long it lasts, how much a 4 month old should sleep, wake windows, and what helps.
body:
# 4 Month Sleep Regression: Signs, How Long It Lasts, and What Helps

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 15, 2026 · **Updated:** November 16, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

The **4 month sleep regression** — also called the **four month sleep regression** or **4th month sleep regression** — is the name many parents give to a stretch when a baby who had started sleeping in longer stretches suddenly wakes more, naps less, or takes longer to settle. It is common, usually temporary, and it does not mean you have done something wrong.

## Short answer

Around 3 to 4 months, many babies move away from newborn-style sleep and toward more mature sleep cycles. That uneven shift is why some families see more night wakings and shorter naps — the classic **signs of 4 month sleep regression**. When it does happen, it often eases over a few days to a few weeks if you keep nights calm and consistent. From 4 to 12 months, the American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) recommends **12 to 16 hours of sleep per 24 hours, including naps**, a range the AASM states is also endorsed by the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP).

### Typical ranges at a glance

Typical ranges from the sources below — not targets every baby must hit, and not a diagnosis.

| Question | Typical range | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| How much should a 4 month old sleep? | 12–16 hours per 24 hours, including naps | AASM (2016), endorsed by the AAP; also NHS |
| How long does the 4 month sleep regression last? | A few days to a few weeks; typically a week or two. Children's Health (regressions in general): two to six weeks | Sleep Foundation; Cleveland Clinic; Children's Health |
| 4 month wake windows | Ages 1–4 months: **1 to 3 hours**. No official 4-month minute count | Sleep Foundation |
| Sleeping through the night? | Many wake more again at 4–5 months. NHS: not routinely through the night until around age 1 | Newcastle Hospitals NHS; Derbyshire NHS |

## What is the 4 month sleep regression?

A sleep regression is when sleep that had been settling seems to go backward: more night wakings, shorter naps, or a baby who suddenly protests bedtime. The phrase **four month sleep regression** is popular because this is often the first time families feel that shift.

Sleep Foundation describes it as a developmental phase in which babies who were sleeping well may start waking more often and have more trouble settling. Cleveland Clinic notes that people often talk about a change around 4 months, but research has not shown regressions happening “like clockwork” at one age for every child. Not all babies have one (Sleep Foundation). Some barely notice a **4th month sleep regression**; others feel it a little earlier or later.

## Signs of 4 month sleep regression (and when it may not be a regression)

**Signs of 4 month sleep regression** often include, according to Sleep Foundation and Cleveland Clinic, more time to fall asleep or restlessness at bedtime; more frequent nighttime awakenings, sometimes with crying; shorter or fewer daytime naps; and more irritability after broken sleep.

**It may not be a regression.** Cleveland Clinic cautions parents not to assume every hard night is one. Check first for illness (fever, a cold, ear pain, or anything that does not feel right); hunger or more frequent feeding; a wet or dirty diaper; discomfort, including teething for some babies (timing varies — ask your pediatrician rather than assuming teething is the cause); a change in the sleep environment; or being too hot or too cold. If your baby has a fever, is feeding poorly, is not wetting diapers as usual, seems to be in pain, or you are uneasy, call your pediatrician.

## When does it start, and how long does the 4 month sleep regression last?

Timing varies by child (Cleveland Clinic). Sleep Foundation places the shift around 3 to 4 months, when sleep starts to consolidate, and notes that some babies struggle at this age, a little earlier, or a little later.

**How long does the 4 month sleep regression last?** Sleep Foundation: in most cases, a **few days to a few weeks**. Cleveland Clinic: **typically a week or two**. Children's Health (Dallas), on infant and toddler regressions in general: often **two to six weeks**.

NHS services also note that night waking often returns around 4–5 months and again around 8–9 months, and that many babies continue to wake at night for at least the first year. If the pattern lasts longer, or is getting worse, check in with your pediatrician.

## Why it happens: sleep cycles are maturing

Newborns sleep in shorter bursts around the clock. They are not born with a steady day–night body clock; that clock develops over time, as Newcastle Hospitals NHS explains. Babies also wake at the end of a sleep cycle and to be fed — brief night waking is normal.

Around 3 to 4 months, Sleep Foundation describes a major transition: sleep starts to **consolidate**, with longer nighttime stretches and naps that are beginning to organize. That shift is not always smooth. Factors can include an uneven move into more consolidated sleep, a greater awareness of surroundings, a disrupted sleep environment, and, for some babies, early separation protest. Cleveland Clinic, quoting Heidi Szugye, DO, IBCLC, also places this among first-year “ebbs and flows,” sometimes alongside growth spurts and new motor skills. Your baby is not “forgetting” how to sleep — their sleep system is being rebuilt.

## A sample 4 month old sleep schedule

**How much should a 4 month old sleep?** The AASM recommends **12 to 16 hours per 24 hours, including naps**, for infants **4 to 12 months**, and states that this consensus is endorsed by the AAP. Derbyshire Community Health Services NHS similarly says that from around 4 months, babies usually sleep **12–16 hours per day**. Sleep Foundation, citing that range, also describes a *typical pattern* (not a second official standard) of about **10 to 12 hours** at night, which may still be broken, plus **three to four daytime naps**.

**Example only — not a schedule your baby must follow**

| Time | What might happen | Sleep (example) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 7:00 a.m. | Wake and feed | — |
| 9:00–10:00 a.m. | Nap 1 | 1 hour |
| 10:00 a.m.–12:15 p.m. | Feed and play | — |
| 12:15–1:30 p.m. | Nap 2 | 1 hour 15 minutes |
| 1:30–3:45 p.m. | Feed and play | — |
| 3:45–4:30 p.m. | Nap 3 | 45 minutes |
| 4:30–6:30 p.m. | Late-afternoon wake | — |
| 6:30 p.m. | Short bedtime routine | — |
| About 7:00 p.m.–7:00 a.m. | Night sleep, with brief wakings and needed feeds | About 10–12 hours, not necessarily uninterrupted |

This example is a mid-teens total inside the 12–16 hour recommendation (about 3 hours of naps plus 10–12 hours at night). A baby closer to 12 or to 16 hours can still be normal if they are growing, feeding well, and reasonably content when awake.

## 4 month wake windows

A **wake window** is the time your baby is awake between one sleep and the next. There is **no official AAP or AASM minute count** for a **4 month old wake window**. The best cited range we found is from Sleep Foundation, which groups **1 to 4 months** and gives a broad typical range of **1 to 3 hours**.

Treat **4 month wake windows** as a loose guide. Watch for yawning, eye rubbing, fussiness, staring off, or your baby's own “tell,” and start a short wind-down before your baby is frantic. During a regression, wake windows can temporarily get shorter or longer (Sleep Foundation). If a numbered window and your baby's cues disagree, follow the baby.

## How to help

Keep a simple, repeatable bedtime — a feed, a clean diaper, a dim room, a song or a book — at about the same time each evening. Cleveland Clinic and Sleep Foundation both emphasize consistency.

Protect day versus night: morning light, ordinary daytime sound, and outdoor time when you can, with nights kept dark and quiet (NHS). Avoid very long daytime naps in fully darkened rooms if they blur day and night (Newcastle Hospitals NHS).

When you can, put babies 4 months and older to bed drowsy, not already deeply asleep, so they can fall asleep in their own sleep space (HealthyChildren.org / AAP).

Respond before your baby becomes very distressed (Newcastle Hospitals NHS). Sleep Foundation suggests waiting a short moment, then offering calm reassurance in a dark, quiet room. You do not have to leave a young baby to cry for a long stretch.

Be gentle with yourself. Many babies still do not sleep through the night even at 12 months (Sleep Foundation). If you are considering formal sleep training, talk with your pediatrician first.

## What can make it worse

A few patterns can accidentally stretch a hard patch:

- Treating every waking as an emergency — or ignoring a baby who may be ill or hungry.
- A stimulating night: bright lights, phones, play, or a long, chatty feed.
- A sleep environment that keeps changing (Children's Health notes that changing where your baby sleeps can make disturbances worse).
- Always falling asleep in a way that cannot be repeated at 3 a.m. Children's Health and HealthyChildren.org caution that a baby who only ever falls asleep while feeding or being held may be upset when they wake alone. You can still comfort at night and gradually offer more chances to finish falling asleep in the crib or bassinet.
- Missing tired cues, or pushing the day too long.
- Very long, late, dark daytime naps that leave your baby under-tired at bedtime (Newcastle Hospitals NHS).
- Unsafe “fixes” such as extra blankets, pillows, an inclined sleeper, or staying swaddled after your baby is trying to roll.

## Safe sleep and when to talk to a pediatrician

Through the first year, follow AAP safe-sleep guidance, as explained on HealthyChildren.org:

- Place your baby **on their back for every sleep** until 1 year. If they can roll both ways and roll after being placed on their back, you need not keep turning them — keep the crib clear.
- Use a **firm, flat, non-inclined** surface that meets safety standards and does not indent under your baby. Surfaces that incline more than 10 degrees are not considered safe for infant sleep.
- Use a **fitted sheet only**. No loose bedding, pillows, quilts, stuffed toys, or bumper pads.
- **Room-share, don't bed-share,** for at least the first six months. HealthyChildren.org: room sharing can decrease the risk of SIDS by as much as 50% and is much safer than bed sharing.
- **Stop swaddling** when your baby is trying to roll. Do not use weighted swaddles or weighted blankets.
- Avoid overheating: about one more layer than you would wear, and no indoor hats after the hospital.

If your baby falls asleep in a car seat, stroller, swing, or carrier, move them to that firm, flat surface on their back as soon as you can.

**Talk to your pediatrician** if you are worried, if growth or feeding drops or wet diapers fall (Sleep Foundation), if breathing during sleep looks or sounds abnormal, if there is a fever or your baby is unusually hard to wake, or if sleep stays very disrupted for weeks (Cleveland Clinic).

## Frequently asked questions

**How long does the 4 month sleep regression last?**  
Usually a few days to a few weeks (Sleep Foundation), typically a week or two (Cleveland Clinic), or often two to six weeks for regressions in general (Children's Health).

**What are the signs of 4 month sleep regression?**  
More night wakings, shorter or skipped naps, taking longer to fall asleep, and a fussier, more tired baby. Consider illness, hunger, discomfort, and a dirty diaper first.

**How much should a 4 month old sleep?**  
AASM recommends 12 to 16 hours per 24 hours, including naps, for infants 4 to 12 months, a range it says is endorsed by the AAP.

**What are typical 4 month wake windows?**  
Sleep Foundation gives **1 to 3 hours** for babies **1 to 4 months**. Use that as a starting point for **4 month wake windows**.

**Do all babies go through a four month sleep regression?**  
No. Not all babies have one (Sleep Foundation), and research has not shown a clockwork change at one exact age (Cleveland Clinic).

## A calmer way to see the pattern (Yorix)

**Yorix** lets you track sleep, feeds, and care, see wake-window and next-sleep-window predictions based on your baby's real day, and ask the in-app AI coach about the pattern you have already logged. It is a support for tired parents — not a medical device and not a diagnosis.

## Related reading

- [Baby Sleep Cycles: Why They Wake After One Cycle](/baby-sleep-cycles)
- [Baby Sleeping on the Stomach: When It Is and Isn't Safe](/baby-sleeping-on-stomach)
- [Sleep Associations: What They Are and How to Change Them](/sleep-associations)
- [When to Move Your Baby From Bassinet to Crib](/when-to-move-baby-to-crib)

- [Sleep regression ages](/sleep-regression)
- [6 month sleep regression](/sleep-regression/6-months)
- [3 month old sleep schedule](/3-month-old-sleep-schedule)
- [4 month old sleep schedule](/4-month-old-sleep-schedule)
- [Wake windows by age](/wake-windows-by-age)
- [Contact naps](/contact-naps)
- [Short naps](/short-naps)
- [Baby waking every hour](/baby-waking-every-hour)

## Sources

All of the following pages were opened and checked for this draft (14 November 2026). Dates below are as shown on the pages when they were checked, where a date was visible.

1. Paruthi S, et al. Consensus Statement of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine on the Recommended Amount of Sleep for Healthy Children: Methodology and Discussion. *Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine*, 2016. Open-access copy: <https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5078711/>. Recommends 12 to 16 hours per 24 hours, including naps, for infants 4 to 12 months; no duration recommendation for infants under 4 months because of wide normal variation and limited outcome data.

2. American Academy of Sleep Medicine. “Recharge with sleep: Pediatric sleep recommendations promoting optimal health.” <https://aasm.org/recharge-with-sleep-pediatric-sleep-recommendations-promoting-optimal-health/>. Same 12–16 hour range; states that the consensus recommendations “are endorsed by the American Academy of Pediatrics.”

3. Sleep Foundation. “4-Month Sleep Regression: Causes, Signs, and Tips for Coping.” Updated 15 July 2025. Medically reviewed by Nilong Vyas, MD, MPH. <https://www.sleepfoundation.org/baby-sleep/4-month-sleep-regression>.

4. Sleep Foundation. “Newborn Wake Windows: What's Normal by Age.” Updated 13 October 2026. <https://www.sleepfoundation.org/baby-sleep/newborn-wake-windows>. Wake-window table (1 to 4 months: 1 to 3 hours) and the 12–16 hour infant range.

5. Cleveland Clinic. “Infant Sleep Regression: What Parents Need To Know.” Published 13 July 2022. <https://health.clevelandclinic.org/the-4-month-sleep-regression-what-parents-need-to-know>.

HealthyChildren.org / American Academy of Pediatrics. “How to Keep Your Sleeping Baby Safe: AAP Policy Explained.” <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/baby/sleep/Pages/A-Parents-Guide-to-Safe-Sleep.aspx>. Back to sleep, firm flat surface, no loose bedding, room-sharing, swaddling limits.

7. HealthyChildren.org / American Academy of Pediatrics. “Getting Your Baby to Sleep.” Last updated 4 June 2024. <https://www.healthychildren.org/english/ages-stages/baby/sleep/pages/getting-your-baby-to-sleep.aspx>.

8. Newcastle Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust. “Sleep (infants 0–12 months).” Page last updated 20 May 2026. <https://www.newcastle-hospitals.nhs.uk/services/great-north-childrens-hospital/childrens-sleep-service/sleep-infants-0-12-months/>.

9. Derbyshire Community Health Services NHS. “How much will my baby sleep in their first year?” <https://derbyshirefamilyhealthservice.nhs.uk/our-services/0-5-years/your-babys-first-year/sleep>.

10. Children's Health (Dallas). “Sleep regression in infants and toddlers.” Timestamps on the page: 8 November 2018 and 3 February 2023. <https://www.childrens.com/health-wellness/sleep-regression-in-infants-and-toddlers>. description: An 18 month old sleep schedule on one nap: 11–14 hours in 24 hours (AASM), a typical day, bedtime, and how this differs from the 15-month and regression pages.
body:
# 18 Month Old Sleep Schedule: Life on One Nap

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 16, 2026 · **Updated:** November 16, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

Eighteen months is often the first stretch of a **settled one-nap day**, not the first time you have heard about one nap. The [15-month sleep schedule](/15-month-old-sleep-schedule) and our [2-to-1 nap transition](/2-to-1-nap-transition) page own the switch itself. The [18-month sleep regression](/sleep-regression/18-months) owns the bump. This page is the ordinary timetable once (or as) that nap has settled — totals, a typical day, and bedtime — not a second sample-day clone of 15 months and not a rewrite of the regression article.

## Short answer

The American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AAP-endorsed) recommends **11 to 14 hours of sleep in 24 hours** for children ages 1 to 2 years, including naps. KidsHealth and Cleveland Clinic use the same toddler range. By 18 months, **most** toddlers are down to **one daytime nap** (KidsHealth; Sleep Foundation describes one nap as typical by 18 to 24 months). That nap is often in the early afternoon and may last from about 1.5 to 3 hours — Sleep Foundation cites that length for a typical 2-year-old nap; 18-month naps are in the same ballpark, not a separate official number. Nights are usually longer than they were at 12 months. If your 18-month-old is still clearly on two naps and is happy, you do not have to force the drop this week; see the transition page.

### Key numbers at a glance

| Question | What the sources say | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Total sleep at 1–2 years | 11–14 hours in 24 hours, including naps | AASM (AAP-endorsed); KidsHealth; Cleveland Clinic |
| Naps at 18 months | Most are on one nap; some are still mid-transition | KidsHealth; Sleep Foundation (18–24 months for one nap) |
| One-nap length | Sleep Foundation: a typical 2-year-old nap is about 1.5 to 3 hours (use as a nearby figure, not an 18-month law) | Sleep Foundation |
| If they are still on two naps | Common in the 12–18 month window; sources disagree on when the morning nap goes (Mayo Clinic often 10–12 months; Boys Town and KidsHealth later). See [2-to-1 nap transition](/2-to-1-nap-transition) | Existing sourced conflict |

## A typical one-nap day (example only)

This is a picture, not a test. Clock times move with your household's morning.

| Time (example) | What might happen |
| --- | --- |
| 6:30–7:30 a.m. | Wake and breakfast |
| Morning | Play, snack, outdoor time if you can |
| 12:00–1:00 p.m. | Lunch, then the nap (often 1.5–3 hours) |
| Afternoon | Snack, play; try not to let the nap run so late that bedtime collapses |
| 6:30–8:00 p.m. | [Bedtime routine](/bedtime-routine-for-baby) and lights out, set so the 11–14 hour total is realistic |

We are not publishing a separate 18-month wake-window chart. Our [wake windows by age](/wake-windows-by-age) guide already covers the first-year numbers; by this age, a consistent wake time, one well-timed nap, and an earlier bedtime on short-nap days usually matter more than a stopwatch.

## Bedtime at 18 months

A predictable routine still earns its keep (the same Mindell evidence we use on the [routine](/bedtime-routine-for-baby) page). If the afternoon nap was short or skipped, move bedtime earlier the way you would during the [2-to-1 transition](/2-to-1-nap-transition), rather than hoping a late, overtired evening will stretch the night. If the nap ran long and bedtime is a battle, the next day's nap may need a slightly earlier cap — without turning every afternoon into a fight.

Night feeds are no longer a given at this age for many toddlers; that is a [night-weaning](/night-weaning) question for your pediatrician, not a schedule rule.

## What this page will not redo

- The step-by-step drop from two naps to one lives on [2-to-1 nap transition](/2-to-1-nap-transition) and, with sample days, on the [15-month](/15-month-old-sleep-schedule) page.
- A sudden burst of night waking, separation protest, or bedtime stalling at this age is often discussed on [18-month sleep regression](/sleep-regression/18-months). Use that page for the bump; use this one for the ordinary day.
- Crib climbing and the later move to a bed are on [crib to toddler bed](/crib-to-toddler-bed). Most 18-month-olds can stay in a crib if it is still safe.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Ask if total sleep is regularly under the 11-hour end of the AASM range and your toddler is struggling by day, if snoring or pauses worry you, or if you are unsure whether a remaining night feed is still needed.

## Frequently asked questions

**How much sleep does an 18-month-old need?**  
11 to 14 hours in 24 hours, including the nap, according to AASM, KidsHealth, and Cleveland Clinic.

**How many naps should an 18-month-old take?**  
Most take one. Some are still shifting from two. Follow the child's actual day, not the birthday.

**What time should an 18-month-old go to bed?**  
Whatever time, plus the nap, adds up to a reasonable total before a consistent morning wake. Many families land in the early-to-mid evening; we do not have an official AAP clock time.

**Is there an 18-month sleep regression?**  
Sleep can get bumpier around language, independence, and the nap change. That is a separate article: [18-month sleep regression](/sleep-regression/18-months).

**Should I drop the pacifier or the crib now?**  
Not because of the birthday. See [pacifier and sleep](/pacifier-and-sleep) and [crib to toddler bed](/crib-to-toddler-bed).

## See the one-nap pattern (Yorix)

body:
# The 2-to-1 Nap Transition: How to Make the Switch

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 16, 2026 · **Updated:** November 16, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

The move from two naps to one is one of the noisier toddler projects. This page is the **method**: when to start, how to slide the morning nap later, and what to do on mixed days. It is not a second [15-month sleep schedule](/15-month-old-sleep-schedule) — that page already has sample days and a shorter step list. It is not the [18-month](/18-month-old-sleep-schedule) "life on one nap" timetable, and it is not a copy of the brief 2-to-1 section on [baby nap schedule by age](/baby-nap-schedule-by-age).

## Short answer

Sources do **not** agree on a single month. Boys Town National Research Hospital describes **15 to 18 months** as the most common window. KidsHealth says most toddlers are down to one nap **by 18 months**. Sleep Foundation uses **18 to 24 months**. Mayo Clinic gives an earlier picture: babies **10 to 12 months** often drop the morning nap, and you can try moving the afternoon nap and bedtime up by about half an hour. We treat **about 12 to 18 months** as the honest range, with mid-toddlerhood as typical, and we do not average Mayo with Boys Town into a fake official week. KidsHealth's clearest sign: a toddler who **fights the morning nap** is probably ready for just an afternoon nap. Slide the morning nap later until it becomes a midday nap, move lunch earlier, and use an earlier bedtime while the new nap stretches.

### Key numbers at a glance

| Source | When the morning nap often goes |
| --- | --- |
| Mayo Clinic (May 2025) | Often at 10–12 months; then shift afternoon nap and bedtime earlier by about 30 minutes |
| Boys Town National Research Hospital | Most commonly 15–18 months |
| KidsHealth | Most toddlers are on one nap by 18 months; fighting the morning nap is a key sign |
| Sleep Foundation | One nap by about 18–24 months |

## Are they ready?

**Probably ready** (practical signs, aligned with KidsHealth and with the readiness list on our 15-month page, not a clinical checklist):

- The morning nap is refused or very short on most days for a week or two.
- When the morning nap does happen, the afternoon nap disappears or bedtime becomes very late.
- They cope reasonably until lunch without that morning sleep.

**Probably not yet:**

- They are a wreck by mid-morning on a skipped morning nap.
- Nights or early mornings get clearly worse when you try.
- They are ill, teething hard, in a new daycare, or otherwise in a bad week. Wait.

If they just finished the [3-to-2 transition](/3-to-2-nap-transition) a few weeks ago, give the two-nap day time to work before you start this one.

## A step-by-step plan

Boys Town describes the usual pattern: you gradually keep the child up longer in the morning so two naps (for example around 9:30 a.m. and 2:30 p.m.) become one midday nap closer to noon, and lunch moves earlier. A practical sequence based on that description — not an official medical protocol:

1. **Push the morning nap later** by a small step every few days (15–30 minutes is a workable increment, the same kind of step we already use on the 15-month page).
2. **Watch the afternoon nap.** If it is crowding bedtime, shorten it slightly rather than letting the whole evening drift. (Sleep Foundation, in a related nap article, prefers shortening a nap to pushing bedtime later when the nap is the problem.)
3. **Move lunch earlier** so they are not starting the new midday nap hungry.
4. **When the "morning" nap lands around late morning to noon, it has become the one nap.** Protect it. The [18-month](/18-month-old-sleep-schedule) page is the picture of a settled version of this day.
5. **Bring bedtime earlier for a stretch.** Mayo Clinic's half-hour shift is a reasonable starting move; some toddlers need more than that on hard days.
6. **Allow mixed days.** Some days will still need two shorter naps. Sleep Foundation notes that a child may go days with one nap and other days with two during a transition. Follow the day's cues instead of ripping up the plan after one odd afternoon.

**Daycare.** Boys Town points out that the room's nap time may not match your child's readiness. Ask how they handle toddlers who are mid-switch, and use weekends to offer the nap your child still needs.

There is no second sample-day timetable on this page on purpose. If you want clock-by-clock examples, use [15 month old sleep schedule](/15-month-old-sleep-schedule).

## If it is not working

Put the morning nap back for a week or two if your toddler is falling apart every late morning, nights have become much worse, or the new "one nap" is a 30-minute collapse followed by a dreadful evening. Try again later. A failed attempt is information about timing, not a character test.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Ask if you are well past 18 to 24 months and two naps still seem required, if total sleep is short of the 11–14 hour AASM toddler range, or if snoring or very restless sleep is part of the picture.

## Frequently asked questions

**When do babies go from 2 naps to 1?**  
Often between 12 and 18 months, sometimes later. Mayo Clinic describes an earlier morning-nap drop than Boys Town or KidsHealth. Follow your child and the signs above.

**How long does the 2-to-1 transition take?**  
Often a few weeks of mixed days. There is no official duration.

**Should I drop to one nap at 12 months?**  
Only if the signs are there. A first birthday is not a deadline.

**What if daycare already has one nap?**  
You may need an earlier bedtime, and some weekend two-nap days, until home and care align better. See also [baby won't nap](/baby-wont-nap).

## See mixed days turn into one nap (Yorix)

**Yorix** can show how often you still have two naps, and whether bedtime moved earlier on one-nap days. The app cannot choose the week to switch and is not a medical device.

## Related reading

- [15 month old sleep schedule](/15-month-old-sleep-schedule)
- [18 month old sleep schedule](/18-month-old-sleep-schedule)
- [Baby nap schedule by age](/baby-nap-schedule-by-age)
- [3-to-2 nap transition](/3-to-2-nap-transition)
- [When do toddlers stop napping](/when-do-toddlers-stop-napping)
- [Short naps](/short-naps)
- [18 month sleep regression](/sleep-regression/18-months)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026.

1. Boys Town National Research Hospital. "Naps: Transitioning from Two Naps to One." <https://www.boystownhospital.org/knowledge-center/transitioning-two-naps-to-one>. 15–18 months as a common window; slide the morning nap later; earlier lunch; daycare mismatch; earlier bedtime or later morning wake if needed.
2. Nemours KidsHealth. "Naps." <https://kidshealth.org/en/parents/naps.html>. Most toddlers are on one nap by 18 months; fighting the morning nap as a sign.
3. Mayo Clinic. "Baby naps: Daytime sleep tips." May 7, 2025. <https://www.mayoclinic.org/healthy-lifestyle/infant-and-toddler-health/in-depth/baby-naps/art-20047421>. Morning nap often dropped at 10–12 months; move afternoon nap and bedtime up about 30 minutes.
4. Sleep Foundation. "When Should Kids Stop Taking Regular Naps?" and "How Long Should a 2-Year-Old Nap?" <https://www.sleepfoundation.org/children-and-sleep/when-do-kids-stop-napping>. One nap by 18–24 months; mixed days during transitions.

# 2 Year Old Sleep Schedule: Naps, Bedtime, and Totals

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 16, 2026 · **Updated:** November 16, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

A two-year-old's "schedule" is mostly a consistent wake time, **one afternoon nap**, and a bedtime that protects the day's total. This is not the [2-year sleep regression](/sleep-regression/2-years) page, which is about stalling, nap strikes, and other bumps. It is also not the [crib-to-bed](/crib-to-toddler-bed) how-to, and it is not a second copy of the [18-month one-nap day](/18-month-old-sleep-schedule).

## Short answer

For ages 1 to 2 years, the AASM (AAP-endorsed) range is still **11–14 hours over a full day, nap included**. At the second birthday, almost all children who still nap take **one nap**. Sleep Foundation, citing research, describes a typical 2-year-old nap as about **1.5 to 3 hours**, and says most children have already dropped to one nap by 18 to 24 months. Night sleep does more of the work than it did at 12 months. Some two-year-olds are already starting to skip the odd nap; that is a nudge toward [when toddlers stop napping](/when-do-toddlers-stop-napping), not an automatic reason to drop it if evenings fall apart.

### The numbers that matter most

| Question | Sourced range or typical figure | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Total sleep at 1–2 years | 11–14 hours over a full day, nap included | AASM; KidsHealth; Cleveland Clinic |
| Naps at age 2 | Usually one, often 1.5–3 hours | Sleep Foundation; KidsHealth |
| Just ahead (age 3–5) | 10–13 hours, which may include a nap | AASM / Cleveland Clinic (preschoolers) |
| When most children stop napping | Mayo Clinic: most have stopped by age 5. Sleep Foundation (citing Weissbluth): almost all still nap at 3; 60% at 4; fewer than 30% at 5 | Mayo Clinic; Sleep Foundation |

## A typical two-year-old day (example only)

Clock times are a sketch. Protect the total, not a famous bedtime on social media.

| Clock time (illustration only) | A possible shape of the day |
| --- | --- |
| 7:00 a.m. | Up for the day |
| Morning | Breakfast, play, or a childcare drop-off |
| Late morning to midday | The stretch since waking is now long; lunch before the rest often helps |
| Roughly 12:30–2:30 p.m. | The nap (Sleep Foundation's typical length is about 1.5–3 hours). A nap that ends very late can shove the evening out |
| Afternoon | A snack, then play or time outside |
| Early to mid evening | The usual [bedtime routine](/bedtime-routine-for-baby), then lights out |

If this looks almost like the 18-month example, that is because the official sleep range has not changed yet. What is different at two is language, boundary-testing, and sometimes a [crib that is no longer safe](/crib-to-toddler-bed) — not a new AASM number.

## Bedtime, not a battle plan

A short, boring, predictable routine still helps (Mindell and colleagues' bedtime-routine research, as used on our routine page). If the nap was skipped, move bedtime earlier rather than "running down the clock." If nights have turned into curtain calls and stalling, that behavior guide belongs on the [2-year regression](/sleep-regression/2-years) page, not here.

We do not invent a single official 2-year-old bedtime. Count backward from the morning wake so the 11–14 hour total, including any nap, is plausible — the approach Cleveland Clinic describes as "clock math."

If a new baby has just arrived and nights have gone sideways, that wobble is covered on [sleep regression](/sleep-regression) — it is a context, not a new official schedule or a fourth regression age. The 11–14 hour total on this page does not change.

## Naps at two: keep, cap, or question

- **Keep** the nap if your child is clearly better for it and bedtime still works.
- **Cap** a very long or late nap if it is the reason bedtime has slid past a reasonable hour. Sleep Foundation notes that, in general, it is better to shorten a nap than to push bedtime later when the nap is the problem — a point they make in the "stop napping" article, and it already applies at two.
- **Question** the nap only if they consistently cannot fall asleep at nap time, nights are late, or mornings are very early, *and* they are fine on days without it. Then read [when toddlers stop napping](/when-do-toddlers-stop-napping) and [baby won't nap](/baby-wont-nap).

Daycare often has a fixed rest period. You may not control the clock there; you can still protect bedtime at home.

## When a doctor should hear about sleep

Bring it up if the 24-hour total is often under 11 hours and days are a struggle, if snoring, gasping, or very restless sleep worries you, or if you want a safety check before a crib-to-bed move.

## Frequently asked questions

**How much sleep does a 2-year-old need?**  
AASM, KidsHealth, and Cleveland Clinic all use 11–14 hours across the whole day, nap included.

**How long should a 2-year-old nap?**  
Sleep Foundation cites about 1.5 to 3 hours as typical. Individual days vary.

**What time should a 2-year-old go to bed?**  
Pick a lights-out that, together with the morning wake and the nap, can still reach a sensible daily total. No AAP clock hour exists.

**Is a 2-year sleep regression real?**  
Sleep can wobble at this age. We treat that as a separate question: [2-year sleep regression](/sleep-regression/2-years).

**Should I move them to a toddler bed at 2?**  
Only if the crib is no longer safe or they are clearly ready. See [crib to toddler bed](/crib-to-toddler-bed).

## Check the 24-hour total (Yorix)

**Yorix** can add the nap and the night so you can see whether you are inside the 11–14 hour range. The app cannot pick a bedtime and is not a medical device.

## Related reading

- [4 Year Old Sleep Schedule: The Preschool Day, With or Without a Nap](/4-year-old-sleep-schedule)

- [3 Year Old Sleep Schedule: With a Nap, or Without](/3-year-old-sleep-schedule)
- [Toddler Bedtime Battles: Stalling, Not a Regression](/toddler-bedtime-battles)
- [Toddler Won't Stay in Bed: After Lights Out](/toddler-wont-stay-in-bed)

- [18 month old sleep schedule](/18-month-old-sleep-schedule)
- [2 year sleep regression](/sleep-regression/2-years)
- [When do toddlers stop napping](/when-do-toddlers-stop-napping)
- [Crib to toddler bed](/crib-to-toddler-bed)
- [How much sleep a baby needs](/how-much-sleep-does-a-baby-need)
- [Baby nap schedule by age](/baby-nap-schedule-by-age)
- [Bedtime routine for baby](/bedtime-routine-for-baby)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026.

1. Paruthi S, et al. AASM pediatric sleep-duration consensus, *Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine*, 2016. 11–14 hours at 1–2 years; 10–13 hours at 3–5 years, including any nap.
2. Nemours KidsHealth. "Naps." <https://kidshealth.org/en/parents/naps.html>. Same totals; one nap is typical by 18 months and through the toddler years.
3. Cleveland Clinic. "How Much Sleep Kids Need." 4 June 2024. <https://health.clevelandclinic.org/recommended-amount-of-sleep-for-children>. AASM ranges; counting backward from wake time.
4. Sleep Foundation. "How Long Should a 2-Year-Old Nap?" <https://www.sleepfoundation.org/napping/how-long-should-a-2-year-old-nap>. About 1.5–3 hours; one nap by 18–24 months.
5. Sleep Foundation. "When Should Kids Stop Taking Regular Naps?" Updated 23 July 2025. <https://www.sleepfoundation.org/children-and-sleep/when-do-kids-stop-napping>. Weissbluth-cited nap prevalence by age; shortening a nap rather than delaying bedtime.
6. Mayo Clinic. "Baby naps: Daytime sleep tips." May 7, 2025. Until about age 3, most children still take an afternoon nap of 1–2 hours; most have stopped by age 5.

body:
# The 3-to-2 Nap Transition: A Practical Plan

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 16, 2026 · **Updated:** November 16, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

This is a **process** page: what to do when a third nap starts to fail. It is not a second nap chart. How many naps are typical at each age already lives on [baby nap schedule by age](/baby-nap-schedule-by-age), and the 6- to 9-month schedule pages already show example days. Use those for the map; use this page for the messy week of the switch.

## Short answer

There is no official AAP week when every baby must drop from three naps to two. Mayo Clinic suggests cutting a **late-afternoon third nap at about 9 months**, so bedtime can come earlier. Huckleberry, which we treat as an app example rather than a clinical source, describes many babies finishing the switch by about 8 months. Ireland's HSE says children usually reduce to two naps a day at **6 to 9 months**. Those windows overlap but are not identical, so think "sometime in the second half of the first year," driven by your baby's day, not a birthday. When the third nap is refused, or it pushes bedtime too late, let the first two naps be the day's sleep, and **bring bedtime earlier** on no-third-nap days.

### Key numbers at a glance

| Question | What the sources say | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Official "drop by this week" rule | None from AAP or AASM | — |
| Mayo Clinic timing | Try cutting a late-afternoon third nap at about 9 months | Mayo Clinic, May 2025 |
| HSE (Ireland) | Usually down to two naps at 6–9 months | HSE |
| What to do when the third nap goes | Bring bedtime earlier (even 30–60 minutes is a practical step many families use; Mayo also uses a half-hour shift in a related nap-drop context) | Mayo Clinic; our nap-by-age page |

## Signs the third nap is done — or not

Practical signs, not a clinical checklist:

**Probably ready**

- The third nap is fought or skipped on most days for a week or more.
- When it happens, bedtime slides too late, or the night gets worse.
- On days you skip it and offer an earlier bedtime, your baby copes.

**Probably not yet**

- The first two naps are still very short, and late afternoon is a wreck without a third rest.
- Your baby is younger than the usual window and is still happily taking three naps.
- Illness, vaccines, or [travel](/baby-sleep-and-travel) is temporarily scrambling days. Wait if you can.

This drop is not the same as the later [2-to-1 transition](/2-to-1-nap-transition). Doing both in the same month is usually too much.

## A practical plan (not an official 7-day protocol)

No medical body publishes a day-by-day 3-to-2 script, so treat the steps below as a working plan, not a prescription.

1. **Watch a week, don't panic after one skip.** One refused third nap is information, not a verdict.
2. **Protect the first two naps.** If your baby will take a slightly longer morning or midday nap, that makes the late-afternoon gap easier. Do not cap those naps just to "save" a third one that is already failing.
3. **On days without a third nap, move bedtime earlier.** The goal is to avoid a long, [overtired](/overtired-baby) evening. A 30- to 60-minute shift is a common practical move; Mayo Clinic uses a half-hour shift when discussing a later nap drop.
4. **Keep the [routine](/bedtime-routine-for-baby) the same**, just earlier.
5. **Expect mixed days** for a week or two: some three-nap days, some two. That is the transition, not a failure.
6. **If two-nap days look worse after a week or two** — much more night waking, very early mornings, or a baby who falls apart by 4 p.m. even with an early bedtime — put the third nap back for a while and try again later.

If you want to see a three-nap day and a two-nap day side by side, use the [7-month sleep schedule](/7-month-old-sleep-schedule) and the [8-month](/8-month-old-sleep-schedule) page, not a new chart here.

## What can go wrong

- Dropping the third nap because a schedule you saw online said "8 months," while your baby still needs it.
- Keeping a late third nap that lands at 5 p.m. and then wondering why bedtime is 9:30.
- Treating every short mid-transition nap as a new problem. See [short naps](/short-naps) if 30-minute naps were already the pattern.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Ask if your baby is well past 9 months, still seems to need three naps, and nights or growth worry you, or if sleep fell apart and is not recovering after you put a nap back.

## Frequently asked questions

**When do babies go from 3 naps to 2?**  
Often in the 6- to 9-month range, with Mayo Clinic highlighting about 9 months for cutting a late-afternoon nap. Individual babies differ.

**Should I wake them from the second nap to "fit in" a third?**  
Usually no, if the third nap is the one that is failing. Let the two better naps stand and use an earlier bedtime.

**How long does the transition last?**  
Often a messy week or two of mixed days. There is no official duration.

**Is this the 8-month regression?**  
Not necessarily. Sleep can wobble when naps change, and [8-month sleep regression](/sleep-regression/8-months) has its own page. Fix the day first; don't assume a named regression.

## Watch mixed days fade (Yorix)

**Yorix** can show whether you are actually having more two-nap days than three, and whether bedtime moved earlier on the short days. The app cannot tell you the right week to drop a nap and is not a medical device.

## Related reading

- [Baby nap schedule by age](/baby-nap-schedule-by-age)
- [8 month old sleep schedule](/8-month-old-sleep-schedule)
- [7 month old sleep schedule](/7-month-old-sleep-schedule)
- [2-to-1 nap transition](/2-to-1-nap-transition)
- [Short naps](/short-naps)
- [Overtired baby](/overtired-baby)
- [Wake windows by age](/wake-windows-by-age)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026.

1. Mayo Clinic. "Baby naps: Daytime sleep tips." May 7, 2025. <https://www.mayoclinic.org/healthy-lifestyle/infant-and-toddler-health/in-depth/baby-naps/art-20047421>. Cut a late-afternoon third nap at about 9 months; half-hour shifts in a later nap-drop context.
2. Health Service Executive (Ireland). "Naps for babies and toddlers." <https://www2.hse.ie/babies-children/sleep/naps-babies-and-toddlers/>. Usually two naps at 6–9 months.
3. Nemours KidsHealth. "Naps." <https://kidshealth.org/en/parents/naps.html>. At 4–12 months, most babies take 2–3 daytime naps (the drop happens inside that span).
4. Our [baby nap schedule by age](/baby-nap-schedule-by-age) page already cites these sources and notes Huckleberry as an app example (many babies finishing 3-to-2 by about 8 months) — not a clinical standard.

# 3 Year Old Sleep Schedule: With a Nap, or Without

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 16, 2026 · **Updated:** November 16, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

Three is a schedule age, not a new "regression" we have chosen to publish. The American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AAP-endorsed) recommends **10 to 13 hours of sleep in 24 hours** for children ages 3 to 5, including any nap. KidsHealth and Cleveland Clinic use the same preschool range. This page maps **a working day at age 3**: the daily total, two sample timetables (nap still in, nap already gone), and how a fixed preschool start changes the evening. It is not a second [2-year-old sleep schedule](/2-year-old-sleep-schedule), and it is not a copy of [when toddlers stop napping](/when-do-toddlers-stop-napping). That article owns the drop itself — signs, a step-by-step change, and what to do to bedtime when the nap goes.

## Short answer

At 3, some children still take a regular afternoon nap; many are giving it up, or have already given it up (KidsHealth: many preschoolers get all of their sleep at night). For those who still nap, KidsHealth says most sleep about an hour, and that a regular time plus a short naptime routine helps. Cleveland Clinic notes that preschoolers who wake too early or have trouble falling asleep at night may not need the afternoon nap. If the nap stays, it still counts toward the 10–13 hour total. If it goes, bedtime usually needs to move earlier so the night can carry the whole amount — details on the nap-drop page.

There is no official AAP clock time for lights out. Set bedtime so that, with or without the nap, the 24-hour total is realistic before a reasonably consistent morning, especially if preschool or childcare has a fixed start.

### Key numbers at a glance

| Topic | Sourced figure | Who says so |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Daily total, ages 3–5 | 10–13 hours, counting a nap if they still take one | AASM consensus (endorsed by the AAP); restated by KidsHealth and Cleveland Clinic |
| The afternoon sleep | Some 3-year-olds still nap; many have already stopped. KidsHealth: among those who still do, most sleep about an hour | KidsHealth; Cleveland Clinic |
| Screens | Off at least 1 hour before bedtime; out of the bedroom | KidsHealth preschool sleep |
| If the nap is ending | Do not rebuild the drop here | [When do toddlers stop napping](/when-do-toddlers-stop-napping) |

## A typical day at 3 (examples only)

Clock hours below are sketches. Move them to match your kitchen and the preschool door.

**If they still nap**

| Clock time (sketch) | A possible shape of the day |
| --- | --- |
| 7:00 a.m. (give or take) | Up and breakfast |
| Morning | Play, time outside if you have it, then lunch |
| Early afternoon | The nap, often around an hour — KidsHealth's usual length, not a requirement |
| Afternoon | Snack and play. If the nap ends late, the evening will almost always slip |
| Early evening | Dinner, the [routine](/bedtime-routine-for-baby), and lights out chosen so 10–13 hours in a day is still reachable |

**If they no longer nap**

| Clock time (sketch) | A possible shape of the day |
| --- | --- |
| 7:00 a.m. (or earlier if preschool is early) | Up and breakfast |
| Midday | Lunch, then **quiet time** even without sleep (KidsHealth: a chance to slow down) |
| Afternoon | Snack, play; watch for a late-day crash |
| Earlier evening than the nap-day plan | Dinner and bedtime moved up so the night can hold most or all of the 10–13 hours |

We will not add a separate wake-window table for this birthday. A steady morning, a clear decision about the afternoon sleep, and a slightly earlier lights-out on no-nap days do more work now than a timer.

## Bedtime and preschool mornings

The same short wind-down is still worth doing every night. If evenings have become a negotiation, that is [toddler bedtime battles](/toddler-bedtime-battles), not a schedule failure. If the child is scared of the room, use [fear of the dark](/fear-of-the-dark). Night terrors, which are different from nightmares, are on [night terrors](/night-terrors).

Preschool does not invent a new official sleep number, but it does invent a morning deadline. Guard the night. A late lights-out rarely produces an easy preschool morning. If the class still offers a rest period, treat that as a maybe-nap, not as a reason to keep a late home bedtime on days they do not sleep there.

## Boundaries with our other toddler pages

- The decision and the steps to drop a nap live on [when toddlers stop napping](/when-do-toddlers-stop-napping).
- The 2-year timetable, and the 2-year regression, stay on those pages. Three-year-olds are in the 3–5 year AASM band, not the 1–2 year 11–14 hour band.
- We are not adding a "3-year sleep regression" article in this batch. If sleep suddenly falls apart, look at schedule, fears, bedtime stalling, illness, or a move to a bed — and ask the pediatrician if you are unsure.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Bring it up if your child is often below 10 hours in a day and looks worn out or hard to manage, if snoring, pauses, or mouth breathing worry you ([baby snoring and mouth breathing](/baby-snoring-and-mouth-breathing)), or if nightmares or night terrors keep returning.

## Frequently asked questions

**How much sleep does a 3-year-old need?**  
The AASM range for ages 3–5 is 10–13 hours in a day, counting a nap if they still take one. KidsHealth and Cleveland Clinic use that same band.

**Should a 3-year-old still nap?**  
Some do; many do not. Watch how the night looks after a nap or a skipped nap, rather than obeying the birthday. Use the nap-drop page if you are making the change.

**What time should a 3-year-old go to bed?**  
Choose a lights-out that, together with any afternoon sleep, still lands inside a sensible daily total before the morning you actually need. The AAP does not publish a clock time.

**Is there a 3-year sleep regression?**  
Preschool, a bigger imagination, and a fading nap can all make nights uneven. We are not publishing a separate "3-year regression" guide; use this timetable plus the battles and fears pages, and call a clinician if the change is sudden or severe.

## Check the 24-hour total at age 3 (Yorix)

**Yorix** can show whether nights and any remaining nap are adding up to the 10–13 hour range, and whether no-nap days are really ending earlier at night. The app cannot set bedtime for you and is not a medical device.

## Related reading

- [4 Year Old Sleep Schedule: The Preschool Day, With or Without a Nap](/4-year-old-sleep-schedule)

- [Toddler Won't Stay in Bed: After Lights Out](/toddler-wont-stay-in-bed)

- [How much sleep a baby needs](/how-much-sleep-does-a-baby-need)
- [2 year old sleep schedule](/2-year-old-sleep-schedule)
- [When do toddlers stop napping](/when-do-toddlers-stop-napping)
- [Toddler bedtime battles](/toddler-bedtime-battles)
- [Fear of the dark](/fear-of-the-dark)
- [Night terrors](/night-terrors)
- [Bedtime routine for baby](/bedtime-routine-for-baby)
- [Crib to toddler bed](/crib-to-toddler-bed)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026.

1. Paruthi S, et al. "Recommended Amount of Sleep for Pediatric Populations: A Consensus Statement of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine." *Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine*, 2016. 10–13 hours for 3–5 years, including naps. AAP-endorsed.
2. Nemours KidsHealth. "Sleep and Your Preschooler." Date reviewed June 2020. About 10–13 hours; many no longer nap; those who do often sleep about an hour; quiet time if there is no nap; routine and screen limits. <https://kidshealth.org/en/parents/sleep-preschool.html>.
3. Cleveland Clinic. "How Much Sleep Kids Need: Recommended Hours by Age." 4 June 2024. 10–13 hours at 3–5 years, which may include a nap; early waking or hard bedtimes can mean the nap is ready to go. <https://health.clevelandclinic.org/recommended-amount-of-sleep-for-children>.

title: The 5 S's for Soothing a Crying Baby | Yorix
heading: The 5 S's for Soothing a Crying Baby (Product-Neutral)
description: The 5 S's — swaddle, side-stomach, shush, swing, suck — soothe a fussy baby. Side or stomach is for holding, not sleep, and no product is required.
body:
# The 5 S's for Soothing a Crying Baby (Product-Neutral)

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 16, 2026 · **Updated:** November 16, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

The "5 S's" are a popular soothing framework named by pediatrician Harvey Karp in *The Happiest Baby on the Block* and explained on the Happiest Baby site: **swaddle, side or stomach position, shush, swing, and suck**. This page is a **product-neutral** guide to that framework and, just as important, to the safety limits that official bodies already set. It is not a sleep-training method, not a [colic](/colic) treatment list, and not a review of any bassinet or noise machine.

We attribute the *name* and the five-item list to Karp / Happiest Baby. The safety rules — back for every sleep, hip-healthy swaddling, never shaking, no overnight sleep in a swing — come from the AAP, the International Hip Dysplasia Institute's swaddle guidance we already use on [how to swaddle a baby](/how-to-swaddle-a-baby), and related pages. Where Karp's commercial site promotes branded products, we leave those out.

## Short answer

The 5 S's are a way to comfort a **fussy, awake** baby, often in the first months. Used carefully, they borrow sensations many babies found familiar before birth: snug holding, rhythmic sound, gentle motion, and sucking. The one rule you cannot loosen is this: **side or stomach is for calming in your arms, never for sleep**. Karp's own explanation says you may hold a baby on the side or stomach, but it is not safe to place them that way to sleep; the back is the only safe sleep position. After the baby settles, put them down on their back in a clear crib or bassinet, the same way [safe sleep for babies](/safe-sleep-for-babies) describes.

Swaddling is the first S. It must leave the hips free to bend, and it must stop when rolling starts — including in any device. Gentle rocking is not shaking. A baby swing is not an overnight bed. Sucking can mean a feed or, once breastfeeding is going well if you are nursing, a [pacifier](/pacifier-and-sleep).

### The five S's at a glance

| The S | What it means here | The safety limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Swaddle | A snug wrap that can reduce startle and help some babies settle | Hips loose and flexed; stop as soon as rolling starts; not tight on the chest. See [how to swaddle a baby](/how-to-swaddle-a-baby) |
| Side or stomach | Hold the baby on the side, tummy, or over your shoulder while you soothe | **In arms only, while you are awake.** Then place on the back to sleep (Karp; AAP) |
| Shush | Steady, fairly strong white noise or a shushing voice | Keep volume reasonable; do not rest a speaker against the baby's ear (see official noise advice on our safe-sleep hub if you use sound) |
| Swing | Small, rhythmic motion — a rock, a walk, a gentle bounce — while you support the head | Never shake. Do not leave a baby to sleep in a swing or sitting device ([car-seat sleep](/baby-sleeping-in-car-seat)) |
| Suck | Feeding, or a pacifier | If breastfeeding, wait until nursing is well established before a dummy (AAP / our pacifier page; Karp agrees) |

## What the 5 S's are — and are not

Karp frames the first three months after birth as a "fourth trimester," and he describes a "calming reflex" that responding to womb-like rhythm can trigger. That framing is his, from his book and site. It is a popular way to think about newborn fussiness; it is **not a formal medical diagnosis** and not a claim we can independently verify from AAP or NHS pages. We mention it only so you know where the method's story comes from.

The 5 S's will not fix hunger, a dirty diaper, illness, or pain. They are a soothing sequence, not a reason to delay a feed or a call to the doctor. They also will not replace a [bedtime routine](/bedtime-routine-for-baby) later in the first year, and they are not a substitute for [gentle sleep training](/gentle-sleep-training) or any other method once a family is ready for that conversation.

Evening fuss that is not colic has its own page: [the witching hour](/witching-hour). If crying meets the clinical picture of colic, or you are worried something is medically wrong, use [colic](/colic) and call your pediatrician.

## How to use them without fighting safe sleep

There is no official AAP protocol that says "do the five S's in this exact order." Parents who use the framework often layer more than one S at a time — for example, a swaddled baby, held on their side in your arms, with a shush and a gentle rock. A practical, safety-first way to think about it:

1. Check the basics first: hunger, diaper, temperature, a burp, illness.
2. If you swaddle, follow hip-healthy wrapping and stop when signs of rolling appear. Our swaddle page owns the how-to and the stop-date.
3. Hold, don't place, on the side or stomach. The moment the baby is going down for a nap or the night, turn them onto their back in their own firm, flat space.
4. Use a steady shush or white noise if it helps. You do not need a branded track.
5. Rock or walk with the head and neck supported. If you feel angry or at the end of your rope, put the baby down on their back in the crib and step away for a few minutes. **Never shake a baby.**
6. Offer a feed if they are hungry, or a pacifier if that is already part of your plan.

If the baby falls asleep in your arms or in a sling, move them to the crib or bassinet on their back as soon as you can do so safely. Motion and holding are for settling, not for all-night sleep in a device.

## When the 5 S's are not the right tool

See a clinician if crying is sudden and severe, the baby has a fever (100.4°F or 38°C or higher in a baby 3 months or younger is an immediate call), is not feeding, is vomiting forcefully, is hard to wake, or has trouble breathing. Karp's site estimates that a small share of colicky crying has a medical cause such as a food intolerance, infection, or reflux; we will not treat that percentage as a diagnosis threshold. Trust your instincts and get help.

## Frequently asked questions

**Can I let my baby sleep on their side after the 5 S's settle them?**  
No. Side and stomach are for holding while you soothe. Sleep is on the back (Karp's own caution; AAP policy).

**Is this sleep training?**  
No. It is a soothing pattern for fussy periods, mainly in young infants. Sleep training, including [gentle methods](/gentle-sleep-training), is a later, separate decision. See [when to start sleep training](/when-to-start-sleep-training).

**Do I need a special bassinet or swaddle to do the 5 S's?**  
No. The framework is older than any one product. This article does not recommend a brand.

**What if my baby hates the swaddle?**  
Some do. You can still use holding, sound, motion, and sucking. See "What if my baby hates the swaddle?" on [how to swaddle a baby](/how-to-swaddle-a-baby).

## See which evenings are actually fussy (Yorix)

**Yorix** can show you when crying and sleep cluster in the day, which is useful when you are deciding whether this is an evening fuss window or something to take to the pediatrician. The app cannot soothe a baby and is not a medical device.

## Related reading

- [Responsive Settling: Help That Can Fade, Not a Second Methods Table](/responsive-settling)

- [How to swaddle a baby](/how-to-swaddle-a-baby)
- [Safe sleep for babies](/safe-sleep-for-babies)
- [Pacifier and sleep](/pacifier-and-sleep)
- [Colic](/colic)
- [The witching hour](/witching-hour)
- [Baby sleeping on the stomach](/baby-sleeping-on-stomach)
- [Baby sleeping in a car seat](/baby-sleeping-in-car-seat)
- [Gentle sleep training](/gentle-sleep-training)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026.

1. Karp H. "Using the 5 S's to Soothe a Crying Baby." Happiest Baby. Accessed 15 November 2026. Origin of the named framework: swaddle, side-stomach, shush, swing, suck; states that side or stomach is for holding, not for sleep. Cited as the source of the name and list only; we do not use product claims. <https://www.happiestbaby.com/blogs/baby/the-5-s-s-for-soothing-babies>.
2. Moon RY, Carlin RF, Hand I; AAP Task Force on Sudden Infant Death Syndrome and the Committee on Fetus and Newborn. "Sleep-Related Infant Deaths: Updated 2022 Recommendations." *Pediatrics*, 2022. Back to sleep; firm, flat surface; no sitting devices for sleep. <https://publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article/150/1/e2022057990/188304/Sleep-Related-Infant-Deaths-Updated-2022>.
3. HealthyChildren.org (AAP). "Swaddling: Is it Safe?" Hip-healthy wrap; stop when rolling starts. <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/baby/diapers-clothing/pages/Swaddling-Is-it-Safe.aspx>.
4. HealthyChildren.org (AAP). "Where We Stand: Back To Sleep." Last updated 9 September 2026. <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/baby/sleep/Pages/Where-We-Stand-Back-To-Sleep.aspx>.

title: Baby Crying in Their Sleep: When to Step In | Yorix
heading: Baby Crying in Their Sleep: When to Step In
description: Why babies cry out in their sleep during active (REM) sleep, how that differs from a true night waking or a night terror, and when you should step in.
body:
# Baby Crying in Their Sleep: When to Step In

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 16, 2026 · **Updated:** November 16, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

A whimper from the crib that fades in 30 seconds is not the same event as a baby who is up and hungry. **Crying out during sleep** is often part of [active sleep](/baby-sleep-cycles). This page is about that in-between moment. It is not [night wakings](/survive-night-wakings-new-parents), not [newborn grunting](/newborn-grunting-in-sleep), and not [night terrors](/night-terrors), which are a deep-sleep event usually seen in older toddlers and preschoolers.

## Short answer

Newborns and young infants spend a large share of sleep in **active (REM) sleep**. Sleep Foundation notes that this stage can include irregular breathing, twitches, mouthing, and brief sounds, and that babies often surface at the end of a roughly 50-minute cycle. A short cry, moan, or whimper that settles without a full wake-up is frequently the baby moving through that light stage — not a request you missed. A pause before you pick them up can tell you which it is (the same idea we use on the cycles page). If the cry builds, they sound fully awake, or a feed or comfort is clearly needed, respond. Very young babies may still need those night calories; see [should you wake a sleeping baby](/should-you-wake-a-sleeping-baby).

### Key numbers at a glance

| Question | What the sources say | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Why sleep can be noisy | Newborns spend about 50% of sleep in REM / active sleep, versus about 20% in adults | Sleep Foundation (sleep cycles) |
| Typical baby cycle length | About 50 minutes, versus about 90 in adults | Sleep Foundation, citing El-Shakankiry |
| Night terrors vs this | Night terrors: usually toddlers/preschoolers, early in the night, child is not truly awake and will not remember | HealthyChildren.org; NHS |

## What "crying in their sleep" often is

In active sleep, a baby may look restless, briefly open their eyes, or make a sound that would worry you if they were up. KidsHealth describes newborns as light, noisy sleepers with no day-night sense yet. That noisiness includes cries that do not always mean "I am awake."

At the end of a cycle they may fully wake. If falling back to sleep depends on feeding, rocking, or being held, they will need that help again — a [sleep association](/sleep-associations). That is a true waking, and it belongs with your usual night plan, not with "ignore every sound."

## When to step in — and when to wait a moment

A practical split, not an official AAP minute count (we are not inventing a "wait five minutes" rule):

**A short pause is reasonable when:**

- The sound is brief, and their body still looks asleep or only fidgety.
- The cry fades as quickly as it started.
- They have already been fed on the schedule your pediatrician wants.

**Go in when:**

- The cry grows and they sound fully awake.
- You are in the early weeks and a feed may be due.
- Something looks wrong: color change, hard work to breathe, a cry you have never heard, or they are unusually hard to settle. That is medical, not a sleep-cycle drill.
- Older toddlers who sit up screaming, glassy-eyed, and do not recognize you early in the night may be having a [night terror](/night-terrors) — a different playbook (do not try to wake them; keep them safe).

Always pick them up or move them if they have fallen asleep in an unsafe place: a sofa, a [car seat after you have arrived](/baby-sleeping-in-car-seat), or a swing.

## What does not help

- Turning every rustle into a full feed and play session, which can accidentally create a new night association.
- Leaving a newborn who may need calories because a saying told you never to interrupt sleep.
- Labeling ordinary active-sleep sounds as night terrors in a two-month-old.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Ask if crying in sleep is new and intense, comes with breathing pauses or color change, happens as much when they are awake, or you cannot tell whether they are in pain. Record a short video if you can do so safely.

## Frequently asked questions

**Why is my baby crying in their sleep but not waking up?**  
They may be in active sleep or at the light end of a cycle. Watch for a moment before you intervene.

**Should I wake a baby who is crying in their sleep?**  
Usually no, if they settle and look otherwise well. Wake or pick them up if a feed is due, they are truly up, or anything about their breathing or color worries you.

**Is this a night terror?**  
Usually not in a young infant. Night terrors are typically described in toddlers and preschoolers, early in the night, with no memory afterward.

**Could they be hungry?**  
Yes, especially in the first months. If the pause does not settle the cry and a feed is plausible, feed them.

## Log the time, not every sound (Yorix)

**Yorix** is useful for true wakings and feeds, not for every 20-second whimper. The app cannot tell active sleep from pain and is not a medical device.

## Related reading

- [Baby sleep cycles](/baby-sleep-cycles)
- [Baby twitching in sleep](/baby-twitching-in-sleep)
- [Newborn grunting in sleep](/newborn-grunting-in-sleep)
- [Night terrors](/night-terrors)
- [Survive night wakings](/survive-night-wakings-new-parents)
- [Sleep associations](/sleep-associations)
- [Should you wake a sleeping baby](/should-you-wake-a-sleeping-baby)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026.

1. Sleep Foundation. "Baby Sleep Cycles." Updated 27 August 2026. <https://www.sleepfoundation.org/baby-sleep/baby-sleep-cycle>. Active/REM features; ~50% REM in newborns; ~50-minute cycles; babies often surface between cycles.
2. Nemours KidsHealth. "Sleep and Your Newborn." <https://kidshealth.org/en/parents/sleepnewborn.html>. Newborns are light, noisy sleepers; no day-night sense yet.
3. HealthyChildren.org (AAP). "Nightmares, Night Terrors & Sleepwalking." Last updated 9/21/2023. <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/preschool/Pages/nightmares-and-night-terrors.aspx>. How night terrors differ (older children, early night, no memory).
4. NHS. "Night terrors and nightmares." <https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/night-terrors/>. Do not wake a child from a night terror; different from ordinary night crying.

title: Baby Sleep and Travel: Planes, Hotels, and Jet Lag | Yorix
heading: Baby Sleep and Travel: Planes, Hotels, and Jet Lag
description: How to protect baby sleep when you travel: hotel cribs and pack-and-plays, car-seat naps, jet lag (adjust 2–3 days before), and what not to drop on vacation.
body:
# Baby Sleep and Travel: Planes, Hotels, and Jet Lag

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 16, 2026 · **Updated:** November 16, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

Travel scrambles days, but it does not rewrite [safe sleep](/safe-sleep-for-babies). This page is about **sleep on the way and at the destination**: jet lag, hotels, and what to do when the only nap happens in a car seat. It is not a packing list for every country, and it is not a second [car-seat safety](/baby-sleeping-in-car-seat) essay — we will link that rule, not repeat the whole airway explanation.

## Short answer

Bring the same basics you use at home: a **firm, flat, clear** crib, bassinet, or play yard, baby on their **back**, in your room if they are still in the first months. HealthyChildren.org (Claire McCarthy, MD, FAAP) says not to relax those habits in a hotel: resist putting the baby in the adult bed; ask for a portable crib or pack-and-play when you book; check that it meets current standards and is in good repair. The AAP's family-travel tips (updated 5 February 2025) add: **to reduce jet lag, adjust the child's sleep schedule 2 to 3 days before departure**, and after you arrive, use **daylight and outdoor or brightly lit time** to help the clock shift. A car-seat nap is for the journey; move them to a flat sleep space as soon as you arrive (AAP, NHS, Lullaby Trust — see our car-seat page).

### Key numbers at a glance

| Question | What the sources say | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Jet lag, before you go | Adjust the child's sleep schedule 2–3 days before departure | HealthyChildren.org travel tips, 5 February 2025 |
| After arrival | Be active outside or in bright light during daylight hours | Same article |
| Driving breaks | Plan to stop about every two hours | Same article |
| Hotel sleep space | Portable crib or play yard; inspect it; do not default to the adult bed | HealthyChildren.org hotel safety, 18 June 2026 |
| Car-seat naps | Okay while travelling; out of the seat as soon as you arrive | AAP; NHS; Lullaby Trust |

We are not inventing a "one hour of shift per day" jet-lag formula. HealthyChildren.org's sourced instruction is the 2- to 3-day pre-adjustment plus daylight. For a one-hour change, our [daylight saving](/daylight-saving-baby-sleep) page (a few minutes a day for about a week) is the closer playbook.

## Hotels and rentals

McCarthy's hotel article is the practical checklist:

- Request a crib or play yard when you book. Inspect hardware, the mattress, and fit of the sheet. If it looks wrong, ask for a replacement or use your own travel play yard.
- Put the crib away from cords, lamps, TVs, and anything that could fall.
- Do a "safety crawl" on arrival for dropped pills, pens, and other small objects.
- Never leave a child alone in a hotel room, even with a monitor, including for a meal in the attached restaurant.
- Gate or block stairs if the layout has them; lock balcony doors; watch water (bathtub, toilet, pool).
- Anchor or make tip-able furniture and TVs harder to pull over, as you would at home after a [crib-to-bed](/crib-to-toddler-bed) move.

The same AAP travel-tips page warns that cribs or play yards provided when you travel internationally — and in the U.S. — may not meet current standards. If you have any doubt, ask for a replacement or choose another option.

A familiar [sleep sack](/sleep-sacks), a small [lovey if they are over 12 months](/when-can-baby-sleep-with-a-blanket), and the usual [bedtime routine](/bedtime-routine-for-baby) are the portable parts of home. A new apartment sofa is not a crib.

## Camping, and very hot or cold nights away from home

Safer sleep does not pause in a tent. Red Nose and the Lullaby Trust both treat sleep away from home as the same rules in a different building (or in no building): **on the back**, on a **firm, flat**, approved surface, with a clear space and no loose adult bedding. A pillow nest on an air mattress, a baby on a quilt between adults, or a car seat left at the edge of a tent is not a campsite exception.

Bring a travel crib, play yard, or other approved product that still fits the baby, and use only its own mattress. Keep the sleep space off a soggy groundsheet and away from heater vents and stove fumes. In hot weather, Red Nose’s summer advice and the Lullaby Trust’s hot-weather pages agree with [how to dress a baby for sleep](/how-to-dress-baby-for-sleep): light layers, no hat for sleep, shade, and a check of the chest — not an extra blanket “in case.” In the cold, add a layer or a well-fitting sleep bag; do not use a hot-water bottle, a heating pad, or a heavy duvet in the baby’s space, and do not bring the baby into an adult sleeping bag.

If the only option looks unsafe, it is better to change the plan than to improvise a nest. Temperature and dressing details stay on the dressing page; this section is the travel-and-camping frame.

## Planes, cars, and the "they've finally fallen asleep" problem

**Cars.** Use a correctly installed, rear-facing seat for as long as the seat allows (AAP). Stop about every two hours (HealthyChildren.org). Never leave a child alone in a car. If they sleep in the seat, that is a travel nap; when you get there, move them — the full argument is on [baby sleeping in a car seat](/baby-sleeping-in-car-seat).

**Planes.** The AAP recommends exploring ways for each child to have their own seat and to ride in an FAA-approved car safety seat, even though the FAA allows children under 2 on a lap. Booster seats cannot be used on aircraft but can usually be checked. For ear pain on descent, the same page suggests nursing or a bottle for infants, and chewing gum or a drink through a straw for older children. Talk to your pediatrician before flying with a newborn who has heart or lung problems, or within two weeks of an ear infection or ear surgery.

A stroller nap in the terminal is still a sitting-device nap. Move them to a flat, safe space when you reasonably can.

## Jet lag and time zones

Two to three days before a trip that crosses time zones, start sliding bedtime and wake time toward the destination clock (HealthyChildren.org). After you land, get daylight in the local day, and keep nights as boring and dark as you can — the same contrast idea as [day-night confusion](/newborn-day-night-confusion) and [DST](/daylight-saving-baby-sleep).

Do not skip needed feeds to "force" the new clock in a young baby. Safety and calories come first; the schedule can be messy for a few days.

If you are only changing the clock by one hour, a gentler nudge is enough. If several hours are involved, expect several off days, not a single heroic night.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Ask before long-haul travel with a preterm or recently discharged baby, before flying after an ear infection, or if you need vaccine or malaria-prevention advice for international trips (AAP travel tips). After you return, mention sleep that has not recovered after a couple of weeks, or any breathing concern that started on the trip.

## Frequently asked questions

**How do I handle jet lag with a baby?**  
Shift the schedule 2–3 days before you go, then use local daylight. Do not invent a steeper protocol than that unless your pediatrician gives you one.

**Is a hotel crib safe?**  
It can be, if it meets current standards and is in good repair. Inspect it. If it does not look right, ask for another or use your own play yard.

**Can they sleep in the bed with us "just on vacation"?**  
The AAP still does not recommend bed-sharing. Vacation tiredness is a reason to be more careful, not less. See [bed-sharing](/bed-sharing-and-co-sleeping).

**What if the only nap is in the car?**  
Use it for the drive, then move them when you arrive. Build a crib nap at the destination when you can.

## Keep the log, loosen the clock (Yorix)

**Yorix** can show how nights drifted across time zones, which is useful when you are resetting after a trip. The app cannot make a hotel crib safe and is not a medical device.
