title: Bed-Sharing vs Room-Sharing: What the Evidence Says | Yorix
heading: Bed-Sharing and Co-Sleeping: What the Evidence Says
description: Co-sleeping vs bed-sharing vs room-sharing: the AAP's 2022 advice, how UK guidance differs, higher-risk situations, and why sofas are especially dangerous.
body:
# Bed-Sharing and Co-Sleeping: What the Evidence Says

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 16, 2026 · **Updated:** November 16, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

"Co-sleeping" is a slippery word. Some people use it to mean **room-sharing** — the baby sleeps in your room, on a separate crib or bassinet. Others use it to mean **bed-sharing** — the baby sleeps on the same surface as an adult, or even on a sofa. Those two arrangements are not equally safe. This page is about that distinction, and about a real disagreement between U.S. and UK public-health advice. The full ABC checklist lives on our [safe sleep](/safe-sleep-for-babies) hub; we will not repeat it here.

## Short answer

The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) **recommends room-sharing and cannot recommend bed-sharing under any circumstances**, including with twins. Room-sharing for at least the first 6 months can lower SIDS risk by as much as 50%, according to HealthyChildren.org. Sofas and armchairs are in a worse category still: the AAP cites a risk of sleep-related death up to 67 times higher. The NHS and Lullaby Trust agree that a baby's own clear cot or Moses basket, in your room, is the safest place. They also publish a "when not to bed-share" list (alcohol, smoking, drugs that cause drowsiness, prematurity, or birth weight under 2.5 kg / 5.5 lb) and, for families who do share a bed, harm-reduction steps. That is not the same as the AAP's "we cannot recommend it." We show both rather than picking a quieter middle.

### Key numbers at a glance

| Question | What the sources say | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AAP position on bed-sharing | Avoid under any circumstances, including with twins | HealthyChildren.org (AAP 2022) |
| How long to room-share | At least the first 6 months | AAP 2022; NHS; Lullaby Trust |
| Room-sharing and SIDS | Can decrease risk by as much as 50% | HealthyChildren.org (AAP) |
| Sofa or armchair with a baby | Risk of sleep-related death up to 67 times higher | HealthyChildren.org (AAP) |
| Extra risk if someone is impaired | More than 10 times higher when bed-sharing with someone who is fatigued or has used alcohol, drugs, or sedating medicines | HealthyChildren.org (AAP) |
| Extra risk under 4 months | 5 to 10 times higher when bed-sharing | HealthyChildren.org (AAP) |
| How common is bed-sharing? | Sleep Foundation cites research that as many as 60% of U.S. infants under 1 bed-share at least sometimes | Sleep Foundation (updated 15 July 2025) |

## First, get the words straight

Sleep Foundation's co-sleeping article, medically reviewed in 2025, usefully splits the language:

- **Room-sharing:** the baby has their own approved crib, bassinet, or play yard in the same room.
- **Bed-sharing / surface-sharing:** the baby and a caregiver sleep on the same bed, couch, chair, or floor.
- **Rooming-in:** the hospital version of room-sharing in the first day or two after birth.

Lullaby Trust uses "co-sleeping" as an umbrella for bed, sofa, or chair sharing, and treats room-sharing as a separate, recommended practice. When a friend says they "co-sleep," it is worth asking which of these they mean.

## “Breastsleeping” and the “Safe Sleep Seven”

These are **popular parent-education names**, not official AAP, NHS, or Lullaby Trust protocols. **Breastsleeping** is a term some breastfeeding advocates use for sleeping in close contact while nursing. The **“Safe Sleep Seven”** is an unofficial checklist circulated in some parent communities (a list of conditions under which those authors consider bed-sharing lower risk).

We name them here because people search for them. We will not reprint the unofficial list as if it were a medical standard, and we will not average it with the AAP’s advice already in the next section (the AAP recommends room-sharing **without** bed-sharing). UK advice that overlaps — and the places it does not — stays in the UK section already on this page. If a book or a forum says the “seven” make bed-sharing official policy, that is not accurate. Use this page’s sourced comparison, not a third checklist.

## Why the AAP draws a hard line

The 2022 AAP policy, in parent language on HealthyChildren.org, is unambiguous: based on the evidence, the AAP recommends that parents **avoid bed-sharing**, and it is "unable to recommend bed-sharing under any circumstances." The reasons are suffocation, entrapment, overlay, and a higher rate of sudden unexpected infant death. Pillows, duvets, a soft mattress, and an adult who does not reliably wake all add risk that a bare crib does not.

The policy is not a moral judgment about closeness or breastfeeding. The AAP wants the baby nearby — in your room — because that makes feeds and checks easier and is associated with lower SIDS risk. If you bring the baby into the bed to feed or comfort them, the advice is to put them back in their own space before you go to sleep. If there is any chance you might doze off, first remove pillows and loose bedding, then move the baby back as soon as you wake. That is damage control, not a recommended sleep plan.

The AAP also flags situations in which bed-sharing is especially hazardous (figures from HealthyChildren.org):

- alcohol, marijuana, medicines, or drugs that make it harder to wake (more than 10 times higher)
- a parent who smokes or vapes, or who smoked in pregnancy
- a baby younger than 4 months (5 to 10 times higher), or a baby who was preterm or low birth weight (2 to 5 times higher)
- anyone other than a parent in the bed, including other children
- a sofa, armchair, waterbed, or other soft surface

## Where UK advice overlaps — and where it does not

NHS and Lullaby Trust start in the same place: the **safest** spot is the baby's own firm, flat, clear cot or Moses basket, in your room, for at least 6 months. They are just as firm as the AAP about **sofas and armchairs**: never fall asleep there with a baby. They also tell you **not** to share a bed if the baby was premature or under 2.5 kg (5.5 lb) at birth, or if anyone in the bed smokes, has drunk alcohol, or has taken medicine or drugs that cause drowsiness.

The difference is tone after that list. The AAP stops at "we cannot recommend bed-sharing." Lullaby Trust, acknowledging that many families share a bed on purpose or by accident, then lists ways to make an adult bed less hazardous if it happens: keep pillows and adult duvets away from the baby, no slatted or decorative headboards that can trap a head, no other children or pets in the bed, no gap between mattress and wall, never leave a baby alone on an adult bed, place the baby on their back, and consider a well-fitting sleep bag as the baby's own layer. They do not recommend pods or nests on the adult mattress.

We are not going to turn those harm-reduction points into a Yorix "how to bed-share safely" guide, because the AAP does not consider any routine bed-sharing arrangement recommendable. If your family does share a bed, read Lullaby Trust's page in full, talk honestly with your pediatrician, and at the very least stay off sofas and out of the high-risk situations above.

Sleep Foundation notes that some countries where bed-sharing is common also have low SIDS rates, but it is not clear whether bed-sharing itself is protective there or whether other factors (more breastfeeding, less smoking, better access to care, firmer, clearer sleep surfaces) explain the difference. That uncertainty is another reason not to treat another country's rate as a green light.

## Room-sharing is the recommended middle

A crib or bassinet next to the adult bed gives you the access that many families want from bed-sharing, without the shared-surface risk. The AAP, NHS, and Lullaby Trust all ask for this for **at least the first 6 months**. Older AAP wording said "ideally the first year"; the 2022 policy uses the six-month minimum. When you are ready to discuss a later move, see [when to move baby to their own room](/when-to-move-baby-to-own-room).

Accidental bed-sharing still happens, especially during night feeds. Planning the baby's own surface within arm's reach makes it easier to put them back. If you think you might fall asleep while feeding, do not do that feed on a sofa.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Tell your baby's doctor what actually happens at night, even if you worry about being judged. Sleep Foundation makes the same point: pediatricians know that many families bed-share at least sometimes, and they can talk about your baby's age, birth history, and smoking or medication in the home. Call urgently if a baby has been in an unsafe sleep situation and you are worried about their breathing.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is co-sleeping the same as bed-sharing?**  
Not always. Ask which arrangement someone means. Room-sharing is recommended; bed-sharing is not, on AAP advice.

**Is bed-sharing safer if I am breastfeeding?**  
Breast milk is associated with a lower SIDS risk, but the AAP still does not recommend bed-sharing as the way to get that benefit. Bring the baby into the bed to feed if you want, then return them to their own space.

**What if I already bed-share?**  
Know the high-risk situations (alcohol, smoke, drowsiness, prematurity, low birth weight, sofas) and have an honest conversation with your pediatrician. The safest change is a crib or bassinet in your room.

**Can twins share our bed?**  
The AAP says no, including with twins. Lullaby Trust advises against bed-sharing with more than one baby at a time because of a greater risk of accidents. See [twins and sleep](/twins-and-sleep).

**Are in-bed sleepers or "sidecar" cribs a loophole?**  
The AAP has said it cannot recommend for or against some bedside or in-bed products until more research is done. If you use a product, it still needs to meet current safety standards and must not become a soft, inclined, or cluttered nest. When in doubt, a standalone, approved bassinet or crib is the clearer choice.

**Can I let my newborn sleep on my chest?**
A hold while you are awake and watching is comfort, not a sleep space. If you fall asleep with a baby on your chest on a sofa or armchair, the risk is higher than in a clear crib. Put them on their back, in their own firm, flat space, when you need to sleep. This page already explains room-sharing without bed-sharing (AAP) and the UK overlap.

## Log nights without turning them into a verdict (Yorix)

**Yorix** can record night feeds and wakings, which is useful when you are discussing sleep with your pediatrician. It cannot tell you that a shared bed is safe, and it is not a medical device. Safe sleep still depends on the surface and the habits, not on an app.

## Related reading

- [Safe sleep for babies](/safe-sleep-for-babies)

Moon, MD, FAAP. <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/baby/sleep/Pages/A-Parents-Guide-to-Safe-Sleep.aspx>. No bed-sharing under any circumstances, including twins; room-share at least 6 months; 50% and 67-times figures; risk multipliers.
2. Moon RY, et al. "Sleep-Related Infant Deaths: Updated 2022 Recommendations." *Pediatrics*, 2022;150(1):e2022057990. <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35726558/>.
3. Sleep Foundation. "Co-Sleeping." Updated 15 July 2025. Medically reviewed by Nilong Vyas, MD, MPH. <https://www.sleepfoundation.org/baby-sleep/co-sleeping>. Definitions; ~60% figure; room-sharing benefits; higher-risk situations; cultural context.
4. NHS. "Sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS)." <https://www.nhs.uk/baby/caring-for-a-newborn/sudden-infant-death-syndrome-sids/>. Own cot in the same room for at least 6 months; do not bed-share if preterm, <2.5 kg, smoking, alcohol, or sedating drugs; never a sofa.
5. The Lullaby Trust. "Co-sleeping with your baby." Last reviewed 1 February 2025; updated 3 August 2026. <https://www.lullabytrust.org.uk/safer-sleep-advice/co-sleeping/>. Safest place is a separate space; when not to co-sleep; harm-reduction if a bed is shared; no sofa; no pods or nests; not more than one baby in the adult bed.
6. NHS. "Helping your baby to sleep." <https://www.nhs.uk/baby/caring-for-a-newborn/helping-your-baby-to-sleep/>. Same-room sleep for at least 6 months.
7. Nemours KidsHealth. "Sleep and Your Newborn." Medically reviewed by Elana Pearl Ben-Joseph, MD. <https://kidshealth.org/en/parents/sleepnewborn.html>. Room-share without bed-share.

description: A baby bedtime routine that actually helps: what to include, how long it should last, what the research shows, and a simple plan from the newborn weeks onward.
body:
# Bedtime Routine for Baby: A Simple, Evidence-Backed Wind-Down

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 16, 2026 · **Updated:** November 16, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

A **bedtime routine for baby** is a short, predictable sequence you repeat before sleep: the same few steps, in the same order, most nights. It is one of the least flashy ideas in infant sleep, and one of the better studied. You do not need a perfect nursery or a 10-step ritual. You need something you can actually do when you are tired.

## Short answer

Start a simple routine as early as you like — NHS and Sleep Foundation both encourage one from the early months — and keep it to about **20 to 30 minutes**, or a little longer if a bath is included. A common pattern is feed, wash or change, pajamas, dim light, a book or lullaby, then into the crib. Research led by Jodi Mindell has found that a consistent nightly routine can help young children fall asleep faster, sleep longer, and wake less, with improvements sometimes seen in only a few nights, and that doing it more consistently is associated with better sleep. The AAP later promotes **Brush, Book, Bed** once teeth and books are part of the evening. Put your baby down **drowsy but awake** once you are past the early newborn weeks, so they get practice falling asleep in their own sleep space.

### Key numbers at a glance

| Question | What the sources say | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| How soon can a routine help? | One study found improvements after only a few nights of a consistent routine | Mindell et al., 2017, summarized by Sleep Foundation |
| How long should it last? | Around half an hour for most children, a little longer if there is a bath | Sleep Foundation |
| How common are toddler/baby sleep struggles? | As many as 20–30% of babies and toddlers have trouble sleeping | Sleep Foundation, citing research |
| Screens before bed | AAP: keep screens out of bedrooms; turn them off at least 60 minutes before bedtime | HealthyChildren.org |
| "Brush, Book, Bed" | AAP structure for evenings once toothbrushing is in play | HealthyChildren.org / AAP |

## What a bedtime routine is — and why it works

Sleep Foundation describes a routine as a consistent, repetitive set of activities carried out before bed every night. The repetition itself is the point. It gives the baby a cue that sleep is next, gives you a script when you are exhausted, and, in older babies, builds self-care and a sense of security.

Mindell and Williamson (2018), in *Sleep Medicine Reviews*, reviewed the wider benefits: better sleep, better parent–child connection, and skills that matter later, such as attention. An earlier trial (Mindell, Telofski, Wiegand, and Kurtz, 2009) found that a nightly routine improved infant and toddler sleep and maternal mood. A 2015 paper (Mindell, Li, Sadeh, Kwon, and Goh) found a **dose-dependent** pattern: more consistent use of a routine was associated with better sleep. That is a useful, unromantic finding. A routine you actually do five nights a week will beat a beautiful routine you only attempt on weekends.

## A simple routine you can scale by age

NHS suggests a bath, a change into night clothes and a fresh nappy, putting the baby down, a story, dim lights, a kiss, and a lullaby or a wind-up mobile. Sleep Foundation's list for children is similar: a feed or snack, a bath or diaper change, teeth and toilet (when relevant), a book, a song, a cuddle, a short chat about the day, then lights out.

You can grow into that, rather than start with all of it.

**Newborns.** Keep it short and quiet. A feed, a change, a dim room, and a few minutes of holding or a soft song is enough. NHS's day/night contrast matters more than a clock: ordinary light and noise by day, low light and little talking at night. Do not worry if bedtime moves around in the first weeks; see [newborn sleep schedule](/newborn-sleep-schedule).

**About 3 to 6 months.** Many families pick a slightly more stable "start of night." HealthyChildren.org suggests, from around 4 months, putting babies down drowsy rather than already asleep, so they can learn to fall asleep in their own crib. A bath does not have to happen every night to "count." If a bath is overstimulating, wash the face and hands and save the tub for earlier in the day. Do baths help every baby sleep? TCB and others discuss that; the honest answer is "sometimes," and it is not required.

**Older babies and toddlers.** Add toothbrushing when teeth are present. The AAP's Brush, Book, Bed is a tidy way to end the evening: brush, read, then bed, with no snacks or bottles after brushing. Sleep Foundation notes that a stuffed animal or comfort blanket can help some toddlers with separation — but only when it is age-safe; loose objects stay out of the crib in the first year. See [safe sleep](/safe-sleep-for-babies) and [sleep sacks](/sleep-sacks).

A worked example, not a rule:

1. Close the kitchen, dim the main lights (5 minutes).
2. Bath or a simple wash, then pajamas (10 minutes).
3. Feed if a bedtime feed is still part of your plan (10–15 minutes). Try to finish the feed before the baby is deeply asleep if you are working on falling asleep in the crib.
4. Book or song in a dim room (5–10 minutes).
5. Into the crib, kiss, leave.

If this regularly lasts an hour, shorten it. Sleep Foundation warns that a drawn-out routine delays bedtime and is hard to keep up on a busy night — and an [overtired baby](/overtired-baby) is harder to settle, so starting before the yawns turn into a second wind matters.

## Dos and don'ts that actually have a basis

**Do** repeat the same order most nights, and share the routine between caregivers when you can, so it does not belong to only one parent. **Do** keep the bedroom dark, cool enough for your climate, and fairly quiet; a dim night light is fine if you need it for feeds. **Do** shift bedtime in small steps (Sleep Foundation suggests about 15 minutes) if you need to move it.

**Don't** start when your baby is already past the point of no return. **Don't** park a baby in front of a phone or TV to "wind down"; the AAP wants screens off at least an hour before bed and out of the bedroom. **Don't** let the last step be a bottle left in the crib. **Don't** use the routine as a time for rough play or a scary story. **Don't** treat weekend late nights as a full reset; Sleep Foundation cautions against shifting wake time by more than about an hour when you can help it, at least for older children. For babies, a slightly later weekend morning is common, but a wildly different schedule makes Monday harder.

## A routine is not a whole sleep plan

It will not, by itself, fix [hourly waking](/baby-waking-every-hour), [false starts](/false-starts), or a bedtime that is two hours too late. It works with [age-appropriate totals](/how-much-sleep-does-a-baby-need), a safe crib, and, if you choose, a settling method you have already read about. It is also not a failure if you skip the bath when you get home late. Do the last two or three steps and start again tomorrow.

A popular daytime slogan, **eat–play–sleep** (or feed–play–sleep), is the same idea in a different order of the day: a flexible, cue-led pattern, not a rigid law, and not a newborn schedule. The longer caveat lives on [newborn sleep schedule](/newborn-sleep-schedule).

## When to talk to your pediatrician

If bedtime is a nightly battle despite a consistent, short routine, or if your baby seems in pain, has noisy breathing, or cannot settle in a way that feels new and extreme, ask for help. A routine is a habit, not a treatment for illness or a medical sleep disorder.

## Frequently asked questions

**When should I start a bedtime routine?**  
As early as you want a cue for "this is night." Even a two-step newborn version counts. It becomes more useful as sleep starts to organize in the first months.

**How long should a baby bedtime routine be?**  
About 20–30 minutes is a realistic target; a bit longer with a bath. If it regularly runs past 45–60 minutes, it is probably delaying sleep.

**What if my partner and I do it differently?**  
The same order matters more than the same singing voice. Agree on the steps and on who does what, then let each adult use their own style.

**Does a routine have to include a bath?**  
No. NHS includes a bath as an option, not a requirement.

**Can I use the same routine when we travel?**  
Yes, and that is one of its strengths. A book and the same song still work in a pack-and-play. Keep the [safe sleep](/safe-sleep-for-babies) rules wherever you are.

**What is a good bedtime for a 12 week old?**
There is no official AAP clock. The week-12 snapshot is on [12 week old baby sleep](/12-week-old-baby-sleep). A short, same-order routine matters more than a 7:00 p.m. target.

## Keep the timing honest (Yorix)

**Yorix** can show you when the last nap ended and when night sleep actually started, which makes it obvious if the "routine" is starting so late that your baby is already overtired. You can also log the night itself to see whether a slightly earlier start helped. It is a support for tired parents, not a medical device and not a diagnosis.

## Related reading

- [4 Year Old Sleep Schedule: The Preschool Day, With or Without a Nap](/4-year-old-sleep-schedule)
- [Cluster Feeding: Not Reverse Cycling, Not a Witching-Hour Diagnosis](/cluster-feeding)
- [Melatonin and Children's Sleep: Not a Do-It-Yourself Sleeping Pill](/melatonin-and-childrens-sleep)
- [Responsive Settling: Help That Can Fade, Not a Second Methods Table](/responsive-settling)
- [Sleep After Separation or Divorce: Two Homes, One Predictable Night](/sleep-after-separation-or-divorce)

- [Baby Sleep Cues: How to Read Sleepy Signs](/baby-sleep-cues)
- [Crib to Toddler Bed: When and How to Switch](/crib-to-toddler-bed)
- [Daylight Saving Time and Baby Sleep: Spring and Fall](/daylight-saving-baby-sleep)
- [Fear of the Dark and Other Nighttime Fears](/fear-of-the-dark)
- [Night Terrors vs Nightmares: How to Tell Them Apart](/night-terrors)
- [Nursing to Sleep: When It Is Normal, and What to Change Later](/nursing-to-sleep)
- [Sleep Associations: What They Are and How to Change Them](/sleep-associations)
- [Toddler Bedtime Battles: Stalling, Not a Regression](/toddler-bedtime-battles)
- [Toddler Won't Stay in Bed: After Lights Out](/toddler-wont-stay-in-bed)

- [Overtired baby](/overtired-baby)
- [How much sleep does a baby need](/how-much-sleep-does-a-baby-need)
- [When do babies sleep through the night](/when-do-babies-sleep-through-the-night)
- [Wake windows by age](/wake-windows-by-age)
- [Safe sleep for babies](/safe-sleep-for-babies)
- [Newborn sleep schedule](/newborn-sleep-schedule)
- [When to start sleep training](/when-to-start-sleep-training)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026.

1. Sleep Foundation. "Bedtime Routines for Children." Updated 23 July 2025. Medically reviewed by Ealena Callender, MD, MPH, FACOG. <https://www.sleepfoundation.org/children-and-sleep/bedtime-routine>. Benefits, 20–30% figure, 30-minute length, Mindell citations, dos and don'ts, screens, 15-minute shifts.
2. Mindell JA, Telofski LS, Wiegand B, Kurtz ES. "A nightly bedtime routine: impact on sleep in young children and maternal mood." *Sleep*, 2009;32(5):599–606. <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19480226/>.
3. Mindell JA, Leichman ES, Lee C, Williamson AA, Walters RM. "Implementation of a nightly bedtime routine: How quickly do things improve?" *Infant Behavior & Development*, 2017;49:220–227. <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28985580/>.
4. Mindell JA, Li AM, Sadeh A, Kwon R, Goh DY. "Bedtime routines for young children: a dose-dependent association with sleep outcomes." *Sleep*, 2015;38(5):717–722. <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25325483/>.
5. Mindell JA, Williamson AA. "Benefits of a bedtime routine in young children: Sleep, development, and beyond." *Sleep Medicine Reviews*, 2018;40:93–108. <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29195725/>.
6. NHS. "Helping your baby to sleep." <https://www.nhs.uk/baby/caring-for-a-newborn/helping-your-baby-to-sleep/>. Example routine; day/night contrast.
7. HealthyChildren.org (AAP). "Getting Your Baby to Sleep." Last updated 4 June 2024. <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/baby/sleep/Pages/getting-your-baby-to-sleep.aspx>. Drowsy but awake from about 4 months; calm nights.
8. HealthyChildren.org (AAP). "Healthy Sleep Habits: How Many Hours Does Your Child Need?" <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/healthy-living/sleep/Pages/healthy-sleep-habits-how-many-hours-does-your-child-need.aspx>. Screens off at least 60 minutes before bed; Brush, Book, Bed mention; regular daily routine.
9. HealthyChildren.org (AAP). "Brush, Book, Bed." <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/healthy-living/oral-health/Pages/Brush-Book-Bed.aspx>.
10. American Academy of Sleep Medicine. "Study shows institution of a consistent nightly bedtime routine improves sleep in infants and toddlers as well as maternal mood." <https://aasm.org/study-shows-institution-of-a-consistent-nightly-bedtime-routine-improves-sleep-in-infants-and-toddlers-as-well-as-maternal-mood/>. (Press summary of Mindell 2009.)

body:
# Crib to Toddler Bed: When and How to Switch

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 16, 2026 · **Updated:** November 16, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

A crib that still works is not a late milestone. The move to a toddler bed or a low "big-kid" bed is a **safety and readiness** decision, not a birthday present. This page is the process guide. The [2-year sleep regression](/sleep-regression/2-years) mentions the switch in passing when sleep is already bumpy; it is not the how-to.

## Short answer

There is **no official age** when every child must leave the crib. Cleveland Clinic, quoting pediatrician Laura O'Connor, MD, says most toddlers switch between **18 months and 3 years**, and that there is no harm in staying in a safe crib. The same article, attributing the line to the American Academy of Pediatrics, says a toddler has outgrown the crib if they are **taller than 35 inches (89 cm)**, or if the rail is at mid-chest (nipple line) when they stand, or if they are **climbing out** even with the mattress at its lowest setting. Climbing out is the clearest "move now" signal, because a fall from a crib rail is a longer drop than a roll from a low bed. The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission defines a toddler bed as a crib-mattress-sized bed for a child **not younger than 15 months** and weighing **no more than 50 lb (22.7 kg)**. If the crib is still safe, many families wait — and that is reasonable.

### Key numbers at a glance

| Question | What the sources say | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Typical window | Most toddlers switch between 18 months and 3 years; no magic age | Cleveland Clinic (1 October 2025) |
| Outgrown the crib (AAP, as cited by Cleveland Clinic) | Taller than 35 inches, or the rail is at nipple line when standing, or they climb out | Cleveland Clinic; AAP |
| Toddler-bed product limits | Intended for a child at least 15 months old and no more than 50 lb (22.7 kg) | CPSC |
| Floor mattress as a stopgap | HealthyChildren.org (Rachel Moon, MD, FAAP): while you wait for a bed, place the crib mattress on the floor | HealthyChildren.org, updated 1 August 2022 |

## When to wait, and when not to

Cleveland Clinic's advice is to weigh which arrangement is **safer tonight**. A bed is easy to get out of. A crib that a climber can tip over or fall from is no longer the safer option.

**Reasons to wait**, if the crib is still safe:

- They are content in it and are not climbing out.
- Sleep is already hard (illness, a [2-year sleep bump](/sleep-regression/2-years), a new sibling, [potty training or a move](/baby-sleep-and-travel)). Cleveland Clinic suggests one big change at a time when you can.
- They still need high sides to stay put, and they have not shown they can follow a "stay in bed" rule.

**Reasons to move now:**

- Repeated climbing, even with the mattress down and (if you use one) a [sleep sack](/sleep-sacks) that has not stopped it.
- They have reached the height or rail-line limits above.
- The crib is damaged, recalled, or missing parts.

Do not move a 15-month-old only because a toddler bed's box says that age is allowed. That is a product minimum, not a developmental green light. Do not move them only because a younger baby needs the crib, if a pack-and-play or a second safe crib would do for the infant instead.

## How to make the switch

HealthyChildren.org's "Big Kid Beds" article, by Rachel Y. Moon, MD, FAAP (updated 1 August 2022), and Cleveland Clinic describe the same unglamorous method:

1. **Talk about it first.** Cleveland Clinic suggests explaining that a bed is a "big-kid" step and that the rule is to stay in it after you leave.
2. **Childproof again, at their height.** Cords, unanchored dressers and TVs, unguarded stairs, unlocked windows, bathrooms, and anything climbable. A gate at the top of the stairs is essential; some families also gate the bedroom door. Moon also recommends childproof latches or taped-shut lower drawers so they cannot be used as steps, and keeping large toys that could injure a falling child out of the way.
3. **Keep the [bedtime routine](/bedtime-routine-for-baby) identical.** The furniture changes; the order of the evening should not.
4. **Start with naps if you can**, so the first experiments happen while you are awake (Cleveland Clinic).
5. **Put them down drowsy, then walk them back.** Moon's steps: tell them to stay in bed until you come; if they get up, calmly and quietly lead them back; praise them briefly for being in the bed, then leave. She warns that "twenty farewell appearances in one evening is by no means an unusual number." Keep the return boring. Extra attention — even annoyed attention — can reward the exit.
6. **Do not make the adult bed the prize.** Both sources say to avoid rewarding breakouts with a family-room party or a regular place in your bed. Comfort them, then return them.
7. **Use a comfort item that is now allowed.** After 12 months, a small [blanket or lovey](/when-can-baby-sleep-with-a-blanket) can be reasonable. A pillow is still a soft object; wait until they are in a bed and your pediatrician is comfortable with it.

A convertible crib that drops a side into a daybed is one way to keep the same mattress. A floor mattress is a safe temporary option while you set up the room (Moon). We are not ranking brands.

## Bunk beds, bed rails, and why not to use a crib tent

This page is the furniture move out of a crib. What the child sleeps in *next* still has limits.

**Bunk beds.** HealthyChildren.org (last updated 5 September 2013): children love them, and they can be dangerous (a fall from the top, or the upper bunk collapsing onto the lower). If you use one anyway, **do not allow a child younger than 6 years to sleep on the top bunk** — they do not yet have the coordination to climb safely or to stay from falling. Other precautions on that page: place the bunk in a corner so two sides are walled; the top mattress must fit snugly and cannot ride over the edge; attach a ladder and use a night-light so the child can see it; install a top-bunk guardrail with a gap **no wider than 3½ inches**, and check the child cannot roll under it when the mattress compresses; mattress supports should be fastened slats or wires, not a loose frame; no jumping or roughhousing on either bunk. If you separate the bunks into twins, remove leftover connectors.

**Bed rails.** Use only a rail made for that bed, installed as the maker says, if a clinician or the bed’s age-and-design instructions call for one. Do not improvise with pillows or a gap that can trap a head or chest. This is not a shopping review; if the child is still in a crib, rails on an adult bed are the wrong product.

**Crib tents and “safety” nets over a crib.** Do not use them. They are not a recommended way to keep a climber in. Mesh or fabric over a crib can loosen, trap, or become a climbing-and-fall hazard, and they fight the bare-crib rule already on [safe sleep](/safe-sleep-for-babies). If a child is climbing out, that is a reason to plan the toddler-bed move on this page, not to zip the crib shut. HealthyChildren.org’s lists of sleep products to avoid include add-ons that make a crib less bare or less safe; a tent is in that family, not in the “helpful accessory” family.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Ask if you are unsure whether a climb or a height measurement means the crib is unsafe, if the child has unusual muscle tone or a medical reason they cannot use a low bed yet, or if weeks of walking-back have not settled and you want a plan that fits their development.

## Frequently asked questions

**When should I transition my toddler from a crib to a bed?**  
When the crib is no longer safe (climbing, 35 inches, or rail at mid-chest), or when they are clearly ready and you have childproofed. Many families wait toward the later end of the 18-month-to-3-year window.

**Is 18 months too early?**  
It can be, if they are not climbing and the crib still fits. It can be necessary if they are already getting out. Follow safety first, not the calendar.

**Should I use a toddler bed or a twin bed?**  
Either can work if it is low, stable, and used within its limits. CPSC's toddler-bed definition assumes a full-size crib mattress and a child 15 months to 50 lb. Guardrails, if you use them, should not create a gap a child can slide into.

**What if they keep getting up?**  
Walk them back the same way each time, stay calm, and keep the room safe. This is normal in the first nights. See also [sleep associations](/sleep-associations).

**Can I wait until after a vacation or a new baby?**  
If the crib is still safe, yes. Cleveland Clinic prefers not to stack big changes. If they are climbing, safety wins.

**Can a toddler sleep with a pillow, or on a mattress on the floor?**
Pillows stay out of infant cribs. For a toddler in a bed, follow the dentist- and pediatrician-advised, age-appropriate bedding already discussed with your clinician, and keep the space clear of hanging cords and top-heavy furniture. A mattress on the floor is a household setup, not an AAP "floor bed" protocol; if you use one, it still needs a clear, smoke-free, safe room (no adult pillows piled as bumpers). This is not a product review.

## Log the move, then give it a week (Yorix)

**Yorix** can show whether nights changed after the date you switched beds. The app cannot tell you that a crib is still safe, and it is not a medical device. Recheck the rail and the room.

## Related reading

- [Fear of the Dark and Other Nighttime Fears](/fear-of-the-dark)
- [Toddler Bedtime Battles: Stalling, Not a Regression](/toddler-bedtime-battles)
- [Toddler Won't Stay in Bed: After Lights Out](/toddler-wont-stay-in-bed)

- [2 year old sleep schedule](/2-year-old-sleep-schedule)
- [2 year sleep regression](/sleep-regression/2-years)
- [When to move baby from bassinet to crib](/when-to-move-baby-to-crib)
- [When can a baby sleep with a blanket](/when-can-baby-sleep-with-a-blanket)
- [Bedtime routine for baby](/bedtime-routine-for-baby)
- [18 month old sleep schedule](/18-month-old-sleep-schedule)
- [Safe sleep for babies](/safe-sleep-for-babies)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026.

1. Cleveland Clinic. "When and How To Transition to a Toddler Bed." Reviewed by Laura O'Connor, MD. 1 October 2025. <https://health.clevelandclinic.org/from-crib-to-toddler-bed>. 18 months to 3 years; no magic age; AAP 35-inch and nipple-line limits; climbing; wait if the crib is still safe; room-proofing; start with naps; walk them back.
2. HealthyChildren.org (AAP). "Big Kid Beds: When to Switch From a Crib." By Rachel Y. Moon, MD, FAAP. Last updated 8/1/2022. <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/healthy-living/sleep/Pages/Big-Kid-Beds-When-To-Make-the-Switch.aspx>. Same routine; calm returns; floor mattress as a stopgap; gates; furniture tip-over and drawer-as-step hazards.
3. U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission. "Toddler Beds" (FAQ). <https://www.cpsc.gov/FAQ/Toddler-Beds>. Product intended for a child not less than 15 months of age and weighing no more than 50 lb (22.7 kg); crib-mattress dimensions.
4. Cleveland Clinic. "When To Lower Your Baby's Crib Mattress." <https://health.clevelandclinic.org/when-to-lower-crib-mattress>. Most toddlers in a crib until at least 18 months; move if they climb or outgrow the crib.


5. [HealthyChildren.org (AAP). “Bunk Beds: Safety Information for Parents.” Last updated 5 September 2013. No top bunk under age 6; corner placement; snug mattress; attached ladder; guardrail gap no more than 3½ inches; secured slats; no roughhousing.](https://www.healthychildren.org/English/healthy-living/sleep/Pages/Bunk-Beds-Safety-Information-for-Parents.aspx)

6. [HealthyChildren.org (AAP). “Inclined Sleepers and Other Baby Registry Items to Avoid.” Use as the companion “do not add unsafe sleep products / keep the crib bare” source when discussing crib tents.](https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/baby/sleep/Pages/Inclined-Sleepers-and-Other-Baby-Registry-Items-to-Avoid.aspx)

title: Daycare and Baby Sleep: Two Rooms, One Baby | Yorix
heading: Daycare and Baby Sleep: A Context Page, Not a New Regression
description: Daycare and baby sleep: two environments, safe sleep in child care, and how to adjust nights at home — not a new 'regression age' article.
body:
# Daycare and Baby Sleep: A Context Page, Not a New Regression

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 16, 2026 · **Updated:** November 16, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

Starting childcare, or moving rooms at a familiar center, often changes naps and then nights. This is a **context page**: two sleep environments, what to ask the carers, and how to adjust at home. It is not a new "daycare sleep regression" age article, and it does not invent a new official sleep number. Totals still come from [how much sleep a baby needs](/how-much-sleep-does-a-baby-need). If the only issue is a nap that will not start, or a nap that ends after one cycle, use [baby won't nap](/baby-wont-nap) and [short naps](/short-naps).

## Short answer

Childcare is a different room, a different schedule, and usually more than one baby. Many families see shorter or later naps at first, then a bumpier bedtime or earlier morning at home. That is an adjustment, not a diagnosis. The useful work is practical: share your baby's current rhythm, ask how naps are actually going, and protect the night if the day ran short — often with a slightly earlier bedtime, the same idea we use on nap-transition pages.

Safe sleep does not loosen at daycare. U.S. *Caring for Our Children* (CFOC) basics, which follow the AAP's 2022 recommendations, say programs should have written safe-sleep policies, that staff who care for infants should be trained before they start, and that infants should be placed **on the back**, on a **firm, flat, non-inclined** surface, with a tight fitted sheet and a clear crib. You can — and should — ask how that is carried out at the setting you are using. The full home list stays on [safe sleep for babies](/safe-sleep-for-babies).

If your baby is still on a number of naps the classroom does not offer, you may be looking at an earlier [3-to-2](/3-to-2-nap-transition) or [2-to-1](/2-to-1-nap-transition) than you had planned, or at a gap you fill at home. There is no official AAP week that says "drop a nap because of daycare."

### What to ask, and what to adjust at home

| At the setting | At home |
| --- | --- |
| Written safe-sleep policy, back for every infant sleep, firm flat crib or cot, no loose bedding | Keep the same rules; do not "catch up" with a sofa or a seat |
| When the group naps, how long, and whether they will try a second nap if your baby still takes two | If only one nap happened and the afternoon is long, move bedtime earlier rather than hoping a late night will fix it |
| Whether they will follow a slightly earlier or later put-down for *your* baby, or must follow a room schedule | Weekends: keep a similar morning when you can, so Monday is not a new timezone |
| How they will tell you about a short nap, a refused nap, or a late wake | If daycare naps are solid but home naps fail, use the same wind-down you use at night, not a more exciting living room |

If breastfeeding is also shifting, with long days away and heavier nights, see [reverse cycling](/reverse-cycling) before you start [night weaning](/night-weaning).

## This is not a new regression age

Sleep can wobble when a big change lands — a new room, a new carer, a first full week. That can look like a [regression](/sleep-regression), and it may overlap with an age that already has a bump (for example 8 or 12 months). Treat the *cause* as the change of context, not as a new official month on the calendar. If the only new variable is teething, illness, or a skill leap, use those pages instead.

Travel days and the clock change are separate: [baby sleep and travel](/baby-sleep-and-travel), [daylight saving](/daylight-saving-baby-sleep).

## When to talk to your pediatrician (or the program)

Ask the program if sleep practice there does not match back-to-sleep, a flat crib, or a clear sleep space. Ask the pediatrician if total sleep is regularly short and your child is struggling, if you are unsure whether a remaining day nap should be kept, or if snoring or pauses worry you.

## When a grandparent, babysitter, or other carer has the baby

The same two-environment problem this page already describes at daycare also happens in a relative’s house. Lullaby Trust and Red Nose both publish safer-sleep advice for other carers: everyone who puts the baby down should know **back, firm and flat, clear space, no smoke**, and that sofas and armchairs are not beds. Write it down if that helps. A babysitter does not need a second set of rules.

If the routine falls apart at a grandparent’s house (late nights, a different crib, extra holding), keep your home pattern on the days you have, and ask for the safe-sleep basics even when the schedule slips. Caring for Kids and CFOC material already used on this page still apply in child care; for a one-off evening, the [safe sleep](/safe-sleep-for-babies) list is enough.

## Frequently asked questions

**Why won't my baby nap at daycare?**  
A new room and a group schedule are a lot. Give it more than two days, share the home rhythm, and adjust bedtime if the day was short. Persistent refusal belongs on [baby won't nap](/baby-wont-nap).

**Should I drop a nap to match the classroom?**  
Only if your baby's days and nights actually support the drop. Follow the transition pages, not the signup form.

**Is a "daycare sleep regression" real?**  
The phrase is popular. The useful idea is a context change, not a new developmental stage we have given its own month.

**What if grandparents will not follow our bedtime?**  
Ask for the safe-sleep basics even if the clock is different. You can return to your usual routine at home. This page is about two environments, not a family argument we can referee.

## See how daycare days change the night (Yorix)

**Yorix** can show whether naps at care are shorter than naps at home, and whether bedtime moved in response. The app cannot set a classroom schedule and is not a medical device.

## Related reading

- [Safe sleep for babies](/safe-sleep-for-babies)
- [Baby won't nap](/baby-wont-nap)
- [Short naps](/short-naps)
- [3-to-2 nap transition](/3-to-2-nap-transition)
- [2-to-1 nap transition](/2-to-1-nap-transition)
- [Reverse cycling](/reverse-cycling)
- [Baby sleep and travel](/baby-sleep-and-travel)
- [How much sleep a baby needs](/how-much-sleep-does-a-baby-need)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026.

1. Child Care Technical Assistance Network. *Caring for Our Children* Basics, "3.1.4.1 Safe Sleep Practices and Sudden Unexpected Infant Death Risk Reduction." Accessed 15 November 2026. Written policies; pre-service training; follow AAP 2022: back to sleep, firm flat non-inclined surface, tight fitted sheet. <https://childcareta.acf.hhs.gov/cfoc/basic/chapter/3/3.1.4.1>.
2. Moon RY, et al. AAP 2022 safe-sleep policy. The same back, bare, flat rules apply for every sleep, including in the care of non-parent caregivers. <https://publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article/150/1/e2022057990/188304/Sleep-Related-Infant-Deaths-Updated-2022>.
3. Paruthi S, et al. AASM pediatric sleep-duration consensus, 2016. Age totals do not change because a baby is at daycare; used by reference via our how-much-sleep page.

4. [The Lullaby Trust. Safer sleep in childcare: checklist for families.](https://www.lullabytrust.org.uk/baby-safety/being-a-parent-or-caregiver/safer-sleep-in-childcare-checklist-for-families/)

description: How to handle daylight saving time with a baby: spring-forward and fall-back on one page, AAP timing tips, and why there is no overnight reset. Evergreen.
body:
# Daylight Saving Time and Baby Sleep: Spring and Fall

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 16, 2026 · **Updated:** November 16, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

The clock changes twice a year in much of the United States and Europe, and babies do not care what the government decided. This is one evergreen page for **both spring-forward and fall-back**. HealthyChildren.org's daylight saving article (updated 26 October 2026, by Anna Esparham, MD, FAAP) is the main parent-facing AAP source we use here. We are not giving a country-by-country calendar; check when your local clocks change.

## Short answer

Start nudging naps and bedtime **a few minutes each day, beginning about a week before** the change, then use morning daylight and a steady [bedtime routine](/bedtime-routine-for-baby) to help the body clock catch up. HealthyChildren.org says that in **spring**, getting children to bed or up in the morning can be a challenge, though the spring change may be a little easier on young children who already wake early. **Fall** can lead younger children to crash early and then wake too early. Most kids, in that article's words, adjust **within about a week**. Newborns already have messy clocks — see [day-night confusion](/newborn-day-night-confusion) — so a 1-hour shift is often less dramatic for a 4-week-old than for a 10-month-old with a set bedtime. We are not recommending melatonin for babies.

### Key numbers at a glance

| Question | What the sources say | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| When U.S. clocks change | Spring-forward: second Sunday in March; fall-back: first Sunday in November | HealthyChildren.org (2026) |
| How to prepare | Nudge naps and bedtime a few minutes each day, starting about a week before | HealthyChildren.org |
| How long adjustment often takes | About a week for most children | HealthyChildren.org |
| Screens | Off at least 1 hour before bed | HealthyChildren.org |
| Melatonin | Discussed in the same article for some children, after a pediatrician conversation — not infant advice we will repeat as a dose or a plan | HealthyChildren.org |

Sleep Foundation's bedtime-routine article, already used on our routine page, mentions shifting bedtime in 15-minute steps over a few days. That is a more specific increment than HealthyChildren.org's "a few minutes." We treat 15 minutes as one workable example, not as an AAP mandate.

## Spring: clocks jump forward (you lose an hour)

On the new clock, a baby who used to wake at 6:30 may now wake at 7:30, and the bedtime that felt "on time" will feel early for their body. The painful part is often the first morning, when you need to be somewhere at a new, earlier time.

HealthyChildren.org's approach:

- In the week before, move naps and bedtime a little later each day, so Sunday is less of a cliff.
- On the days after, open curtains and get **morning daylight**. Light is the strongest clock cue you have.
- Keep the routine in the same order even if the clock time is slightly off for a few days.
- Protect bedtime from screens for at least an hour.

If you did not prepare, you can still shift a few minutes later each day after the change. Do not keep the baby up a full extra hour on Saturday night and hope for the best; that is a good way to get an [overtired](/overtired-baby) bedtime.

## Fall: clocks fall back (you gain an hour)

The same 6:30 wake can become 5:30 on the new clock, and a toddler may be exhausted at a late-afternoon hour that used to be mid-afternoon. HealthyChildren.org flags early crashes and early mornings as the typical fall pattern.

In the week before, nudge naps and bedtime a little **earlier** each day. After the change, still use morning light, but do not start the day at 5 a.m. with a full "morning" (bright play, breakfast theater) if you are trying to slide wake-up later. Keep the room dark until a reasonable wake window, then go into daylight. For a baby who already wakes early, see [early morning waking](/early-morning-waking) — the clock change can aggravate a pattern that was already there.

## Newborns, older babies, and what "a week" looks like

Under about 8 weeks, many babies do not have a clock-stable bedtime yet. A light-and-dark contrast still helps, but you do not need a minute-by-minute DST project. From the age when a [schedule](/baby-nap-schedule-by-age) actually exists, the week-before nudge is more useful.

One-year-olds and toddlers often feel the change more because their bedtime is more set. Hold the routine and the new clock, rather than negotiating a moving target every night.

If you also need to [wake a baby](/should-you-wake-a-sleeping-baby) for a feed, keep the medical plan and shift the "extra" schedule pieces, not the required calories.

## What we are not recommending

HealthyChildren.org mentions melatonin at low pediatric doses for some children, only after talking to a pediatrician, and as part of a larger sleep plan. **That is not advice for infants.** We are not listing doses, and we are not suggesting a supplement as a daylight-saving shortcut for a baby. If a clinician raises melatonin for an older child, that conversation belongs with them.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Ask if sleep was already a serious problem before the clock change and is still off two weeks later, or if you are considering any sleep aid. Call sooner if the baby seems unwell, not merely "on the wrong clock."

## Frequently asked questions

**How do I handle daylight saving with a baby?**  
Shift naps and bedtime by a few minutes a day for about a week, use morning light, and keep the routine. Expect about a week to adjust.

**Is spring or fall harder?**  
HealthyChildren.org: in spring, bedtime and morning can both be a struggle, but the change may be a little easier on young early risers and harder on teens. In fall, younger children may crash early and wake earlier than usual.

**Should I keep my baby on "old time"?**  
You can delay the shift by a day or two if a Sunday event is optional, but living on a private time zone usually becomes messy once childcare or work is involved.

**Can I use the clock change to fix a late bedtime?**  
Sometimes, in the spring, because the new clock already moves social time earlier relative to the body. Make only one project at a time if you can.

**Does this apply outside the United States?**  
The method is the same whenever clocks move by an hour. The March and November dates above are the U.S. ones; the UK and EU change on different dates.

## Watch the week, not the hour (Yorix)

**Yorix** can show whether bedtime and morning wake drifted in the week after the change. The app cannot reset a body clock and is not a medical device. Use the log to see whether the "few minutes a day" plan is actually happening.

## Related reading

- [Baby Sleep and Travel: Planes, Hotels, and Jet Lag](/baby-sleep-and-travel)

- [Bedtime routine for baby](/bedtime-routine-for-baby)
- [Early morning waking](/early-morning-waking)
- [Newborn day-night confusion](/newborn-day-night-confusion)
- [Overtired baby](/overtired-baby)
- [Should you wake a sleeping baby](/should-you-wake-a-sleeping-baby)
- [Wake windows by age](/wake-windows-by-age)
- [How much sleep a baby needs](/how-much-sleep-does-a-baby-need)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026.

1. HealthyChildren.org (AAP). "Daylight Saving Time: Don't Lose Sleep Over It." By Anna Esparham, MD, FAAP, DABMA, DABOIM. Last updated 10/26/2026. <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/healthy-living/sleep/Pages/daylight-saving-time-dont-lose-sleep-over-it.aspx>. U.S. change dates; nudge naps and bedtime a few minutes a day about a week before; spring vs fall (fall early crash/early wake in younger kids; spring may be a little easier on young early risers); about a week to adjust; light, screens, routine. The same article mentions melatonin for some children only after talking to a pediatrician — not used here as infant advice.
2. Sleep Foundation. "Bedtime Routines for Children." Updated 23 July 2025. <https://www.sleepfoundation.org/children-and-sleep/bedtime-routine>. 15-minute bedtime shifts as one example of a gradual change.
3. NHS. "Helping your baby to sleep." <https://www.nhs.uk/baby/caring-for-a-newborn/helping-your-baby-to-sleep/>. Daylight and a calm, consistent night routine as general clock cues.

title: Fear of the Dark: Toddler Nighttime Fears | Yorix
heading: Fear of the Dark and Other Nighttime Fears
description: Fear of the dark is a waking nighttime fear, unlike a night terror. What helps: a calm routine, dim light, honest comfort — and skip rituals like monster spray.
body:
# Fear of the Dark and Other Nighttime Fears

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 16, 2026 · **Updated:** November 16, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

Fear of the dark is a **waking** problem. The child is aware, can usually tell you something is scary, and will remember it in the morning. That is the opposite of a [night terror](/night-terrors), in which the child is not fully awake, may not know you, and typically has no memory of the episode. Nightmares — bad dreams the child can recall — sit closer to this page than to night terrors (HealthyChildren; KidsHealth).

This is also not [separation anxiety and sleep](/separation-anxiety-and-sleep), though the two can overlap at bedtime. Separation anxiety is "don't leave me." Fear of the dark is "this room is not safe." A child can have both. We will not retell the regression articles, and we will not write a science essay on night-light color — that remains a possible later topic.

## Short answer

Nighttime fears are common. KidsHealth notes that younger children may struggle to tell imagination from reality, and that many preschool-age children are afraid of the dark and of what might be under the bed or in a closet. Cincinnati Children's says it is normal for young children to worry about safety and security at bedtime, and that most children have nighttime fears at some point.

What helps, according to those sources and to KidsHealth's preschool-sleep page, is a calm, predictable routine, a quiet comfortable room, a **dim night light** if it helps the child feel safe, a comfort object when age-safe, and brief, serious reassurance. What does not help is teasing the fear, or building a nightly theater of "monster spray" and closet checks that teach the child you also believe something is in the room (Cincinnati Children's). KidsHealth's preschool advice is to avoid lying with the child until they fall asleep as a new every-night pattern, because it can make solo settling harder; Cincinnati Children's says an occasional stay until they fall asleep can be all right if fear is intense, but not night after night. We treat that as a **nuance, not a fight**: comfort is allowed; a brand-new all-night presence can become the only way the child will sleep.

Screens and scary stories before bed make this worse (KidsHealth, Cincinnati Children's). Turn screens off at least an hour before bedtime and keep them out of the bedroom (KidsHealth preschool sleep).

### Fear of the dark versus night terrors versus nightmares

| | Fear of the dark / bedtime fear | Nightmare | Night terror |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Is the child awake? | Yes, at bedtime or after a waking | Yes, after a dream; they can usually be comforted | No — they may look terrified but are not fully awake |
| Will they remember it? | Yes | Often yes | Typically no |
| When? | Settling, or after waking in the night | More often in the second half of the night | Often in the first part of the night |
| What to do | Reassure, keep the plan boring and kind | Comfort, keep the visit short, back to bed | Keep them safe, do not try hard to wake them. See [night terrors](/night-terrors) |

## What to do in the evening, and after a scare

By day, Cincinnati Children's suggests giving the child a chance to talk about the fear, without forcing the conversation, and without agreeing that a monster is real. You can say the room is safe and that you are there to keep it that way. You do not need a ritual that "clears" the closet.

At bedtime:

- Keep the [routine](/bedtime-routine-for-baby) the same length on easy nights and scared nights, as much as you can, so fear does not earn an hour of extra entertainment.
- A dim night light or a door left slightly open is a reasonable comfort (Cincinnati Children's, KidsHealth). Bright light that turns the room into daytime is less useful. We are not claiming a special color of light unless a later, sourced article can support it.
- A lovey or blanket belongs only in a sleep space that is old enough for it.
- If the child calls out, Cincinnati Children's suggests going back, asking what is wrong, and answering with safety ("we are here to make sure you are safe in your own bed") rather than starting a hunt.
- If they come to your room, take them back calmly. The goal is for the bed to feel like the safe place, not for the dark hall to become the path to your mattress every night — unless you have chosen a family-bed arrangement on purpose, with the safety limits that still apply for younger children.

After a nightmare, the same short-comfort rule holds (KidsHealth preschool): soothe, return them to their bed, keep the visit brief. If nightmares are frequent or the child seems distressed by day, talk with the pediatrician.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Ask if fears are taking over daytime life, if the child cannot sleep in their room at all for a long stretch, if you cannot tell night terrors from nightmares, or if snoring, pauses, or unusual daytime sleepiness are also in the picture (see [baby snoring and mouth breathing](/baby-snoring-and-mouth-breathing)).

## Frequently asked questions

**Is a night light all right?**  
Yes, if it is dim and the child sleeps with it. KidsHealth and Cincinnati Children's both treat it as a reasonable comfort. This page does not recommend a color.

**Should I check the closet for monsters?**  
Cincinnati Children's advises against building rituals that treat imagined figures as real (including "monster spray"). Take the fear seriously; do not join the story.

**How is this different from a night terror?**  
The child with a night terror is not truly awake and usually will not remember it. Details and first aid are on [night terrors](/night-terrors).

**My 2-year-old suddenly will not go to bed. Is it fear or a regression?**  
It can be either, or both. Use [2-year sleep regression](/sleep-regression/2-years) for a time-limited bump, [toddler bedtime battles](/toddler-bedtime-battles) for ongoing stalling, and this page if the child can tell you they are scared.

## Note whether the scare is at bedtime or later (Yorix)

**Yorix** can help you record whether a hard night started at lights-out or hours later, which is one clue when you and the pediatrician are sorting fear or a nightmare from a night terror. The app cannot treat anxiety and is not a medical device.

## Related reading

- [4 Year Old Sleep Schedule: The Preschool Day, With or Without a Nap](/4-year-old-sleep-schedule)
- [Sleep After Separation or Divorce: Two Homes, One Predictable Night](/sleep-after-separation-or-divorce)

- [Night Lights and Baby Sleep: Color Claims, and What We Can Source](/night-lights-and-baby-sleep)
- [Toddler Won't Stay in Bed: After Lights Out](/toddler-wont-stay-in-bed)

- [Night terrors](/night-terrors)
- [Separation anxiety and sleep](/separation-anxiety-and-sleep)
- [Toddler bedtime battles](/toddler-bedtime-battles)
- [2-year sleep regression](/sleep-regression/2-years)
- [3 year old sleep schedule](/3-year-old-sleep-schedule)
- [Bedtime routine for baby](/bedtime-routine-for-baby)
- [Crib to toddler bed](/crib-to-toddler-bed)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026.

1. Nemours KidsHealth. "Childhood Fears and Worries." Young children may not tell real from imagined; many fear the dark and bedtime "monsters"; comfort, short honest goodbyes, do not mock the fear. <https://kidshealth.org/en/parents/anxiety.html>.
2. Nemours KidsHealth. "Sleep and Your Preschooler." Date reviewed June 2020. About 10–13 hours' sleep; dim night light if afraid of the dark; comfort object; avoid falling asleep with you as a new pattern; screens off at least an hour before bed; brief comfort after a night waking. <https://kidshealth.org/en/parents/sleep-preschool.html>.
3. Nemours KidsHealth. "Nightmares." Accessed 15 November 2026. Recalled bad dreams; comfort and back to bed. <https://kidshealth.org/en/parents/nightmare.html>.
4. Cincinnati Children's. "Helping to Overcome Bedtime Fears." Accessed 15 November 2026. Nighttime fears are common; do not build "monster" rituals; night light and open door can help; occasional stay until asleep is all right, but not night after night; no scary media. <https://www.cincinnatichildrens.org/health/b/bedtime-fears>.
5. HealthyChildren.org (AAP). "Nightmares, Night Terrors & Sleepwalking in Children." Contrast with night terrors (not fully awake, usually no memory). <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/preschool/pages/nightmares-and-night-terrors.aspx>.

body:
# Gentle Sleep Training: Chair, Fading, and Pick Up / Put Down

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 16, 2026 · **Updated:** November 16, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

The comparison of sleep-training methods already lives on [sleep training methods explained](/sleep-training-methods-explained). [Ferber](/ferber-method-baby-sleep) and [cry it out](/cry-it-out-method) have their own how-to pages. This article is the **practical walk-through of the slower, stay-close approaches** people usually mean by "gentle" or "no-cry": the chair method (camping out), pick up / put down, and bedtime fading. It is not a rewrite of the comparison table, and it is not a new age-sliced training page for 5, 6, or 9 months — that job stays on [when to start sleep training](/when-to-start-sleep-training).

## Short answer

"Gentle sleep training" is not one official protocol. It is a family of plans that keep the parent nearby or keep responses fairly prompt, and that change sleep habits over days or weeks rather than over a few nights. Sleep Foundation notes that these slower approaches can still involve crying, and that they often take longer than cry-it-out or Ferber — fading or camping out may run up to about two weeks in that description. Cleveland Clinic describes pick up / put down as more time-consuming and demanding than those two methods.

None of these plans is for a newborn. Sleep Foundation, in line with our readiness page, places formal training after about 4 to 6 months, with many clinicians more comfortable around 6 months. If your baby is younger, unwell, or still needs frequent night calories, wait and talk with the pediatrician. A consistent [bedtime routine](/bedtime-routine-for-baby) and putting the baby down drowsy, as HealthyChildren describes from about 4 months, is a reasonable foundation without picking a branded method.

### Which plan is which? (and a naming conflict)

Sources do not all use "fading" the same way. We keep the split our methods page already uses, and we flag the clash:

| Name we use here | What you actually do | What sources call it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Chair method / camping out | After the routine, stay in the room and gradually sit farther from the crib over nights | Sleep Foundation treats "fading" and "camping out" / the chair method as the same family. KidsHealth New Zealand describes camping out for **primary-school** children, so we do not copy that night-by-night distance plan as a baby protocol |
| Pick up / put down | Pick up to calm, put down still awake, repeat | Cleveland Clinic; Sleep Foundation (often discussed for roughly 4–8 months) |
| Bedtime fading | Temporarily move bedtime closer to when the child actually falls asleep, then ease it earlier | A different idea from "fade your presence." Our methods page notes support in an AASM review and a 2016 trial. KidsHealth New Zealand also describes bedtime fading, including for older children |

There is no single AAP method sheet for any of these. The steps below are high-level, sourced where a clinical site describes them, and should be adapted with your pediatrician.

## Before you start

Use the readiness and "when not to start" advice on [when to start sleep training](/when-to-start-sleep-training). In short: the baby should be past the newborn period, you should have a feeding plan for the night, and you should not begin in the middle of an illness, a big household change, or a situation your clinician wants you to wait on. If the issue is mainly a strong feed-to-sleep habit, read [nursing to sleep](/nursing-to-sleep) and [sleep associations](/sleep-associations) first — you may only need a slow change to the start of the night, not a full formal method.

Agree the plan with every caregiver. Gentle methods fail most often when one adult sits in the chair and another rocks to sleep the next night.

## Chair method (camping out), in outline

Sleep Foundation's description: go through the bedtime routine, put the baby down drowsy, and stay nearby until they fall asleep. Over subsequent nights, move yourself a little farther — for example from beside the crib, then farther across the room, then toward the door — while offering only limited talking or touching. The parent remains in view for a stretch of this process.

Expect some protest. You are visible, which some families find easier than leaving the room, and which can also make it harder to stay quietly consistent. Sleep Foundation says this usually takes longer than leaving-the-room methods. KidsHealth New Zealand's camping-out page is written for school-age children who can be told "this is sleep time, not play time," and it mentions a range of about 7 to 21 nights; treat that as context for older children, not as a baby guarantee.

If the baby is asleep and later wakes, return to the place you had reached in the plan and stay until they settle again, rather than starting from zero with rocking or a feed that is no longer needed. Needed feeds still happen.

## Pick up / put down, in outline

Cleveland Clinic describes a loop: when the baby fuss or cries after you put them down, pick them up to soothe, then put them back down **before** they fall asleep in your arms, and repeat as needed. The aim is that the last moment of falling asleep happens in the crib, not on your chest. Sleep Foundation places this approach especially in a mid-infancy window (it cites about 4 to 8 months) when babies can begin to practice independent settling but still respond to being held.

The honest difficulty, which Cleveland Clinic also flags, is the number of repetitions. If crying starts the moment the back touches the mattress, you may be picking up and putting down many times in one evening. That is why some families find it "gentler" in theory and exhausting in practice. It is a valid choice; it is not automatically easier.

Do not use this as a wrestling match with a baby who is ill, very hungry, or too young. Put the baby down on their back, in a clear crib, every time.

## Bedtime fading, in outline

This is a clock change, not a presence change. If a child is taking a long time to fall asleep, a temporary later bedtime — closer to their actual sleep-onset time — can reduce long, frustrated evenings (KidsHealth New Zealand; our methods page). After they are falling asleep more easily, shift bedtime earlier in small steps (our methods page mentions about 15 minutes every few days as a typical pattern). Keep the morning wake time reasonably steady, or the whole day slides.

Bedtime fading can be combined with a chair plan, but you do not have to do both. It is often useful for toddlers as well as older babies.

## What "no-cry" does and does not promise

Marketing language sometimes implies that a gentle method means no tears. Sleep Foundation is clearer: crying is still common, especially with chair / fading, because the baby can see you and still wants the old pattern. The difference is how you respond, and how slowly you change the pattern — not a guarantee of silence. If a plan only works when you rock or feed the baby all the way to sleep every night, it is a [sleep association](/sleep-associations) you have kept, not a training method you have finished.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Ask first if your baby was premature (use [corrected age](/preemie-sleep)), has reflux, poor weight gain, or breathing concerns, or if you are unsure whether night feeds are still needed. Stop and call if the baby seems unwell, or if sleep is getting worse in a way that does not match a short adjustment period.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is gentle sleep training effective?**  
Sleep Foundation says several methods can work and that the better fit is the one the family can use consistently. Direct trial evidence is thinner for chair and pick up / put down than for some leaving-the-room methods — our methods page already records that. "Gentle" is a preference and a pace, not a separate proof of superiority.

**Will my baby still cry?**  
Often, yes, at least some. The selling point is a closer parent and a slower change, not zero crying.

**Can I combine this with Ferber later?**  
Some families start gentle and later switch. If you do, pick one plan at a time and give it a fair stretch, rather than changing rules every night. See [Ferber](/ferber-method-baby-sleep) if you need that how-to.

**Is this appropriate for naps?**  
Naps are often harder. A short, consistent try at the same approach can be reasonable once nights have a plan; a dedicated nap-training article is not what this page is. See [baby won't nap](/baby-wont-nap) and [short naps](/short-naps) for daytime sleep problems.

## See whether the new plan is actually sticking (Yorix)

**Yorix** can show how long settling takes at the start of the night and whether night wakings are changing over a week, which is more useful than judging a gentle method on a single hard evening. The app cannot run a method for you and is not a medical device.

## Related reading

- [Responsive Settling: Help That Can Fade, Not a Second Methods Table](/responsive-settling)

- [Self-Soothing: A Skill That Grows, Not a Method](/self-soothing)
- [Sleep Training Methods Explained: A Side-by-Side Comparison](/sleep-training-methods-explained#why-naps-are-often-harder-than-nights)

- [Sleep training methods explained](/sleep-training-methods-explained)
- [When to start sleep training](/when-to-start-sleep-training)
- [Ferber method](/ferber-method-baby-sleep)
- [Cry-it-out method](/cry-it-out-method)
- [Sleep associations](/sleep-associations)
- [Nursing to sleep](/nursing-to-sleep)
- [Bedtime routine for baby](/bedtime-routine-for-baby)
- [Baby won't sleep in the crib](/baby-wont-sleep-in-crib)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026.

1. Sleep Foundation. "Sleep Training: What It Is, When to Start, and How to Do It." Accessed 15 November 2026. Readiness often 4–6 months; fading / camping out / chair described as gradual distance with the parent in the room, often up to about two weeks; pick up / put down often discussed at about 4–8 months; gentler plans can still involve crying and usually take longer. <https://www.sleepfoundation.org/baby-sleep/sleep-training>.
2. Cleveland Clinic. "Pick Up Put Down Sleep Training Method." Accessed 15 November 2026. Pick up to calm, put down drowsy / awake, repeat; can be slow and demanding; compared with cry-it-out and Ferber. <https://health.clevelandclinic.org/pick-up-put-down-method>.
3. KidsHealth New Zealand (Starship / Paediatric Society of New Zealand, from Murdoch Children's Research Institute content). "Camping Out Method For Managing Sleep Problems" and "Bedtime Fading for Managing Sleep Problems." Camping out is written there for primary-school children (about 7–21 nights). Bedtime fading: temporarily use the child's actual sleep time, then adjust. <https://www.kidshealth.org.nz/camping-out-method-for-managing-sleep-problems> and <https://www.kidshealth.org.nz/bedtime-fading-for-managing-sleep-problems>.
4. HealthyChildren.org (AAP). "Getting Your Baby to Sleep." Last updated 4 June 2024. From about 4 months, put babies down drowsy rather than already asleep; regular cycles often appear around then. <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/baby/sleep/Pages/Getting-Your-Baby-to-Sleep.aspx>.
5. NHS. "Helping your baby to sleep." Accessed 15 November 2026. Patterns vary; a calm routine and a consistent approach, without a branded method. <https://www.nhs.uk/baby/caring-for-a-newborn/helping-your-baby-to-sleep/>.
