description: How much sleep a baby needs by age, with AASM and National Sleep Foundation ranges side by side, plus newborn variation and when to call the pediatrician.
body:
# How Much Sleep Does a Baby Need? A Chart From Newborn to Age 5

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 16, 2026 · **Updated:** November 16, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

"How much sleep does a baby need?" sounds as if there should be one official number. There is not. There are two widely used charts, they do not match at every age, and healthy babies sit on a wide range around them. This page is a **totals chart** — hours in 24 hours, naps included — not a daily schedule. For sample days and wake windows, use the month guides linked below and our [wake windows by age](/wake-windows-by-age) and [nap schedule by age](/baby-nap-schedule-by-age) pages.

## Short answer

The American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM), in a 2016 consensus statement endorsed by the American Academy of Pediatrics, recommends **12 to 16 hours per 24 hours** for infants 4 to 12 months, **11 to 14 hours** at 1 to 2 years, and **10 to 13 hours** at 3 to 5 years, naps included. The AASM did **not** issue a recommendation for the first 3 months, because the evidence was not strong enough. The National Sleep Foundation's 2015 ranges, which Sleep Foundation and KidsHealth still quote, suggest **14 to 17 hours** from 0 to 3 months and **12 to 15 hours** from 4 to 11 months — a slightly different infant band. Cleveland Clinic, looking at the whole first year, says babies often sleep **11 to 17 hours** a day. Use the charts as a range, not a daily target your baby must hit.

### Key numbers at a glance

| Age | AASM (AAP-endorsed) | National Sleep Foundation (2015) | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0–3 months | No official AASM number | 14–17 hours in 24 hours | Sleep Foundation also notes healthy newborns may sleep as few as 11 or as many as 19 hours |
| 4–12 months | 12–16 hours (4–12 months) | 12–15 hours (listed as 4–11 months) | The upper end differs by one hour; both include naps |
| 1–2 years | 11–14 hours | 11–14 hours | Includes naps |
| 3–5 years | 10–13 hours | 10–13 hours | Includes any remaining nap |
| 6–12 years | 9–12 hours | 9–11 hours (NSF school-age band is slightly narrower) | Shown for completeness; this page focuses on babies and toddlers |
| 13–18 years | 8–10 hours | 8–10 hours | AASM teenager range |

KidsHealth's parent summary uses 14–17 hours at 0–3 months and 12–16 hours at 4–12 months — that is, NSF at the start of infancy and AASM after 4 months. We would rather show both original charts than blend them silently.

## Why the official bodies disagree a little

The AASM consensus (Paruthi and colleagues, published in the *Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine* in 2016) reviewed hundreds of studies and then recommended ranges that "promote optimal health." The AAP endorsed those ranges. The panel started at 4 months because newborn sleep is so variable, and because high-quality studies in the first months were limited.

The National Sleep Foundation's 2015 update (Hirshkowitz and colleagues, in *Sleep Health*) is the other chart you will see. It includes a newborn band and uses 4–11 months rather than 4–12 months, with a slightly lower upper limit (15 vs 16 hours). Neither chart is "wrong." They are two expert groups drawing similar, not identical, lines.

Cleveland Clinic's first-year article (reviewed 15 June 2023) describes an even wider everyday range of 11 to 17 hours and tells parents to ask their pediatrician what is normal for their baby. That is a useful reminder: a single night or week outside a chart is not, on its own, a diagnosis.

## What "hours in 24 hours" actually includes

Every figure in the table is **total sleep**, nights plus naps. A 6-month-old who sleeps 11 hours at night and 3 hours across two or three naps is inside the AASM range. A toddler who dropped to one nap and sleeps 11 hours at night plus a 2-hour nap is inside the 1–2 year range. If you only count night sleep, you will think your baby is "short" when they are not.

Newborns are a special case. Their sleep comes in short stretches of one to two hours, around the clock, because they need frequent feeds and their body clock is still maturing. Sleep Foundation describes this pattern clearly, and NHS reminds parents that some babies sleep much more than others and that a newborn's pattern is unlikely to match yours. For week-by-week expectations, see [newborn sleep schedule](/newborn-sleep-schedule) and [when do babies sleep through the night](/when-do-babies-sleep-through-the-night).

## What happens when a child regularly gets less — or a lot more

The AASM statement links regularly sleeping in the recommended range with better attention, behavior, learning, memory, emotional regulation, and physical health. Regularly sleeping fewer hours than the range is associated with attention, behavior, and learning problems, and with higher risk of accidents, hypertension, obesity, diabetes, and depression (with additional self-harm risks discussed for teenagers). HealthyChildren.org, summarizing the AAP's support for these guidelines, also lists irritability, poor concentration, headaches, and a harder time at school when children are routinely short on sleep, and notes that enough sleep supports the immune system and mental health.

"More than the range" is less often discussed and is not automatically better. A baby who is suddenly much sleepier than usual, is hard to wake, or is feeding poorly needs a medical check, not a later bedtime. Cleveland Clinic makes this point for babies who seem to sleep "too much," including the possibility of illness.

## How to use the chart without turning it into a test

- Add up a typical 24 hours, not a single night.
- Compare with your baby's mood, feeding, and growth, not only with a neighbor's baby.
- Expect totals to swing during a [sleep regression](/sleep-regression), a cold, or a nap transition. Look at the week, not the day.
- Move bedtime earlier if nights plus naps consistently come in under the range and your child looks exhausted. Do not keep a baby up late in the hope of a longer night — that often backfires; see [overtired baby](/overtired-baby).
- For a day-by-day picture at a specific age, open the matching schedule: [newborn](/newborn-sleep-schedule), [1 month](/1-month-old-sleep-schedule), [2](/2-month-old-sleep-schedule), [3](/3-month-old-sleep-schedule), [4](/4-month-old-sleep-schedule), [5](/5-month-old-sleep-schedule), [6](/6-month-old-sleep-schedule), [7](/7-month-old-sleep-schedule), [8](/8-month-old-sleep-schedule), [9](/9-month-old-sleep-schedule), [10](/10-month-old-sleep-schedule), [11](/11-month-old-sleep-schedule), [12](/12-month-old-sleep-schedule), [15 months](/15-month-old-sleep-schedule).

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Sleep Foundation's wake-window article, and Cleveland Clinic, both suggest checking in if your baby regularly sleeps a lot more or less than the range for their age, or if you notice snoring, long pauses in breathing, or very restless sleep. Call sooner if your baby is unusually hard to wake, is not feeding, has fewer wet diapers, or seems unwell. Charts cannot tell you whether a particular baby has a medical sleep problem.

## Frequently asked questions

**How much sleep does a newborn need?**  
There is no AASM official number. NSF suggests 14–17 hours in 24 hours, and Sleep Foundation notes a healthy range that can run from about 11 to 19 hours, in short stretches.

**How much should a 6-month-old sleep?**  
AASM: 12–16 hours in 24 hours, including naps. Details and example days are on our [6 month old sleep schedule](/6-month-old-sleep-schedule).

**Do the hours have to be in one long night block?**  
No. The recommendations are 24-hour totals. Many babies still wake at night and still meet the range; see [when do babies sleep through the night](/when-do-babies-sleep-through-the-night).

**Is 11 hours enough for a 4-month-old?**  
It is below the AASM 12–16 hour range. One short day is not a crisis; a regular pattern that low, especially if the baby is miserable, is worth a conversation with your pediatrician and a look at naps and bedtime.

**Should I wake my baby to keep them from sleeping "too much"?**  
Not to hit a chart. Newborns sometimes need to be woken for feeds — that is a nutrition question, discussed with your pediatrician, not a way to trim sleep.

## Add up the real 24 hours (Yorix)

**Yorix** logs naps and night sleep so you can see a 24-hour total instead of guessing from a hard night. You can also log feeds and symptoms if you are trying to understand a sleepy or restless stretch. It is a support for tired parents, not a medical device and not a diagnosis.

## Related reading

- [4 Year Old Sleep Schedule: The Preschool Day, With or Without a Nap](/4-year-old-sleep-schedule)
- [Melatonin and Children's Sleep: Not a Do-It-Yourself Sleeping Pill](/melatonin-and-childrens-sleep)

- [18 Month Old Sleep Schedule: Life on One Nap](/18-month-old-sleep-schedule)
- [2 Year Old Sleep Schedule: Naps, Bedtime, and Totals](/2-year-old-sleep-schedule)

- [Baby Sleep Cycles: Why They Wake After One Cycle](/baby-sleep-cycles)
- [Daycare and Baby Sleep: A Context Page, Not a New Regression](/daycare-and-baby-sleep)
- [Preemie Sleep: Use Due Date, Not Just Birthday](/preemie-sleep)
- [When Do Toddlers Stop Napping?](/when-do-toddlers-stop-napping)

- [Wake windows by age](/wake-windows-by-age)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026.

1. Paruthi S, et al. "Recommended Amount of Sleep for Pediatric Populations: A Consensus Statement of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine." *Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine*, 2016;12(6):785–786. <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27250809/>. 12–16, 11–14, 10–13, 9–12, and 8–10 hour ranges; no 0–3 month recommendation.
2. American Academy of Sleep Medicine. "Recharge with sleep: Pediatric sleep recommendations promoting optimal health." <https://aasm.org/recharge-with-sleep-pediatric-sleep-recommendations-promoting-optimal-health/>. Same ranges; endorsed by the AAP.
3. Hirshkowitz M, et al. "National Sleep Foundation's updated sleep duration recommendations: Final report." *Sleep Health*, 2015;1(4):233–243. <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29073398/>. 14–17 hours (0–3 months) and 12–15 hours (4–11 months).
4. HealthyChildren.org (AAP). "Healthy Sleep Habits: How Many Hours Does Your Child Need?" <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/healthy-living/sleep/Pages/healthy-sleep-habits-how-many-hours-does-your-child-need.aspx>. AAP support for AASM; health effects of too little sleep.
5. Nemours KidsHealth. "Kids and Sleep." Medically reviewed by Mary L. Gavin, MD. Date reviewed January 2021. <https://kidshealth.org/en/parents/sleep.html>. 14–17 hours (0–3 months), 12–16 hours (4–12 months), and later AASM-aligned ranges.
6. Sleep Foundation. "How Much Do Newborns Sleep?" Updated 30 September 2026. Medically reviewed by Pranshu Adavadkar, MD. <https://www.sleepfoundation.org/baby-sleep/how-much-do-newborns-sleep>. 11–19 hour variation; short stretches; circadian development.
7. Sleep Foundation. "When Do Babies Sleep Through the Night?" Updated 11 August 2026. <https://www.sleepfoundation.org/baby-sleep/when-do-babies-sleep-through-night>. NSF 14–17 and 12–15 figures; AASM/AAP have no 0–3 month recommendation.
8. Cleveland Clinic. "Sleep in Your Baby's First Year." Last updated 15 June 2023. <https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/articles/14300-sleep-in-your-babys-first-year>. 11–17 hours in the first year; ask the pediatrician if you are worried about too much sleep.

heading: How to Dress a Baby for Sleep: Layers, Heat, and Room Temperature
description: How to dress a baby for sleep: the 'one extra layer' rule, signs of overheating, sleep sacks vs blankets, and why room-temperature advice differs by country.
body:
# How to Dress a Baby for Sleep: Layers, Heat, and Room Temperature

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 16, 2026 · **Updated:** November 16, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

Parents worry about two opposite mistakes: a baby who is too cold, and a baby who is bundled into a higher risk of overheating. **How to dress a baby for sleep** is mostly about that balance. The rule you will see in AAP parent advice is simple — about **one more layer** than an adult would need in the same room — and then there is a messy disagreement about what temperature the room itself should be.

## Short answer

Dress your baby in light layers that match the room, usually a onesie or similar base layer plus, if needed, a wearable blanket (a [sleep sack](/sleep-sacks)). Keep **loose blankets, quilts, and hats** out of the sleep space in the first year. Feel the **chest or back**, not the hands, to judge warmth. Signs of overheating include sweating, damp hair, flushed cheeks, and a hot chest. On room temperature, sources do not agree on a single number: NHS and Lullaby Trust recommend **16–20°C** (61–68°F); some U.S. pages mention **68–72°F** (20–22°C); the AAP's 2022 safe-sleep policy itself does not set a range. Use a comfortable room, watch the baby, and adjust layers rather than chasing one "perfect" thermostat setting.

### Key numbers at a glance

| Question | What the sources say | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| How many layers? | In general, one more layer than an adult would wear in the same room | AAP / HealthyChildren.org; Sleep Foundation |
| UK room-temperature range | 16–20°C (about 61–68°F) | NHS; Lullaby Trust |
| U.S. figures often quoted | 68–72°F (20–22°C) | HealthyChildren.org "hours of sleep" page; Sleep Foundation discussion of studies |
| Does the 2022 AAP policy set a temperature? | No. It says to dress for the ambient temperature and avoid overheating | Sleep Foundation, summarizing the 2022 policy |
| Hats during indoor sleep | Do not put a hat on your baby indoors once you are home from the hospital | AAP / HealthyChildren.org |
| Sleepwear to have on hand | About four to six pieces is usually enough, because babies grow quickly | Sleep Foundation, citing MedlinePlus |

## Start with the baby, not the thermostat

Babies are not as good as older children at regulating temperature. They also sweat less, which is one reason overheating is treated as a SIDS risk, not just a comfort issue. The AAP's practical test is clothing: if you are comfortable in a long-sleeved shirt, your baby often needs that plus one light layer, not a fleece suit, a swaddle, and a blanket.

A typical starting point:

- **Mild room:** a short- or long-sleeved bodysuit, plus a [sleep sack](/sleep-sacks) if you want a wearable layer.
- **Cooler room:** add a light footed sleeper under the sack, or a slightly heavier sack, not a quilt.
- **Warm room or hot weather:** a single bodysuit, or a very light sack, may be enough. If you are in a T-shirt and still warm, your baby does not need an extra layer on top of that simply because "babies should be bundled."

Sleep Foundation notes that a onesie is often a good base layer, that several thin layers are easier to adjust than one thick garment, and that sleep gowns with an open bottom can make night diaper changes easier. Buttons and ties should be secure; nothing — including a pacifier — should be clipped to clothing with a cord.

## Why the room-temperature numbers disagree

This is worth spelling out, because charts on parenting sites often pick one range and present it as a universal rule.

- **NHS** tells parents not to let a baby get too hot or too cold and to keep the room at **16–20°C**.
- **Lullaby Trust** uses the same **16–20°C** range and suggests a room thermometer.
- A **HealthyChildren.org** article on how much sleep children need says the AAP and other medical organizations recommend avoiding overheating and head covering "and temperatures between 68°F to 72°F for infants and children."
- **Sleep Foundation** (updated 11 June 2026) says some studies have found **68–72°F** comfortable, then immediately adds that **the AAP refrains from providing a specific temperature range** in its policy and instead focuses on dressing for the room. The same article notes that what feels right can depend on local climate, and that strong air-conditioning or heavy winter heating can be unhelpful.

Those ranges overlap only at the warm end of the UK advice and the cool end of the U.S. figures (around 20°C / 68°F). A room at 72°F (22°C) is above the UK range; a room at 16°C (61°F) is below the U.S. figures people often quote. We are not going to declare a winner. If you live with NHS or Lullaby Trust advice, 16–20°C is the range to aim for. If you follow U.S. pediatric material, a mid-to-high 60s to low 70s Fahrenheit room, plus the one-layer rule, is the usual starting point. In both cases, **the baby's chest** is a better guide than the number on the wall.

Place the crib away from radiators, air conditioners, and sunny windows. Sleep Foundation cautions that heating has been studied as a SIDS risk factor, and that a fan, if you use one in warm weather, should not blow directly on the baby. An older California study (Coleman-Phox, Odouli, and Li, 2008) found that fan use at higher room temperatures was associated with a lower SIDS risk; that is one study, not a reason to point a fan at a newborn.

## How to tell if your baby is too hot or too cold

Feel the **chest, back, or tummy**. Hands and feet are often cooler and can fool you into adding a layer the baby does not need.

Sleep Foundation lists common signs of overheating: sweating, damp hair, red or rashy skin, reddened cheeks, quicker breathing, and a chest that is noticeably hot. The AAP similarly flags sweating, a hot chest, and flushed skin. If those appear, remove a layer and cool the room. Do not put a hat on a sleeping baby indoors; hats can contribute to overheating and can slip over the face.

If a baby is too cold, the skin on the chest may feel cool, and they may seem unsettled. Add a light layer or a wearable blanket. Sleep Foundation also lists pale or grey skin, breathing difficulty, limpness, vomiting, poor feeding, and unusual irritability as possible signs of hypothermia — those are medical signs, not a cue to pile on blankets. Seek urgent care if they appear.

If your baby has a fever, ask your pediatrician before you add layers. Over-bundling a feverish baby can make things worse.

## A sweaty head, and a fan in the room

A damp scalp is a common reason parents add — or remove — a layer. Heads shed heat, so a slightly moist hairline is not, by itself, proof that the baby is dangerously hot. Check the **chest or back**, as the section above already says. If that skin is hot, sweaty, or flushed, take off a layer and cool the room. If the chest feels comfortable and the baby is otherwise well, you often need to change nothing. A sweaty head plus fever, unusual sleepiness, or fast breathing belongs in a call to the pediatrician, not in an extra blanket — see [sick baby sleep](/sick-baby-sleep).

A room fan can make a warm room more comfortable. Keep cords out of reach and do not point a strong airflow at a newborn’s face. A fan is **not** a SIDS-prevention device and does not replace the safer-sleep steps on [safe sleep](/safe-sleep-for-babies). For how warm a wearable blanket should feel, including TOG labels, see [sleep sacks](/sleep-sacks).

## Blankets, sleep sacks, swaddles, and what stays out of the crib

For the first year, AAP safe-sleep advice is to keep loose blankets, pillows, quilts, and stuffed toys out of the crib. Warmth should come from clothes or a wearable blanket that cannot ride up over the face. That is the job of a [sleep sack](/sleep-sacks). A [swaddle](/how-to-swaddle-a-baby) is a newborn option only, and it has to stop when rolling starts.

Do not use weighted blankets, weighted sleepers, or weighted swaddles. The AAP and KidsHealth both rule those out.

**TOG ratings** (a measure of how warm a garment is) appear on many sleep-sack labels and in unofficial charts that pair a TOG number with a room temperature. We did not find a TOG table in the AAP, NHS, or Lullaby Trust pages we opened for this article, so we are not reproducing a manufacturer chart here. If a label uses TOG, treat it as a starting hint and still check your baby's chest.

## A word on "keep them warm so they sleep longer"

Comfort matters, but "warmer is sleepier" is not a safe rule. Overheating is one of the SIDS risks the AAP, NHS, and Lullaby Trust all highlight. A slightly cool, steadily dressed baby is the aim, not a flushed, sweaty one who looks "cozy."

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Get in touch if your baby's chest stays very warm or very cool after you change the room and the clothing, if they have a fever, or if they were born early — Sleep Foundation notes that preterm babies can take longer to regulate temperature and may need slightly warmer conditions with close watching for overheating. Call urgently for the hypothermia-type signs listed above, or if breathing looks hard.

## Frequently asked questions

**What should a newborn wear to sleep?**  
Usually a light base layer plus, if the room is not warm, a swaddle or a sleep sack. No loose blanket, no hat indoors, no weighted product.

**Is 72°F too warm?**  
It is inside the 68–72°F band some U.S. sources quote, and it is above the NHS/Lullaby Trust 16–20°C range. If the room is 72°F, dress down (often a single layer) and watch for sweating.

**Can I use a blanket if I watch the baby?**  
For the first year, AAP advice is to skip loose blankets in the sleep space, even when you are nearby. A wearable blanket is the usual alternative.

**How do I dress my baby for sleep in summer?**  
Lighter layers, a cooler room if you can, and extra attention to sweating. A fan in the room may help comfort, but do not aim it at the baby, and do not use it as a reason to ignore the rest of [safe sleep](/safe-sleep-for-babies).

**Are fleece pajamas enough on their own?**  
In a cool room, often yes, sometimes with a light sack. Fleece plus a heavy sack plus a hat is usually too much.

## Log the room and the layers (Yorix)

If you want a record of what you tried, **Yorix** can store sleep times and any symptoms you log (for example, that your baby felt sweaty at 2 a.m.). That can make it easier to see whether a hot night lined up with extra waking. The app does not measure room temperature and is not a medical device.

## Related reading

- [When Can a Baby Sleep With a Blanket or Lovey?](/when-can-baby-sleep-with-a-blanket)

- [Safe sleep for babies](/safe-sleep-for-babies)
- [Sleep sacks](/sleep-sacks)
- [How to swaddle a baby](/how-to-swaddle-a-baby)
- [White noise for baby sleep](/white-noise-for-baby-sleep)
- [Newborn sleep schedule](/newborn-sleep-schedule)
- [How much sleep does a baby need](/how-much-sleep-does-a-baby-need)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026.

1. HealthyChildren.org (AAP). "How to Keep Your Sleeping Baby Safe: AAP Policy Explained." <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/baby/sleep/Pages/A-Parents-Guide-to-Safe-Sleep.aspx>. One extra layer; no hats indoors; no weighted products; wearable blankets instead of loose blankets; overheating signs.
2. HealthyChildren.org (AAP). "Healthy Sleep Habits: How Many Hours Does Your Child Need?" <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/healthy-living/sleep/Pages/healthy-sleep-habits-how-many-hours-does-your-child-need.aspx>. Mentions 68°F to 72°F for infants and children, plus avoiding overheating and head covering.
3. Sleep Foundation. "How to Dress a Baby for Sleep." Updated 13 October 2026. Medically reviewed by Nilong Vyas, MD, MPH. <https://www.sleepfoundation.org/baby-sleep/how-to-dress-baby-for-sleep>.
4. Sleep Foundation. "Ideal Sleeping Temperature for a Baby." Updated 11 June 2026. Medically reviewed by Nilong Vyas, MD, MPH. <https://www.sleepfoundation.org/baby-sleep/best-room-temperature-for-sleeping-baby>. 68–72°F in some studies; AAP policy has no set range; signs of heat and cold; fan study.
5. NHS. "Sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS)." <https://www.nhs.uk/baby/caring-for-a-newborn/sudden-infant-death-syndrome-sids/>. Room temperature 16–20°C.
6. The Lullaby Trust. "Safer sleep advice for babies." Updated 9 October 2026. <https://www.lullabytrust.org.uk/safer-sleep-advice/>. 16–20°C; avoid overheating.
7. Nemours KidsHealth. "Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS)." July 2022. <https://kidshealth.org/en/parents/sids.html>. Dress for the room; no overbundling; no head covering; no weighted products.
8. Coleman-Phox K, Odouli R, Li DK. "Use of a fan during sleep and the risk of sudden infant death syndrome." *Archives of Pediatrics & Adolescent Medicine*, 2008. <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18838649/>.
9. MedlinePlus. "Baby supplies you need." Cited by Sleep Foundation for the four-to-six sleepwear pieces figure. <https://medlineplus.gov/ency/patientinstructions/000541.htm>.

description: How to swaddle a baby safely: a hip-healthy wrap, always on the back, signs of overheating, and when to stop — as soon as your baby tries to roll.
body:
# How to Swaddle a Baby Safely — and When to Stop

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 16, 2026 · **Updated:** November 16, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

Swaddling is a thin wrap that holds a newborn's arms snug and can calm the startle (Moro) reflex. Many families find it useful in the first weeks. It is optional, not a requirement, and it has rules. The two that matter most: keep the wrap **hip-healthy** (legs free to bend up and out), and **stop as soon as your baby shows signs of trying to roll**, which can be as early as 2 months.

## Short answer

If you swaddle, use a light blanket or a commercial wrap, place your baby **on their back** every time, and leave enough room at the hips and knees for the legs to flex and fall open. Do not wrap the chest so tightly that breathing looks strained. Watch for overheating. Do not use a **weighted** swaddle. Stop swaddling at the first attempts to roll — Sleep Foundation notes this may start at 2 months and, for most babies, means stopping by around 3 months — and move to a [sleep sack](/sleep-sacks) with free arms if you still want a wearable layer.

### Key numbers at a glance

| Question | What the sources say | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| When to stop swaddling | As soon as the baby shows signs of trying to roll, which may be as early as 2 months; often around 3 months | Sleep Foundation, citing AAP/NICHD; International Hip Dysplasia Institute (IHDI) |
| Safe sleep position while swaddled | Always on the back | AAP; IHDI; Sleep Foundation |
| Weighted swaddles | Do not use weighted blankets, sleepers, or swaddles | AAP / KidsHealth / Sleep Foundation |
| Arms in or out | Sleep Foundation states this has no impact on safety | Sleep Foundation (updated 13 October 2026) |
| Evidence that swaddling is safer than layered clothes | None found — Sleep Foundation, citing NICHD, says there is no evidence swaddling is safer than dressing in layers | Sleep Foundation / NICHD |

## Why parents swaddle — and what it does not do

A systematic review in *Pediatrics* (van Sleuwen and colleagues, 2007), cited by the IHDI, found that swaddling can reduce crying and help some infants settle. Sleep Foundation adds that it may calm some babies, but **it is not a SIDS-prevention method**. NICHD, as quoted there, says there is no evidence that swaddling is any safer than dressing a baby in ordinary layered sleepwear. If your baby sleeps well without a wrap, you do not need to start.

Swaddling also adds heat. That is useful in a cool room and a risk in a warm one. Combine this page with [how to dress a baby for sleep](/how-to-dress-baby-for-sleep) and the [safe sleep](/safe-sleep-for-babies) checklist rather than treating the wrap as a complete sleep plan.

## Hip-healthy wrapping: the rule that is easy to miss

Improper swaddling is a known risk for **developmental dysplasia of the hip**. The International Hip Dysplasia Institute's position is specific: infant hips should sit in slight flexion and abduction during swaddling. The knees should also be slightly flexed. The legs must not be tightly wrapped straight down and pressed together, as if the baby were standing at attention. That "straight down" position can loosen the joints and damage the soft cartilage of the socket.

In practice:

- After you wrap the arms and chest, leave a loose pouch for the legs so they can bend up and fall out, the way they sat in the womb.
- Commercial swaddles should have a loose sack or pouch for the legs and feet. Even some products can confine the thighs if you pull the fastening too tight — the IHDI warns about this.
- An alternative, also endorsed by the IHDI, is to swaddle only the upper body and leave the legs completely free.

The IHDI describes one common method: fold a square cloth to make a straight edge; place the baby's shoulders at that edge; wrap one side over the arm and chest and tuck; repeat on the other side; then twist or fold the bottom and tuck it behind the baby **only after** you have left the legs bent up and out. Watch a clinician or a trusted video if you are unsure — a written list is easier to get tight at the hips than you think.

## How to swaddle without making breathing or heat worse

Sleep Foundation's safety points, which track AAP advice, are:

- **Back only.** A swaddled baby who ends up face-down cannot easily roll back. That is the core danger once rolling starts, and it is why a belly-sleeping swaddle is never acceptable.
- **Not too tight across the chest.** A baby who struggles to breathe, or whose chest cannot rise easily, is wrapped too tightly.
- **Light fabric.** A thin muslin or a purpose-made wrap is enough. Thick quilts trap heat and add loose fabric if they come undone.
- **Watch for overheating:** sweating, damp hair, flushed or red cheeks, skin that is hot to the touch, or quicker breathing. If you see those signs, loosen or stop the swaddle and remove a layer. See the dressing article for more on temperature.
- **No weighted products.** The AAP, KidsHealth, and Sleep Foundation all advise against weighted swaddles and weighted blankets. Evidence on their safety is limited, and the extra weight may make it harder for a baby to breathe or may add heat.

If the wrap comes loose, it becomes loose bedding, which does not belong in a safe crib. Re-wrap or switch to a zip or velcro swaddle sack that stays put — still with a loose hip pouch.

## When to stop, and how to come out of the swaddle

Stop when your baby starts **trying to roll**, not on a birthday. Sleep Foundation says this may begin at 2 months and that for most babies swaddling should stop around 3 months. The IHDI adds that once a baby can roll onto their stomach, a swaddle increases the risk of ending up face-down.

A simple transition many families use, described across baby-sleep sites and consistent with the "arms can be in or out" safety note:

1. One arm out for a few days, then both arms out, still using a sack for the legs if you like.
2. Or go straight to a [sleep sack](/sleep-sacks) with free arms, which is the AAP's preferred wearable blanket once the wrap is gone.
3. Expect a few bumpier nights. That is a reason to change at the start of a calmer stretch of days, not during illness or a [sleep regression](/sleep-regression), if you can help it.

If your baby has started rolling and you are still swaddling, stop at the next sleep. Do not wait for a "perfect" moment.

## “Wrapping,” the startle (Moro), and arms-up sleep

In Australia and the UK, **wrapping** is the usual word for the same skill this page calls swaddling. Red Nose, Raising Children Network, and Karitane wrapping advice follow the same safety limits already here: hips free to bend, chest not tight, no hood, and **stop once the baby can roll**. Use this page’s how-to.

A newborn’s **Moro (startle) reflex** can jerk the arms and briefly wake a baby, including as they drop into light sleep. That reflex is ordinary, and it fades over the early months. Swaddling is sometimes used to make those jerks less of a full wake — it is not a treatment for a diagnosis, and it is not a reason to wrap past the rolling deadline already in the section above.

**Arms-up** (or one arm out) is a common way to come out of the wrap, already listed in the transition steps above. Some babies sleep more happily with hands free or near the face. That is a transition, not a new method. If startle-waking is really a short cycle at the end of a nap, see [baby sleep cycles](/baby-sleep-cycles) and [false starts](/false-starts) rather than tightening the wrap.

## What if my baby hates the swaddle?

Some newborns arch, cry, or work their arms free every time. That is allowed. Swaddling is a tool, not a test you have to pass. Try arms-out, a looser hip pouch, or skip the wrap and use a sleep sack or ordinary layers instead. Soothing with holding, feeding, or a [pacifier](/pacifier-and-sleep) is still available. If your baby seems in pain when the hips are moved, or one leg looks to sit differently from the other, raise that with your pediatrician — those are hip questions, not "fussy swaddle" questions.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Ask before you swaddle if your baby was premature, has a respiratory problem, or has a known hip concern. Ask promptly if you notice uneven thigh creases, limited hip movement, or a clicking hip, or if you are unsure whether rolling attempts have started. And if a wrap ever seems to make breathing harder, take it off and get medical advice.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is swaddling safe?**  
It can be, for a non-rolling baby on their back, in a light, hip-healthy wrap, with no extra loose bedding and no added weights. It is not safer than simple layers, and it becomes unsafe once rolling starts.

**When should I stop swaddling?**  
At the first signs that your baby is trying to roll, which can be as early as 2 months.

**Can I swaddle with arms out?**  
Yes. Sleep Foundation says arms in or out does not change safety. Arms-out is also a useful step when you are stopping.

**Can I swaddle at daycare or with a grandparent?**  
Only if every caregiver knows the back-only rule and the stop-when-rolling rule. A wrap that is safe at 6 weeks can be unsafe at 10 weeks in someone else's care if the baby has started to roll.

**Are velcro or zip swaddle sacks better than a blanket?**  
They can stay in place more reliably, which reduces loose fabric. They still need a loose hip pouch, a light fabric, back sleeping, and a hard stop at rolling.

**Can I use a swaddle and a loose blanket together?**  
No. The wrap replaces the blanket. A second covering adds the loose-bedding risk that [safe sleep](/safe-sleep-for-babies) advice is trying to remove.

## See when rolling starts (Yorix)

**Yorix** can log sleeps and the signs you notice — for example, that your baby rolled in a nap or seemed too warm. That record is a memory aid for you and for whoever you ask about timing the swaddle-to-sack change. It is not a medical device and it cannot tell you that a wrap is safe.

## Related reading

- [The 5 S's for Soothing a Crying Baby (Product-Neutral)](/5-s-soothing-a-crying-baby)
- [Baby Sleeping on the Stomach: When It Is and Isn't Safe](/baby-sleeping-on-stomach)
- [Baby Won't Sleep in the Bassinet or Crib](/baby-wont-sleep-in-crib)

- [Safe sleep for babies](/safe-sleep-for-babies)
- [Sleep sacks](/sleep-sacks)
- [How to dress a baby for sleep](/how-to-dress-baby-for-sleep)
- [Newborn sleep schedule](/newborn-sleep-schedule)
- [1 month old sleep schedule](/1-month-old-sleep-schedule)
- [2 month old sleep schedule](/2-month-old-sleep-schedule)
- [White noise for baby sleep](/white-noise-for-baby-sleep)
- [Contact naps](/contact-naps)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026.

1. Sleep Foundation. "How to Dress a Baby for Sleep." Updated 13 October 2026. Medically reviewed by Nilong Vyas, MD, MPH. <https://www.sleepfoundation.org/baby-sleep/how-to-dress-baby-for-sleep>. Swaddling section: optional, not safer than layers (NICHD), stop at rolling (as early as 2 months, often around 3), back only, not too tight, no weighted swaddles, arms in or out.
2. International Hip Dysplasia Institute. "Hip-Healthy Swaddling" and position statement. <https://hipdysplasia.org/infant-child/hip-healthy-swaddling/>. Legs flexed and abducted, not wrapped straight down; commercial sacks need a loose pouch; back sleeping; stop if the baby can roll to the stomach.
3. van Sleuwen BE, et al. "Swaddling: a systematic review." *Pediatrics*, 2007;120:e1097–e1106. Cited by the IHDI for calming and sleep effects.
4. HealthyChildren.org (AAP). "How to Keep Your Sleeping Baby Safe: AAP Policy Explained." <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/baby/sleep/Pages/A-Parents-Guide-to-Safe-Sleep.aspx>. Wearable blankets as a blanket alternative; no weighted blankets, sleepers, or swaddles; back sleeping; one extra layer.
5. Nemours KidsHealth. "Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS)." Date reviewed July 2022. <https://kidshealth.org/en/parents/sids.html>. No weighted blankets, sleepers, or swaddles.
6. Moon RY, et al. "Sleep-Related Infant Deaths: Updated 2022 Recommendations." *Pediatrics*, 2022. <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35726558/>.
7. Sleep Foundation. "How Much Do Newborns Sleep?" Updated 30 September 2026. <https://www.sleepfoundation.org/baby-sleep/how-much-do-newborns-sleep>. Swaddle only until the baby has learned to roll, usually around 3 months; always on the back.

# Naps on the Go: Stroller, Car, and Wrap — Lifestyle, Then a Flat Surface

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 16, 2026 · **Updated:** November 16, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

This is a **lifestyle** page: the nap that happens in a stroller, a parked or moving car, or a wrap while you are out. It is not [is it safe for a baby to sleep in a car seat](/baby-sleeping-in-car-seat), which is the "can they stay there" safety explainer — use that page for sitting-device risk and unsupervised time. It is not [contact naps](/contact-naps) (the sofa or arms at home). It is not [baby sleep and travel](/baby-sleep-and-travel) (time zones and hotel rooms). Cross-link those; do not rewrite them.

## Short answer

An occasional motion nap is how many days out actually work. The rule that does *not* loosen is the surface when you can change it. CPSC's Safe Sleep "dos" include this, in plain words: **move your baby to their crib, bassinet, play yard, or bedside sleeper if they fall asleep elsewhere.** The AAP's 2022 policy is in the same family: sitting and sitting-style products are not a regular sleep space; when a baby falls asleep in a car seat, stroller, swing, or similar, move them to a firm, flat surface as soon as it is practical.

A wrap or sling while you are awake and watching is a carrying tool, not a crib. The Lullaby Trust points families to the Consortium **TICKS** checks: tight, in view at all times, close enough to kiss, chin off the chest, supported back. They also say "hands-free" feeding in a sling is unsafe, especially under four months. This page does not treat a sling as an approved overnight bed.

If *every* nap only happens on the move, you are in a pattern, not a one-off errand. That can still be a season. It becomes a problem when you cannot transfer at all, or when the "nap" is an unsupervised seat in a hallway or a parked car. For the transfer practice, [contact naps](/contact-naps) is the closer how-to.

### Occasional outing versus everyday motion nap

| Situation | Reasonable? | Do this |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stroller nap on a walk, you are with the buggy | Often, as a day out | Keep the face visible, chin off the chest; on arrival, move to a flat approved surface (CPSC; AAP 2022) |
| Car nap *during a journey* | The trip is the reason for the seat | The seat is for travel. When you arrive, move the baby — do not leave them in a parked car or in a seat indoors. Details: [car-seat sleep](/baby-sleeping-in-car-seat) |
| Supervised wrap or sling, you are awake | Carrying, not a bed | TICKS; no hands-free feed; transfer when you stop (Lullaby Trust; CPSC "fell asleep elsewhere") |
| Every nap, every day, only in motion | A pattern to watch | Work on one crib or flat-surface nap, as on the contact-nap and [won't nap](/baby-wont-nap) pages |
| Baby left to nap in a seat, swing, or parked car | No | Not a sleep space (CPSC: no unsupervised time in products not designed for sleep) |

## Stroller, car, and wrap, in that order

**Stroller.** A walk that produces a nap is common. Stay with the child. Watch the head: a chin on the chest is the same airway problem the car-seat page explains, and we will not repeat the anatomy here. When you get home or to a friend's house, transfer to the approved flat surface. A stroller is not a spare crib for an unattended hour in another room.

**Car.** If the baby falls asleep on the way, finish the journey, then move them. Do not extend the drive only to "protect the nap," and do not carry the seat inside as a bed. Those points live on the car-seat page; this page only adds the lifestyle frame: a travel nap is not a scheduling method.

**Wrap or sling.** You can wear a sleeping baby if you can see the face, keep the airway open, and stay awake. That is TICKS, not a loophole in safe sleep. When you sit down or finish the outing, CPSC's "move them if they fell asleep elsewhere" still applies. A sling overnight, or a sling on a parent's chest while the parent sleeps, is not what this page is defending — [bed-sharing](/bed-sharing-and-co-sleeping) and [safe sleep](/safe-sleep-for-babies) cover adult-bed and surface rules.

Day-to-day totals still come from [how much sleep a baby needs](/how-much-sleep-does-a-baby-need). A short motion nap may need an earlier bedtime, the same idea as on [short naps](/short-naps) and the daycare page.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Ask if motion is the only way your baby will sleep and you cannot transfer them, if you are worried about the airway in a seat or carrier, or if total sleep is regularly short.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is a stroller nap safe?**  
It can be, if you are present, the face is clear, and you move the baby to a flat, approved surface when you can. It is not a substitute crib.

**What if they only sleep in the car?**  
Use the car for journeys. Practice one nap at home on a flat surface. The safety "can they stay in the seat" question is answered on the [car-seat page](/baby-sleeping-in-car-seat).

**Can they nap in a wrap all afternoon?**  
Not as an unsupervised or all-afternoon bed. Supervised carrying with TICKS is one thing; a sleep surface is another.

**Can a baby nap in a swing, bouncer, or "only if I am watching"?**
Use the same move-to-a-safe-sleep-space rule as [baby sleeping in a car seat](/baby-sleeping-in-car-seat). Supervised does not make an incline safe for sleep.

## See which naps actually happened on the go (Yorix)

**Yorix** can help you tag whether a nap was in the crib, the stroller, or the car, so you can see how often motion is doing the work. The app cannot judge a carrier fit and is not a medical device.

## Related reading

- [Baby sleeping in a car seat](/baby-sleeping-in-car-seat)
- [Contact naps](/contact-naps)
- [Safe sleep for babies](/safe-sleep-for-babies)
- [Baby sleep and travel](/baby-sleep-and-travel)
- [Baby won't nap](/baby-wont-nap)
- [Short naps](/short-naps)
- [Daycare and baby sleep](/daycare-and-baby-sleep)
- [Bed-sharing and co-sleeping](/bed-sharing-and-co-sleeping)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026.

1. U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission. "Safe Sleep – Cribs and Infant Products." Accessed 15 November 2026. Move the baby to a crib, bassinet, play yard, or bedside sleeper if they fall asleep elsewhere; do not leave a baby unsupervised in products not designed for sleep; sitting or inclined products over 10° are not for infant sleep. <https://www.cpsc.gov/SafeSleep>.
2. Moon RY, et al. AAP 2022 safe-sleep policy. Sitting devices (car seats, strollers, swings, and similar) are not recommended for routine sleep; move the infant to a firm, flat surface as soon as practical. <https://publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article/150/1/e2022057990/188304/Sleep-Related-Infant-Deaths-Updated-2022>.
3. The Lullaby Trust. "Baby slings and carriers." Accessed 15 November 2026. TICKS: Tight, In view at all times, Close enough to kiss, Keep chin off the chest, Supported back. "Hands-free" feeding in a sling is unsafe, especially under four months, and for pre-term or unwell babies. <https://www.lullabytrust.org.uk/baby-safety/baby-product-information/slings-and-carriers/>.

title: Newborn Day-Night Confusion: How to Reset It | Yorix

description: Why newborns mix up days and nights, how long day-night reversal usually lasts, and a simple light-and-dark plan for the first 8 weeks. Sourced advice.
body:
# Newborn Day-Night Confusion: How to Reset It

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 16, 2026 · **Updated:** November 16, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

A baby who is wide awake from 11 p.m. to 4 a.m. and then sleeps hard at mid-morning is following a well-known newborn pattern: **day-night confusion**, sometimes called day-night reversal. This page is the 0- to 8-week "days and nights are backwards" plan. It is not a second copy of our [newborn sleep schedule](/newborn-sleep-schedule); that article has an example day and wake-window ranges. Here we focus on why the clock feels inverted, and what actually shifts it.

## Short answer

Newborns are not born with a working sense of day and night. KidsHealth is blunt: they have no day/night sense yet, and they wake often to feed. HealthyChildren.org's article on reversing day-night reversal (Jana and Shu) calls the mix-up **temporary**, with no quick fix. The consistent advice from NHS, HealthyChildren.org, and KidsHealth is contrast: **bright, ordinary household light and play by day; dim, quiet, boring care at night.** Most families see nights lengthen over the first weeks as the baby's circadian rhythm starts to settle — not overnight after one "trick."

### Key numbers at a glance

| Question | What the sources say | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Do newborns know day from night? | Not yet | KidsHealth; NHS |
| Is there a quick reset? | No. The pattern is temporary; contrast helps | HealthyChildren.org (Jana & Shu, 2009) |
| Night feeds in the first weeks | Often every 2–3 hours, or about 8–12 feeds in 24 hours | NHS; CDC (feeding context) |
| When longer night stretches may be allowed | KidsHealth: after good weight gain, often after the first couple of weeks, you may not need to wake for every stretch — ask your pediatrician | KidsHealth |
| When "drowsy but awake" is usually introduced | HealthyChildren.org often mentions around 4 months, which is later than this problem | HealthyChildren.org |

## Why days and nights get swapped

Before birth, babies often nap during the day (when you were walking around) and become more active at night. After birth, their body clock is immature. Sleep Foundation's cycle article and KidsHealth both describe frequent, evenly spread sleep rather than a long night and a defined day. Add cluster feeding in the evening, and you can get a baby who "saves" a long stretch for 9 a.m.

This is usually not a sign you have already created a bad habit. It is an immature clock plus a small stomach.

## The contrast plan (no fancy schedule required)

HealthyChildren.org (Jana and Shu) and NHS "Helping your baby to sleep" describe the same contrast, which you can start from the first days at home:

**By day**

- Open curtains. Ordinary daylight is the cue. A short morning walk, weather allowing, adds more.
- Keep the house at a normal daytime volume. You do not have to tiptoe around naps.
- During awake stretches, talk, change, and play a little. Even a newborn benefits from the difference between "day" and "night" handling.
- If they are still asleep when a feed is due in the early weeks, [waking them to eat](/should-you-wake-a-sleeping-baby) may be what your pediatrician wants. That is a growth issue, not a sleep-training issue.

**By night**

- Dim lights. A small lamp is enough for a safe diaper change and feed.
- Keep voices low. No play, no extra burbling "hello" unless you need it.
- Do the feed and the change, then put them back in their [safe sleep space](/safe-sleep-for-babies) in your room.
- Do not start a long, bright "awake window" at 2 a.m. because they look alert. The goal is to make night dull.

There is no evidence-based 3-day "reset" clock we can quote from AAP or NHS. Be suspicious of plans that promise a flipped baby by Friday.

## What not to do

- Do not keep the baby up all day in the hope that exhaustion will create a night. An [overtired baby](/overtired-baby) often sleeps worse, not better.
- Do not darken the room for every daytime nap in the first weeks as if it were a 6-month-old's nursery. Day sleep can happen in ordinary light.
- Do not skip nighttime feeds to "teach" a longer stretch. In the early weeks, feeding comes first. See [should you wake a sleeping baby](/should-you-wake-a-sleeping-baby) and, later, [night weaning](/night-weaning).
- Do not treat this as a reason to [bed-share](/bed-sharing-and-co-sleeping) on a sofa because you are tired of the 2 a.m. party. Keep the baby on their own firm, flat surface in your room.

## How long does it last?

HealthyChildren.org calls day-night reversal temporary. Many parents notice a clearer "night" by 6 to 8 weeks, but we did not find a single official week-by-week deadline in AAP or NHS materials, so treat that window as a common experience, not a guarantee. If at 2 or 3 months the baby is still systematically wide awake all night and asleep all day, mention it at a checkup — and check that daytime light exposure is actually happening.

A more mature night, in the research sense of a longer stretch, is covered in [when babies sleep through the night](/when-do-babies-sleep-through-the-night). That is a later milestone than fixing a backwards clock.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Ask how long you should keep waking for feeds, especially if your baby was preterm, is not back to birth weight, or has a jaundice or blood-sugar plan. Get help sooner if the baby is very hard to wake for those daytime feeds, has fewer wet diapers, or seems unwell, not merely "nocturnal."

## Frequently asked questions

**Why is my newborn awake all night and asleep all day?**  
Their body clock is immature, and some babies keep a "party at night, sleep in the day" pattern for a few weeks. Light by day and boredom by night help it turn.

**How do I fix newborn day-night confusion?**  
Contrast, consistently, not a one-night crash-and-reset. There is no instant official protocol.

**Should I wake them from long daytime naps?**  
Sometimes, in the early weeks, if a long day sleep is crowding out a needed feed or pushing all the "awake" time into the night. Ask your pediatrician what length is too long for *your* baby. See [should you wake a sleeping baby](/should-you-wake-a-sleeping-baby).

**Will a stricter schedule help at 2 weeks?**  
A loose pattern of eat, play, sleep is enough. A minute-by-minute timetable is more than a newborn can follow. Use our [newborn sleep schedule](/newborn-sleep-schedule) as a map, not a test.

**Is this the same as a sleep regression?**  
No. Regressions are discussed later, often around 3–4 months, when [sleep cycles](/baby-sleep-cycles) reorganize. Day-night confusion is a first-weeks clock problem.

## See which hours are actually flipped (Yorix)

**Yorix** can show a 24-hour log of sleep and feeds, which makes a "long morning nap, long night wake" pattern obvious. The app cannot reset a body clock and is not a medical device. Use the log alongside your pediatrician's feeding plan.

## Related reading

- [2 Week Old Baby Sleep: Pieces, Feeds, and 'Sleeping All Day'](/2-week-old-baby-sleep)
- [8 Week Old Baby Sleep: When the Clock Stirs and Naps Stay Short](/8-week-old-baby-sleep)

- [Baby Sleep Cues: How to Read Sleepy Signs](/baby-sleep-cues)
- [Night Lights and Baby Sleep: Color Claims, and What We Can Source](/night-lights-and-baby-sleep)
- [Preemie Sleep: Use Due Date, Not Just Birthday](/preemie-sleep)

- [Newborn sleep schedule](/newborn-sleep-schedule)
- [Should you wake a sleeping baby](/should-you-wake-a-sleeping-baby)
- [How much sleep a baby needs](/how-much-sleep-does-a-baby-need)
- [Baby sleep cycles](/baby-sleep-cycles)
- [Bedtime routine for baby](/bedtime-routine-for-baby)
- [Safe sleep for babies](/safe-sleep-for-babies)
- [When do babies sleep through the night](/when-do-babies-sleep-through-the-night)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026.

1. HealthyChildren.org (AAP). "Reversing Day-Night Reversal." By Laura A. Jana, MD, FAAP, and Jennifer Shu, MD, FAAP. Last updated 11/2/2009. <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/baby/sleep/Pages/Reversing-Day-Night-Reversal.aspx>. Temporary; lights and activity by day; calm, dark, focused care at night; no quick fix.
2. NHS. "Helping your baby to sleep." <https://www.nhs.uk/baby/caring-for-a-newborn/helping-your-baby-to-sleep/>. Day versus night contrast; room-share at least 6 months.
3. Nemours KidsHealth. "Sleep and Your Newborn." <https://kidshealth.org/en/parents/sleepnewborn.html>. No day/night sense yet; frequent feeds; after good weight gain, longer night stretches may be allowed.
4. HealthyChildren.org (AAP). "Getting Your Baby to Sleep." <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/baby/sleep/Pages/Getting-Your-Baby-to-Sleep.aspx>. Night care stays calm and boring; drowsy but awake is a later skill.
5. CDC. "How Much and How Often to Breastfeed." <https://www.cdc.gov/breastfeeding/php/guidelines-recommendations/how-much-and-how-often.html>. Frequent 24-hour feeding in the early weeks (context for why nights stay broken).

description: Night lights and baby sleep: dim light for night cares, what child studies say about color, and why infant-specific red-light rules are not settled.
body:
# Night Lights and Baby Sleep: Color Claims, and What We Can Source

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 16, 2026 · **Updated:** November 16, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

This is a **light-at-night** page: how bright the room should be for a 2 a.m. feed, what we can actually cite about color, and how to treat projectors. It is not [fear of the dark](/fear-of-the-dark), which already allows a dim lamp as comfort and deliberately left color science to a later, sourced article — this one. It is not [white noise](/white-noise-for-baby-sleep). It does not retell the bedtime-routine or toddler-fear plans.

## Short answer

A **dim** lamp for a night change or feed is ordinary, practical advice. Sleep Foundation suggests using a nightlight instead of the overhead light, and, in the newborn period, a **red bulb** so the caregiver can see. That is their wording, and it is about *you* being able to work without flooding the room. It is **not** an infant clinical trial, and their claim that newborns "cannot see the red light waves" should be read as a popular-science shorthand, not as a proven law of infant vision. We mark that part as **unverified as a developmental fact**.

Color-of-light research that *is* published is mostly in **children and preschoolers, not young infants**. A 2018 study of children (mean age 8.9 years) found greater melatonin suppression under 6200 K light than under 3000 K, a difference that did not reach significance in the adult group. A 2026 laboratory paper on 25 consumer nightlights reported that, at the product itself, only 3 of 25 stayed consistently under a 5 lx melanopic-EDI threshold used as a pediatric sleep benchmark; in a typical-use setup, 14 of 25 could get under that 5 lx mark on at least one setting, usually when they were red-toned, dim, and farther from the bed. Those authors recommend dim red or amber, off the direct line of sight, and away from the bed when you can. That is a product-measurement paper, not a night-long trial in cribs.

The AAP's Center of Excellence Q&A on light projectors (December 2025) is clearer on *brightness and duration* than on a required hue: **avoid bright light as bedtime approaches**; keep a projector to a **brief** settle (they give 15–20 minutes as an example), not hours; evening bright, cool-toned artificial light can suppress melatonin. They also say there is **no research** that treats a galaxy projector as the same thing as tablet or TV screen time.

### What we can source — and what we cannot

| Claim | What we can say | Caveat |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dim is better than overhead at 2 a.m. | Sleep Foundation; AAP "avoid bright light close to bedtime" | Intensity matters more than brand |
| Red or amber is "required for babies" | **Not established** as an infant rule | Child and preschool studies, plus a 2026 product paper, support *lower melanopic / warmer* light in older children; do not treat that as a crib-specific law |
| Newborns cannot see red | Sleep Foundation's phrase | **Unverified** as a vision fact on this page |
| Projectors can run all night | AAP: brief soothing, not hours | Not the same evidence base as "screen time," and they say so |
| Any night light is harmless | 2026 paper: many products are bright at the source | Placement and the dimmest setting matter |

## How to use a light, practically

- For a night feed or diaper, keep the room as dim as you can still work in. That is the Sleep Foundation night-care point, and it is enough even if you never buy a "baby" lamp.
- If you want a warmer color, red or amber at the *lowest* setting, out of the baby's direct gaze and farther from the sleep surface, matches what the 2026 product paper found was more likely to stay under their 5 lx melanopic threshold. Many of those dim settings, the authors noted, would not actually help *you* see well.
- Do not aim a bright, cool, or flashing projector at the crib as all-night scenery. If a projector helps a short wind-down, treat it like the AAP's brief-soothe example and turn it down or off for sleep.
- A comfort lamp for a toddler who is afraid of the dark still belongs on the [fear of the dark](/fear-of-the-dark) page: dim, not a second daytime. Color choice can follow the child-study caution above; it is not a different protocol.

There is no CPSC or AAP product standard that certifies a night light as "safe for infant circadian biology." Check only that the object itself cannot fall into the crib or overheat on a sheet — the bare-crib rule on [safe sleep](/safe-sleep-for-babies) still applies.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Ask if you are using a bright lamp all night because the baby seems unable to settle in dim light, or if you have a concern about vision, jaundice follow-up, or a preemie's lighting plan (those are clinical questions; see [preemie sleep](/preemie-sleep)).

## Frequently asked questions

**Is a red night light best for a baby?**  
Warmer, dimmer light is the better-supported direction in *children*. We do not have an infant trial that makes red mandatory. Sleep Foundation's red-bulb tip is for the caregiver during newborn night cares.

**Can I leave a galaxy projector on until morning?**  
The AAP Q&A's recommendation is a short settle, not hours. Bright, cool evening light is the part they warn against.

**Will a night light stop early waking?**  
Unlikely, if the room is already dim. Early waking has its own page: [early morning waking](/early-morning-waking).

## Log whether the room stayed dim (Yorix)

**Yorix** can help you note a rough bedtime and whether a night waking turned into a long, brightly lit stretch. The app cannot measure light and is not a medical device.

## Related reading

- [Melatonin and Children's Sleep: Not a Do-It-Yourself Sleeping Pill](/melatonin-and-childrens-sleep)

- [Fear of the dark](/fear-of-the-dark)
- [Safe sleep for babies](/safe-sleep-for-babies)
- [White noise for baby sleep](/white-noise-for-baby-sleep)
- [Bedtime routine for baby](/bedtime-routine-for-baby)
- [Newborn day-night confusion](/newborn-day-night-confusion)
- [Preemie sleep](/preemie-sleep)
- [Early morning waking](/early-morning-waking)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026.

1. Sleep Foundation. "Babies and Sleep." Accessed 15 November 2026. Use a nightlight rather than overhead lighting for night cares; they suggest a red bulb in the newborn period so the caregiver can see (their wording that newborns "cannot see the red light waves" is reported, not independently verified here). <https://www.sleepfoundation.org/baby-sleep>.
2. American Academy of Pediatrics, Center of Excellence on Social Media and Youth Mental Health. "Light Projectors and Screentime in Infants." Dated 3 December 2025; accessed 15 November 2026. No research equating projectors with tablet or TV screen time; brief 15–20 minute settle is not a problem; avoid bright light close to bedtime; evening bright cool-toned artificial light can suppress melatonin; projectors should not run for hours. <https://www.aap.org/en/patient-care/media-and-children/center-of-excellence-on-social-media-and-youth-mental-health/qa-portal/qa-portal-library/qa-portal-library-questions/light-projectors-and-screentime-in-infants/>.
3. Lee SI, Matsumori K, Nishimura K, et al. "Melatonin suppression and sleepiness in children exposed to blue- and red-enriched light." *Physiological Reports*, 2018. Children (mean 8.9 years) showed greater melatonin suppression at 6200 K than at 3000 K; the same color-temperature contrast was not significant in adults. This is a school-age sample, not infants. <https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5899906/>.
4. Glickman GL, Rothstein-Epp R, Binkowski K, et al. "Quantifying the biological impacts of nightlights: implications for sleep and circadian health in children." *npj Biological Timing and Sleep*, 2026. Twenty-five consumer nightlights; at the source, only 3/25 stayed consistently below 5 lx melanopic EDI; in typical use, 14/25 could do so on at least one setting, mostly dim red-toned units placed farther from the bed. Authors recommend dim red or amber, off the line of sight. Not an infant sleep trial. <https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13046988/>.

title: Night Terrors vs Nightmares: How to Tell Them Apart | Yorix
heading: Night Terrors vs Nightmares: How to Tell Them Apart
description: Night terrors vs nightmares: how they differ, what to do in the moment, when not to wake your child, and when to call the doctor. NHS and AAP advice.
body:
# Night Terrors vs Nightmares: How to Tell Them Apart

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 16, 2026 · **Updated:** November 16, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

A screaming child at 10 p.m. can look like a nightmare, a tantrum, or something medical. **Night terrors** and **nightmares** are different events, at different times of night, and they need different responses. This page is not a second [night-wakings](/survive-night-wakings-new-parents) guide, and it is not the same as a baby [crying in their sleep](/baby-crying-in-sleep) during ordinary active sleep.

## Short answer

**Nightmares** are scary dreams. The child usually wakes, can often remember the dream, and wants comfort. HealthyChildren.org says they can start as early as 6 months and tend to peak between 3 and 12 years, often in the **second half of the night**. **Night terrors** happen in deep, non-dream sleep, usually **early in the night**. The child may scream, thrash, look terrified, and not recognize you — and typically **will not remember** it in the morning. HealthyChildren.org says they occur most often in toddlers and preschoolers; the NHS says they are most common between ages 3 and 8. Do **not** try to wake a child from a night terror (NHS: they may get more upset). Stay calm, keep them safe, and wait it out. If episodes happen at the same time each night, the NHS suggests waking them 15 minutes beforehand, every night for two weeks.

### Key numbers at a glance

| Feature | Night terrors | Nightmares |
| --- | --- | --- |
| When in the night | Early, often in the first few hours (deep sleep) | Later, second half of the night (dream sleep) |
| Is the child awake? | Appears distressed but is not truly awake; may not recognize you | Wakes and can usually be comforted |
| Memory the next day | Typically none | Often can recall the dream |
| How long? | NHS: up to 15 minutes. HealthyChildren.org: can last as long as 45 minutes, though most are much shorter. We are not picking one "correct" outer limit. | Until the child settles after waking |
| Common ages | NHS: most common at 3–8 years. HealthyChildren.org: most often toddlers and preschoolers | HealthyChildren.org: may start at 6 months; peak 3–12 years |

## What a night terror looks like

HealthyChildren.org lists: uncontrollable crying, sweating, shaking or fast breathing, a terrified, confused, or glassy-eyed look, thrashing, screaming, kicking or staring, not realizing you are there, and pushing you away if you try to hold them. After it ends, most children fall straight back to sleep because they were never really awake.

Night terrors can run in families and often travel with [sleepwalking](#sleepwalking-and-sleep-talking). Being very tired, unwell, or off schedule can make them more likely (NHS). They are frightening to watch and usually harmless to the child.

## What to do in the moment

**For a night terror** (NHS and HealthyChildren.org, compiled):

- Stay calm. Your job is safety, not a conversation.
- Do not try to wake them. Do not shake them, turn on bright lights, or insist they "snap out of it."
- Make sure they cannot fall, hit furniture, or leave the room unsafely. HealthyChildren.org: if they try to get out of bed, gently restrain them. NHS: do not try to stop them moving unless there is a risk of injury.
- Tell babysitters what a night terror looks like and what not to do.
- If the same clock time keeps triggering it, try the NHS scheduled-waking plan (15 minutes before, nightly for two weeks), and mention it to your pediatrician.

**For a nightmare** (HealthyChildren.org):

- Go in promptly. Reassure them that they are safe and that dreams are not real.
- Let them tell you about it if they want to. A dim light is fine if it helps.
- When they are ready, help them back to sleep. Look for an obvious scare in the room, such as a shadow, and fix it.

A consistent, calming [bedtime routine](/bedtime-routine-for-baby), enough total sleep (see [how much sleep a baby needs](/how-much-sleep-does-a-baby-need) and the [2-year](/2-year-old-sleep-schedule) or preschool ranges), and less late-evening screen time all reduce the "overtired or overstimulated" fuel that both problems share.

## Sleepwalking and sleep talking

HealthyChildren.org groups these with night terrors as deep-sleep events. The child may have a blank stare, not respond, and be hard to wake. Most return to bed on their own and do not remember it. Do not try to wake them; gently lead them back. Clear trip hazards, block stairs, and lock outside doors. Sleepwalking can run in families.

## Nightmares — what to do when they wake

Nightmares are scary dreams. As the table above already says, the child usually **wakes**, often later in the night, can often **remember** the dream, and wants comfort. HealthyChildren.org: they may start as early as 6 months and tend to peak between 3 and 12 years. Caring for Kids: talk calmly, cuddle, and reassure; do **not** “search for monsters.” Tell a preschooler, simply, that it was a dream. A brief, boring return to their own bed is the goal, not a new every-night sleepover in yours unless you are choosing that for other reasons (see [fear of the dark](/fear-of-the-dark) and [toddler won't stay in bed](/toddler-wont-stay-in-bed)).

If the same nightmare keeps coming back after a frightening event, or the child cannot settle night after night, talk to the pediatrician. Recurring, very distressing dreams are a reason to ask, not a reason to invent a new diagnosis on this page.

**Sleep talking** (murmurs, odd sentences, even a short shout) often happens in the same family of partial arousals as walking or terrors, or in lighter dream sleep. It is usually harmless and not remembered. You do not need to wake the child or have a conversation. Mention it at a visit if it is new, very frequent, or comes with snoring, unusual daytime sleepiness, or other changes. Confusional arousals (looking awake but not making sense, often early in the night) stay on this page with terrors and walking; they are not a new URL.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

The NHS suggests seeing a GP if nightmares continue after age 6, are frequent, or follow a frightening event; if night terrors **start after age 5**; or if they **continue after age 12**. HealthyChildren.org is less age-specific and says to talk with the doctor if night terrors keep happening. Use the lower bar if you are worried: frequent, violent, or injurious episodes, breathing pauses or loud snoring between events, or a child who seems unusually sleepy by day all deserve a medical look. This page cannot tell a night terror from a seizure; that is a clinician's job.

## Frequently asked questions

**What is the difference between night terrors and nightmares?**  
Nightmares: the child wakes from a scary dream and remembers it, usually later at night. Night terrors: early, deep sleep, looks terrified, does not really wake, and usually has no memory.

**Should I wake my child during a night terror?**  
No. Keep them safe and wait.

**Will they remember it?**  
Usually not, which is why it is often worse for you than for them.

**Can babies have night terrors?**  
HealthyChildren.org places night terrors mostly in toddlers and preschoolers. Very young babies who cry out briefly in [active sleep](/baby-sleep-cycles) are more often doing something ordinary — see [crying in sleep](/baby-crying-in-sleep). If you are unsure, ask your pediatrician rather than labeling it.

**Do they mean my child is anxious or traumatized?**  
Not by themselves. Tiredness, illness, and family history are common contributors (NHS). Recurring nightmares after a scary event are a reason to call the doctor.

## Note the clock time (Yorix)

**Yorix** can log the hour an episode started, which helps you see whether it is an early-night pattern and whether the NHS timed-waking idea even applies. The app cannot diagnose a night terror or a seizure, and it is not a medical device.

## Related reading

- [Teeth Grinding in Sleep: Toddler Bruxism, Not a Second Teething Page](/teeth-grinding-in-sleep)

- [Fear of the Dark and Other Nighttime Fears](/fear-of-the-dark)

- [Baby crying in their sleep](/baby-crying-in-sleep)
- [Baby sleep cycles](/baby-sleep-cycles)
- [2 year old sleep schedule](/2-year-old-sleep-schedule)
- [When do toddlers stop napping](/when-do-toddlers-stop-napping)
- [Survive night wakings](/survive-night-wakings-new-parents)
- [Bedtime routine for baby](/bedtime-routine-for-baby)
- [How much sleep a baby needs](/how-much-sleep-does-a-baby-need)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026.

1. HealthyChildren.org (AAP). "Nightmares, Night Terrors & Sleepwalking in Children: How Parents Can Help." Last updated 9/21/2023. <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/preschool/Pages/nightmares-and-night-terrors.aspx>. Nightmare timing and ages; night-terror signs and response; do not wake a sleepwalker; room safety.
2. NHS. "Night terrors and nightmares." Page last reviewed 24 November 2025. <https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/night-terrors/>. Comparison table; most common at 3–8 years; up to 15 minutes; do not wake; scheduled waking 15 minutes before for 2 weeks; when to see a GP.
3. Sleep Foundation. "Night Terrors." <https://www.sleepfoundation.org/parasomnias/night-terrors>. NREM vs REM timing (early vs late night). Duration figures on some Sleep Foundation pages differ from NHS and HealthyChildren.org; we rely on NHS and AAP parent pages for what to do, and we do not treat a single maximum length as settled.


4. [Canadian Paediatric Society, Caring for Kids. “Healthy sleep for your baby and child.” November 2024. Comfort after nightmares; do not search for monsters.](https://caringforkids.cps.ca/handouts/healthy-living/healthy_sleep_for_your_baby_and_child)
