description: What sleep associations are, why a baby who needs rocking or feeding to fall asleep also needs it at 2 a.m., and a gentle plan to change the habit.
body:
# Sleep Associations: What They Are and How to Change Them

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 16, 2026 · **Updated:** November 16, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

If your baby can only fall asleep in your arms, on a breast or bottle, or in a moving swing, you already know the 2 a.m. sequel: when they stir between [sleep cycles](/baby-sleep-cycles), they need that same condition again. That is a **sleep association**. This page explains the mechanism and a gentle way to loosen it. It does not walk through the Ferber, cry-it-out, or other formal methods — those steps live on [when to start sleep training](/when-to-start-sleep-training) and [sleep training methods explained](/sleep-training-methods-explained).

## Short answer

A sleep association is whatever your baby links with falling asleep: feeding, rocking, bouncing, a swing, a car ride, a parent in the room, lights, or sound. Some associations are easy to repeat in the middle of the night (a dark room, a [pacifier](/pacifier-and-sleep), a familiar [sleep sack](/sleep-sacks)). Some are not (being held, being fed to sleep every time, motion). Sleep Foundation's article on sleep-onset association problems notes that 20 to 30% of children have trouble falling or staying asleep, often with a behavioral component, and that bedtime resistance and long night wakings are typical signs. NHS and HealthyChildren.org both warn that always rocking or holding a baby all the way to sleep can make resettling harder later. A consistent [bedtime routine](/bedtime-routine-for-baby) and, from around 4 months, practice with "drowsy but awake" (HealthyChildren.org) are the usual first changes.

### Key numbers at a glance

| Question | What the sources say | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| How common are falling-asleep problems? | 20–30% of children have trouble falling or staying asleep, often behavioral | Sleep Foundation (sleep-onset associations) |
| When "drowsy but awake" is often introduced | Around 4 months | HealthyChildren.org |
| Why nights unravel | Babies often surface at the end of a ~50-minute cycle and need the same conditions to continue | Sleep Foundation (cycles) |
| Newborn feeding to sleep | Normal and often necessary; it is not a "bad habit" in the first weeks | KidsHealth; NHS |

## Helpful associations versus tricky ones

Almost every baby has associations. The useful split is not "good" versus "spoiled." It is **present when they wake** versus **missing when they wake**.

Easier to keep:

- a dark or dim room at night
- a fairly consistent bedtime
- a wearable layer, not a loose [blanket](/when-can-baby-sleep-with-a-blanket)
- white noise at a safe volume, if you use it — see [white noise](/white-noise-for-baby-sleep)
- a pacifier, if you offer one and it is age-appropriate

Harder to repeat eight times a night:

- being fully fed to sleep every time, once night calories are no longer required
- rocking or bouncing to a complete stop
- a [swing or car seat](/baby-sleeping-in-car-seat) as the nap location
- a parent lying down with the baby in an adult bed — which also collides with [safe-sleep](/safe-sleep-for-babies) advice

[Contact naps](/contact-naps) are a special case: they can be a reasonable choice in the day, as long as you stay awake and the position is safe, but they still count as an association if they are the only way sleep happens.

## Why this shows up so clearly around 3 to 4 months

Newborns often feed to sleep and are put down already asleep. That matches their needs. Around the time sleep reorganizes into more mature [cycles](/baby-sleep-cycles), many babies start surfacing fully between cycles. If the only way they know to fall asleep is in your arms, they will call for that at the end of each cycle. Families often experience this as the [4-month sleep regression](/sleep-regression/4-months) or as [hourly wakings](/baby-waking-every-hour).

You did not "create insomnia." You used a tool that used to work around the clock.

## A gentle change plan (without a formal method)

Sleep Foundation lists consistent routines, gradually fading the extra help, and — for some families — structured behavioral methods. NHS and HealthyChildren.org start with the milder end: a predictable wind-down, and putting the baby down after the last feed, drowsy but awake, once they are past the newborn stage.

A plain version of fading, not a script you must follow:

1. Keep the last 20 to 30 minutes of the evening predictable (bath, feed, book, crib — whatever you already do). Put the feed **before** the final put-down if you are trying to uncouple feeding from the exact moment of sleep.
2. For a few nights, reduce the intensity of the help: slightly less rocking, a stiller hold, putting them down a little more awake than yesterday.
3. Stay nearby at first if that helps you keep the experiment going. The goal is that the crib, not your movement, is the last thing they remember.
4. Use the same approach for the first waking of the night, not only at bedtime. Bedtime is easier, but nights are where the association shows.

If you want a more structured approach, or you are deciding whether to use timed checks or a different style, go to [sleep training methods explained](/sleep-training-methods-explained) and [when to start sleep training](/when-to-start-sleep-training). We will not paste those steps here, and we will not tell you that any one method is required.

Skip any plan that puts a baby in an unsafe sleep place "because it is the only way they sleep." Change the association in a crib or bassinet that already meets [safe-sleep](/safe-sleep-for-babies) rules.

## When not to start

Do not overhaul sleep associations in the first weeks, during an illness, in the middle of a major travel week, or if your pediatrician still wants frequent night feeds. A 3-week-old who falls asleep at the breast is doing something normal. See [should you wake a sleeping baby](/should-you-wake-a-sleeping-baby) and [night weaning](/night-weaning) before you treat every night feed as a "habit."

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Ask first if your baby is under 4 months, was premature, has reflux or poor weight gain, or if you are not sure night calories are still needed. Seek help if breathing, snoring, or very restless sleep makes you wonder whether something other than an association is going on.

## Frequently asked questions

**What is a sleep association?**  
Anything your baby uses as a cue to fall asleep. The association becomes a problem when they cannot fall back to sleep without it.

**Is feeding to sleep always bad?**  
No, especially in newborns. It becomes less convenient when they wake for a feed-shaped comfort at times they no longer need the calories.

**How do I change a rocking-to-sleep habit?**  
Fade the rocking, put them down more awake, keep the routine, and be consistent at the first night waking. If you want a formal method, use the training pages rather than this overview.

**Can a pacifier be an association?**  
Yes. The AAP still encourages offering a pacifier at sleep as a SIDS-risk reducer once breastfeeding is established. If you spend the night replacing it, that is a nuisance, not a reason to ignore the safer-sleep advice. See [pacifier and sleep](/pacifier-and-sleep).

**Will this fix short naps?**  
Sometimes, if the nap ends because they cannot link [cycles](/baby-sleep-cycles) without help. Sometimes the nap is just short. See [short naps](/short-naps).

## See what actually happens at sleep onset (Yorix)

**Yorix** can record how a nap or night started (for example, a short note that you rocked to sleep), which makes a pattern easier to discuss. The app cannot change an association for you and is not a medical device.

## Related reading

- [Cluster Feeding: Not Reverse Cycling, Not a Witching-Hour Diagnosis](/cluster-feeding)
- [Responsive Settling: Help That Can Fade, Not a Second Methods Table](/responsive-settling)

- [Baby Won't Sleep in the Bassinet or Crib](/baby-wont-sleep-in-crib)
- [Gentle Sleep Training: Chair, Fading, and Pick Up / Put Down](/gentle-sleep-training)
- [Naps on the Go: Stroller, Car, and Wrap — Lifestyle, Then a Flat Surface](/naps-on-the-go)
- [Nursing to Sleep: When It Is Normal, and What to Change Later](/nursing-to-sleep)
- [Self-Soothing: A Skill That Grows, Not a Method](/self-soothing)

- [Baby sleep cycles](/baby-sleep-cycles)
- [Bedtime routine for baby](/bedtime-routine-for-baby)
- [When to start sleep training](/when-to-start-sleep-training)
- [Sleep training methods explained](/sleep-training-methods-explained)
- [Contact naps](/contact-naps)
- [Survive night wakings](/survive-night-wakings-new-parents)
- [False starts](/false-starts)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026.

1. Sleep Foundation. "Sleep Onset Association Disorder." Updated 21 October 2026. <https://www.sleepfoundation.org/insomnia/sleep-onset-association-disorder>. 20–30% figure; common associations; bedtime resistance and night wakings; routine, fading, and behavioral treatments (mentioned, not copied as steps).
2. HealthyChildren.org (AAP). "Getting Your Baby to Sleep." <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/baby/sleep/Pages/Getting-Your-Baby-to-Sleep.aspx>. Drowsy but awake around 4 months; rocking or holding all the way to sleep can make later resettling harder.
3. NHS. "Helping your baby to sleep." <https://www.nhs.uk/baby/caring-for-a-newborn/helping-your-baby-to-sleep/>. Same caution about always rocking or holding to sleep; consistent routine.
4. Sleep Foundation. "Baby Sleep Cycles." Updated 27 August 2026. <https://www.sleepfoundation.org/baby-sleep/baby-sleep-cycle>. Cycle length and why babies surface between cycles.
5. Nemours KidsHealth. "Sleep and Your Newborn." <https://kidshealth.org/en/parents/sleepnewborn.html>. Newborn feeding-to-sleep is expected.

title: Sleep Sacks: When to Use a Wearable Blanket | Yorix
heading: Sleep Sacks: A Safer Alternative to a Loose Blanket
description: Sleep sacks explained: why a wearable blanket is safer than a loose blanket, how it differs from a swaddle, fit, safety, and when a toddler can use a blanket.
body:
# Sleep Sacks: A Safer Alternative to a Loose Blanket

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 16, 2026 · **Updated:** November 16, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

A **sleep sack** — also called a wearable blanket — is a sleeveless (or short-sleeved) bag that zips or snaps over a baby's usual sleep clothes. It is one of the few extra layers the American Academy of Pediatrics is comfortable with in the crib, because it warms the body without leaving a loose blanket near the face. This page is about that product category, not about room temperature or how to wrap a newborn. Those are in [how to dress a baby for sleep](/how-to-dress-baby-for-sleep) and [how to swaddle a baby](/how-to-swaddle-a-baby).

## Short answer

Yes, a well-fitting sleep sack can be a safe way to keep a baby warm in the first year, when loose blankets should stay out of the crib. Choose a sack that is the right size, does not cover the head or restrict the hips, and is not weighted. A swaddle-style sack that holds the arms has to come off when your baby starts trying to roll. An arms-free sack can continue after that. We did not find a medical-source age at which every child must stop using one; many toddlers keep a wearable blanket until they can use a regular blanket safely, which is after the first birthday at the earliest.

### Key numbers at a glance

| Question | What the sources say | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Loose blankets in the first year | Keep them out of the sleep space; use clothing or a wearable blanket instead | AAP / HealthyChildren.org |
| Weighted sleep sacks | Do not use weighted blankets, sleepers, or swaddles | AAP; KidsHealth |
| Swaddle-style sacks | Stop once the baby shows signs of rolling, which may be as early as 2 months | Sleep Foundation; AAP logic on swaddling |
| Hip room | Legs should be able to bend up and out; a sack should not pin the thighs together | International Hip Dysplasia Institute |
| Ordinary blankets or stuffed toys | Not in the sleep space for the first 12 months | AAP; Sleep Foundation ("When Can Babies Sleep With a Blanket?") |

## Why a sack is not the same thing as a blanket

The risk with a loose blanket is that it can end up over a baby's face or around the neck. A sleep sack goes on like clothing: the zipper or snaps keep it in place, and a properly designed neck opening is too small for the baby's head to slip inside. That is why AAP parent advice names "wearable blankets, like a sleeping sack" as a safer way to add warmth than a quilt or a loosely tucked covering.

It still has to fit. A sack that is far too big can ride up. A sack that is too tight at the chest or hips works against comfort and, if it straightens the legs, against healthy hip position. The IHDI's advice for commercial "sleepsacks specifically designed for swaddling" is that they should have a loose pouch for the legs and feet; the same idea applies to an ordinary arms-free sack — the baby should be able to flex and move the hips.

## Sleep sack vs swaddle

These two get mixed up because some products do both jobs.

| | Swaddle or swaddle sack | Arms-free sleep sack |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Purpose | Limits arm movement to reduce startle in newborns | Adds warmth like a blanket, with arms free |
| When it is appropriate | Only before the baby starts trying to roll | Before and after rolling, if it fits |
| Hip position | Must stay loose at the hips | Must stay loose at the hips |
| Weighted versions | Do not use | Do not use |

If the product holds the arms against the body, treat it as a swaddle and follow the stop-at-rolling rule. If the arms are free, you can keep using it after rolling starts, which is the point of switching from a wrap to a sack.

## Fit, fabric, and what "TOG" can and cannot tell you

Useful fit checks, drawn from AAP and IHDI principles plus ordinary product-safety sense:

- The neck opening cannot slip down over the baby's mouth or up over the face.
- Armholes are snug enough that the baby cannot slip down inside the sack.
- There is room for a diapered baby to frog-leg, not a tight tube around the thighs.
- The fabric is light enough for your room (see the dressing article for the one-extra-layer rule and the 16–20°C vs 68–72°F temperature disagreement).
- There is no hood, no loose ribbon, and no attached toy or pacifier clip.

**TOG** is a lab measure of thermal insulation used on many UK and European sacks. Manufacturer charts often pair 0.5, 1.0, 2.5 TOG and so on with room temperatures. We opened AAP, NHS, and Lullaby Trust safer-sleep pages for this package and did not find an official TOG table, so any such chart should be treated as **unverified by those medical sources** — a label hint, not a clinical standard. Check the baby's chest, not only the number on the tag.

Replace a sack that is worn through, has a broken zipper, or that your baby has grown out of (when the neck opening looks wide or the hips look cramped). Follow the maker's size range, but do not "size up" a long way for longevity if that leaves a loose neck.

## When can a toddler use a regular blanket instead?

Sleep Foundation's page on blankets, and AAP safe-sleep advice, keep soft, loose objects out of the sleep space for the **first 12 months**. After the first birthday the suffocation risk is lower, but a small toddler can still get tangled in a heavy quilt. Many families keep a sleep sack well into the second or third year simply because it stays on. That choice is not something we found a hard AAP cut-off for. When you do introduce a blanket, start with a small, light one and keep the crib or bed otherwise uncluttered. Pillows are a separate, later question and are not needed for infant sleep.

## What a sleep sack will not do

It will not teach a baby to sleep through the night, fix [short naps](/short-naps), or replace [safe sleep](/safe-sleep-for-babies) habits. It will not make an unsafe surface (a sofa, a lounger, a car seat in the house) safe. And a sack under a loose blanket puts you back where you started.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Ask if your baby has a hip condition, was born very early, or seems to overheat in every sack you try. Stop using a product and seek advice if the fabric covers the face, if breathing looks strained, or if the baby works their body down inside the sack.

## Frequently asked questions

**Are sleep sacks safe for newborns?**  
An arms-free sack can be, if it fits and you are not adding loose blankets. A swaddle sack is only for the pre-rolling stage. Newborns can also sleep in ordinary layers with no sack at all.

**Can my baby roll in a sleep sack?**  
In an arms-free sack, yes — and that is expected once rolling starts. That is why the arms need to be out. Practice supervised tummy time so rolling skill can develop.

**Do I need different sacks for summer and winter?**  
Often a lighter and a slightly warmer sack, or a single light sack with a change of clothes underneath, is enough. Follow the room and the baby's chest, not a rigid seasonal wardrobe.

**Can I use a sleep sack in a car seat or stroller?**  
A bulky sack can interfere with harness fit, which is a crash-safety issue, not a sleep-sack issue. Use clothing that allows a snug harness; do not put the harness over a thick bag if it leaves slack. Check the car-seat manual.

**Is a wearable blanket the same as a "sleep bag"?**  
Yes. "Sleep bag," "sleep sack," and "wearable blanket" are names for the same idea.

**What TOG rating should I buy?**  
TOG is a lab insulation number used on many UK and European bags, not an AAP, NHS, or Lullaby Trust medical standard. Use the maker’s chart only as a starting hint, then check the baby’s chest (see “Fit, fabric, and what TOG can and cannot tell you” above, and [how to dress a baby for sleep](/how-to-dress-baby-for-sleep)). Choose a bag that fits the baby’s **weight**, has no hood, and cannot ride up over the face. Do not “size up” so far that the neck opening is loose.

## Note what your baby wore (Yorix)

**Yorix** can log the sleep itself, and you can use a note or symptom entry if a night seemed too hot or too cold. It will not recommend a TOG rating and it is not a medical device.

## Related reading

- [Crib to Toddler Bed: When and How to Switch](/crib-to-toddler-bed)
- [When Can a Baby Sleep With a Blanket or Lovey?](/when-can-baby-sleep-with-a-blanket)

- [How to dress a baby for sleep](/how-to-dress-baby-for-sleep)
- [How to swaddle a baby](/how-to-swaddle-a-baby)
- [Safe sleep for babies](/safe-sleep-for-babies)
- [Newborn sleep schedule](/newborn-sleep-schedule)
- [When do babies sleep through the night](/when-do-babies-sleep-through-the-night)
- [White noise for baby sleep](/white-noise-for-baby-sleep)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026.

1. HealthyChildren.org (AAP). "How to Keep Your Sleeping Baby Safe: AAP Policy Explained." <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/baby/sleep/Pages/A-Parents-Guide-to-Safe-Sleep.aspx>. Wearable blankets as a safer alternative to loose blankets; no weighted blankets, sleepers, or swaddles; one extra layer.
2. Sleep Foundation. "How to Dress a Baby for Sleep." Updated 13 October 2026. <https://www.sleepfoundation.org/baby-sleep/how-to-dress-baby-for-sleep>. Wearable blankets can be safe if they do not restrict movement once rolling starts; no head covering.
3. Sleep Foundation. "When Can Babies Sleep With a Blanket?" Updated 30 September 2026. Medically reviewed by Nilong Vyas, MD, MPH. <https://www.sleepfoundation.org/baby-sleep/when-can-baby-sleep-with-blanket>. No loose blankets under 12 months; wearable blankets or sleep sacks for warmth; stop swaddling once the baby tries to roll.
4. International Hip Dysplasia Institute. "Hip-Healthy Swaddling." <https://hipdysplasia.org/infant-child/hip-healthy-swaddling/>. Commercial sleepsacks need a loose leg pouch.
5. Nemours KidsHealth. "Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS)." July 2022. <https://kidshealth.org/en/parents/sids.html>. No weighted products; no loose bedding in the sleep area.
6. The Lullaby Trust. "Safer sleep advice for babies." <https://www.lullabytrust.org.uk/safer-sleep-advice/>. Clear cot; no bulky or weighted bedding.
7. Moon RY, et al. 2022 AAP policy, *Pediatrics*. <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35726558/>.

description: Toddler bedtime battles are the ongoing stalling of ages 18 months to 4 years — not a regression article, and not the later stay-in-bed guide.
body:
# Toddler Bedtime Battles: Stalling, Not a Regression

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 16, 2026 · **Updated:** November 16, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

Bedtime battles are the **ongoing** evening struggle of toddlerhood and the early preschool years: one more book, one more drink, a sudden need to discuss the day, a body that will not stay on the starting line. This is not a rewrite of [2-year sleep regression](/sleep-regression/2-years) or [18-month sleep regression](/sleep-regression/18-months). Those pages own a time-limited bump. This page is the behavior guide for roughly **18 months to 4 years** when the fight is the new normal, not a two-week blip.

It is also not the later problem of a child who has already been put down and will not **stay** in bed. Curtain calls after lights out, and the walk-back from a toddler bed, deserve their own space; [crib to toddler bed](/crib-to-toddler-bed) covers the furniture move, and a dedicated "won't stay in bed" page is still on our plan. Here we stay on the wind-down fight: getting the evening started, and finished, without a new negotiation every night.

## Short answer

HealthyChildren's bedtime-trouble guidance for toddlers is built around a **predictable, calm routine**, a consistent bedtime, meeting last needs (water, a hug, the bathroom) *before* lights out, and a firm, unexcited response to extra requests. KidsHealth tells preschool families the same story: a regular sequence, screens off at least an hour before bed and out of the bedroom, a quiet room, and no new habit of falling asleep somewhere other than the child's bed. The AAP's Brush, Book, Bed sequence is one ready-made order: teeth, stories, sleep.

If the child is genuinely scared, use [fear of the dark](/fear-of-the-dark). If they are panicked that you are leaving, use [separation anxiety and sleep](/separation-anxiety-and-sleep). If they have just climbed out of a crib, the first question is safety, not willpower — see the crib-to-bed page. And if the whole week is a sudden, new mess around a birthday or a big change, glance at the matching regression article, then come back here for the nightly pattern.

### What "the battle" usually is

| Pattern | Treat it as | Not as |
| --- | --- | --- |
| "One more book / snack / question" every night | Stalling. Close the menu before you start | A medical mystery, unless other signs are present |
| Meltdown as soon as pajamas appear | A too-late or too-stimulating evening, or a child who is simply overloaded | Proof that sleep is impossible at this age |
| Fear talk ("there's a monster") | [Fear of the dark](/fear-of-the-dark) | A stall you should argue with |
| Already in bed, then out again | A stay-in-bed problem (pointer only here) | The same thing as refusing to start bedtime |
| A short bumpy spell at 2 | [2-year sleep regression](/sleep-regression/2-years) | This whole guide, unless it keeps going |

## A plan you can repeat when you are tired

There is no official AAP stopwatch for how long a toddler routine should last, and there is no official clock time for lights out. The [3-year-old sleep schedule](/3-year-old-sleep-schedule) and [2-year-old sleep schedule](/2-year-old-sleep-schedule) own the 24-hour totals. This page owns the process:

- **Pick a bedtime you can keep most nights**, including weekends as much as life allows. A moving target invites a nightly auction.
- **Start the routine before the child is past it.** An overtired toddler often looks "wired," not sleepy ([overtired baby](/overtired-baby) still applies).
- **Announce the plan once**, in the same order. Brush, Book, Bed is one version (HealthyChildren). A bath can sit before that if it calms your child; skip it if it winds them up.
- **Close the kitchen and the request window** as the routine starts. HealthyChildren's idea is to meet water, toileting, and a last hug *before* you leave, then treat later requests as already answered.
- **Turn screens off** at least an hour before bed and keep them out of the room (KidsHealth).
- **Leave with the same short line** you used the night before. A new speech is a new opening.

When the child protests, stay calm and boring. Extra laughter, extra bargaining, and extra books taught as a reward for protest all lengthen the evening. If a fear is real, attend to the fear (see that page) without adding a 20-minute inspection ritual.

Daytime sleep still matters. A late or very long nap can push bedtime later; a dropped nap can mean an earlier night. The *how* of dropping a nap is on [when toddlers stop napping](/when-do-toddlers-stop-napping), not here.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Ask if bedtime takes so long that the child is chronically short of the 10–13 hour (ages 3–5) or 11–14 hour (ages 1–2) AASM totals and is struggling by day, if you suspect pain, breathing problems, or unusual daytime sleepiness, or if you cannot tell stalling from anxiety or a night terror.

## Frequently asked questions

**How long should I let a bedtime battle go?**  
There is no official minute count. A short, identical routine with one clear end is the sourced idea. If you are still in the room 45 minutes later adding chapters, the plan has slipped, not the child.

**Should I give in on "one more book"?**  
Build the book into the routine so it is already included. Adding one after protest teaches the protest. HealthyChildren's "meet needs first, then be consistent" pattern is the better frame.

**Is this the same as a 2-year regression?**  
It can start in the same season. The regression page is for a time-limited bump and its usual causes. This page is the nightly habit if the struggle has become the baseline.

**What if they get out of bed after I leave?**  
That is the stay-in-bed problem. Walk them back calmly if they have a bed they can leave; see [crib to toddler bed](/crib-to-toddler-bed) if the crib is no longer safe. We are not expanding that how-to here.

## See how long the evening is actually taking (Yorix)

**Yorix** can show when the routine starts and when sleep actually begins, which is a clearer picture than a single loud night. The app cannot run bedtime for you and is not a medical device.

## Related reading

- [4 Year Old Sleep Schedule: The Preschool Day, With or Without a Nap](/4-year-old-sleep-schedule)
- [Sleep After Separation or Divorce: Two Homes, One Predictable Night](/sleep-after-separation-or-divorce)

- [Toddler Won't Stay in Bed: After Lights Out](/toddler-wont-stay-in-bed)

- [2-year sleep regression](/sleep-regression/2-years)
- [2 year old sleep schedule](/2-year-old-sleep-schedule)
- [3 year old sleep schedule](/3-year-old-sleep-schedule)
- [Fear of the dark](/fear-of-the-dark)
- [Separation anxiety and sleep](/separation-anxiety-and-sleep)
- [Crib to toddler bed](/crib-to-toddler-bed)
- [Bedtime routine for baby](/bedtime-routine-for-baby)
- [When do toddlers stop napping](/when-do-toddlers-stop-napping)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026.

1. HealthyChildren.org (AAP). "Toddler Won't Go to Sleep? 7 Tips to Help End Bedtime Battles." Accessed 15 November 2026. Predictable routine, consistent bedtime, meet last needs before lights out, calm and firm response to extra requests. <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/healthy-living/sleep/Pages/bedtime-trouble.aspx>.
2. HealthyChildren.org (AAP). "Brush, Book, Bed: How to Structure Your Child's Nighttime Routine." A simple, repeatable order. <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/healthy-living/oral-health/Pages/Brush-Book-Bed.aspx>.
3. Nemours KidsHealth. "Sleep and Your Preschooler." Date reviewed June 2020. Regular routine; screens off at least an hour before bed and out of the bedroom; child falls asleep in their own bed; brief comfort after a waking. <https://kidshealth.org/en/parents/sleep-preschool.html>.
4. Paruthi S, et al. AASM pediatric sleep-duration consensus, 2016. 11–14 hours at 1–2 years and 10–13 hours at 3–5 years, including any nap — used here only as the total the evening should protect. AAP-endorsed.

description: Toddler won't stay in bed: nightly curtain calls after lights out, calm walk-backs, and where an OK-to-wake clock can fit — not the crib-to-bed move.
body:
# Toddler Won't Stay in Bed: After Lights Out

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 16, 2026 · **Updated:** November 16, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

This page is the **nightly encore**: the toddler is already in the bed, the routine is over, and they appear in the hall again. It is not [crib to toddler bed](/crib-to-toddler-bed) (when and how to make the furniture move). It is not [toddler bedtime battles](/toddler-bedtime-battles) (the stalling that delays lights out). It is not the [2-year sleep regression](/sleep-regression/2-years) (a time-limited bump). If they are still in a crib they can climb, start with the safety question on the crib-to-bed page before you treat this as willpower.

## Short answer

KidsHealth's preschool-sleep advice, and HealthyChildren's bedtime-trouble tone, point the same way once the child is up: **take them back calmly, keep the visit short and boring, and do it the same way every time**. Do not start a second evening of snacks, extra chapters, or a new speech. If the child is frightened, use [fear of the dark](/fear-of-the-dark). If they cannot tolerate being alone yet, that is a comfort question, not a prize for leaving the room fifteen times.

Cleveland Clinic's "toddler won't sleep" tips are in the same family: a consistent bedtime, needs met *before* you leave (water, toilet, a last hug), and a firm, unexcited return. There is no official AAP minute-count for how many walk-backs are allowed.

An **OK-to-wake clock** can be a useful *section* of this plan for a toddler who can understand "the clock is still sleepy." It is a household tool, **not an AAP protocol** we can cite as a required device, and it is not for infants. The rule it supports is a consistent morning, not the gadget itself.

### Stay-in-bed versus nearby problems

| Pattern | This page? | Go here |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Will not start the routine, one more book | No | [Toddler bedtime battles](/toddler-bedtime-battles) |
| In bed, then out, repeatedly | Yes | This page |
| Just moved from a crib, or climbing | Safety first | [Crib to toddler bed](/crib-to-toddler-bed) |
| "There's a monster" | If fear is the driver | [Fear of the dark](/fear-of-the-dark) |
| A short bumpy spell at 2 | Maybe both | [2-year sleep regression](/sleep-regression/2-years) |

## A boring walk-back plan

1. Close the request window before you leave. Water, toilet, a last hug, the door or night light already agreed (HealthyChildren; KidsHealth).
2. When they appear, say one short line you can repeat — "it's sleep time, I will walk you back" — and do it with almost no conversation.
3. Put them in the bed, not on the sofa and not in your bed, unless you have chosen a family-bed arrangement on purpose (and only with the safety limits that still apply for younger children; see [bed-sharing](/bed-sharing-and-co-sleeping)).
4. Leave again. The first week can be tedious. A new game, a new snack, or a long lecture teaches the encore.
5. If they are genuinely scared, sit briefly and be present, then still return them to their bed. An every-night stay until they fall asleep can become the new condition (the same nuance we note on the fears page).

Do not use a lock that would trap a child in a room in a fire, and do not turn the walk-back into a chase. If the bed is still so new that they are not safe in it, going back to a crib if it is still appropriate is a safety decision, not a failure — the crib-to-bed page already says waiting is often the better move.

## OK-to-wake clocks (a section, not a separate article)

Once a toddler can follow a simple visual rule, some families use a clock or a lamp that changes color at the allowed morning time. We do not have an AAP or NHS protocol that names a brand or a start age. If you use one:

- Set it to a morning you can actually keep, inside a sensible 24-hour total (11–14 hours at 1–2 years, 10–13 hours at 3–5, AASM, including any nap).
- Teach it in the daytime, not at the first 5 a.m. appearance.
- It does not replace the walk-back at 8 p.m. It only answers "is it morning yet?"

If early waking is the real problem, also see [early morning waking](/early-morning-waking).

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Ask if the nights are so broken that the child is short of the AASM range and struggling by day, if you suspect fear, pain, or breathing problems, or if a new bed has made the room unsafe.

## Frequently asked questions

**How many times should I walk them back?**  
As many as it takes that night, in the same boring way. There is no official cap. Changing the rule on the tenth trip is what usually stretches the problem.

**Should I lie down with them until they stay?**  
An occasional comfort is different from a new every-night requirement. KidsHealth preschool advice is that falling asleep with you, or in another room, can make solo settling harder.

**Will a clock fix it?**  
It may help a child who is testing the morning. It will not replace a consistent walk-back after bedtime, and it is not a medical device or an official AAP tool.

## See how often the encore actually happens (Yorix)

**Yorix** can help you note how many times a night the child is up, and whether mornings are drifting earlier. The app cannot walk a toddler back to bed and is not a medical device.

## Related reading

- [4 Year Old Sleep Schedule: The Preschool Day, With or Without a Nap](/4-year-old-sleep-schedule)
- [Sleep After Separation or Divorce: Two Homes, One Predictable Night](/sleep-after-separation-or-divorce)

- [Toddler bedtime battles](/toddler-bedtime-battles)
- [Crib to toddler bed](/crib-to-toddler-bed)
- [Fear of the dark](/fear-of-the-dark)
- [2-year sleep regression](/sleep-regression/2-years)
- [Early morning waking](/early-morning-waking)
- [2 year old sleep schedule](/2-year-old-sleep-schedule)
- [3 year old sleep schedule](/3-year-old-sleep-schedule)
- [Bedtime routine for baby](/bedtime-routine-for-baby)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026.

1. Nemours KidsHealth. "Sleep and Your Preschooler." Date reviewed June 2020. If the child gets out of bed, calmly take them back; keep night visits short; they should fall asleep in their own bed. <https://kidshealth.org/en/parents/sleep-preschool.html>.
2. HealthyChildren.org (AAP). "Toddler Won't Go to Sleep? 7 Tips to Help End Bedtime Battles." Meet last needs before lights out; consistent, calm, firm response. <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/healthy-living/sleep/Pages/bedtime-trouble.aspx>.
3. Cleveland Clinic. "Tips To Get Your Toddler To Stay In Bed." Accessed 15 November 2026. Consistent plan, needs met first, calm returns. <https://health.clevelandclinic.org/toddler-wont-sleep-tips>.
4. Paruthi S, et al. AASM pediatric sleep-duration consensus, 2016. 11–14 hours at 1–2 years and 10–13 hours at 3–5 years, including any nap — the total a consistent morning should still protect.

body:
# Twins and Sleep: Safety, Co-Bedding, and Routines

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 16, 2026 · **Updated:** November 16, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

Two babies does not mean two copies of a generic schedule. The sleep questions that are specific to twins are about **safety, surfaces, and logistics**: can they share a cot, do they stay in your room, and how do you survive a night when one is always awake? This is not a second [newborn](/newborn-sleep-schedule) or [3-month](/3-month-old-sleep-schedule) article with the word "twins" added.

## Short answer

On **safe sleep**, start from the same rules as for one baby — back, firm, flat, clear, in your room, not in your bed — on our [safe-sleep](/safe-sleep-for-babies) hub, with extra caution because NHS notes that twins and premature or low-birth-weight babies have a **higher SIDS risk**. On **whether two babies can share one cot**, U.S. and UK advice genuinely disagree. The AAP cannot recommend bed-sharing under any circumstances, **including with twins**, meaning each baby should have their own approved sleep surface. NHS says co-bedding in a single cot is "perfectly safe" while they are small enough, if you follow safe-sleep advice: on their backs, heads toward one another with feet at opposite ends, or side by side with feet at the end of the cot, not close enough to touch, and not in a Moses basket. We will not average those into one Yorix rule. Talk to your pediatrician, and do not share an adult bed with one or both babies.

### Key numbers at a glance

| Question | What the sources say | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AAP on twins sharing a sleep surface | Avoid bed-sharing under any circumstances, including with twins — each baby, own space | HealthyChildren.org (AAP 2022) |
| NHS on co-bedding in one cot | "Perfectly safe" while they are small enough, if safe-sleep advice is followed; not in a Moses basket | NHS, "Twins and sleep," reviewed 21 April 2026 |
| How to place co-bedded twins (NHS) | Backs, heads toward each other and feet at opposite ends, or side by side with feet at the end; not close enough to touch | NHS |
| Room-sharing | At least the first 6 months, in the parents' room | AAP; NHS; Lullaby Trust |
| Adult bed and more than one baby | Lullaby Trust: do not bed-share with more than one twin at a time | Lullaby Trust |
| Extra SIDS risk | Twins, preterm, and low-birth-weight babies are at higher risk | NHS SIDS page |

The HealthyChildren.org "Twins: 2 Cribs or 2 Bedrooms?" page returned an access error (HTTP 401) when we tried to open it on 15 November 2026, so we have not quoted it. We rely on the 2022 AAP policy, NHS twins guidance, and Lullaby Trust instead.

## Safety first: one surface or two?

**United States (AAP).** The policy is written for sudden unexpected infant death and suffocation risk. "Bed-sharing" here includes a baby sharing a surface with anyone, including a twin. The practical reading is: two approved cribs, bassinets, or play yards, even if they sit side by side in your room. That arrangement still counts as room-sharing.

**United Kingdom (NHS).** Co-bedding in one cot is described as safe while the babies are small, with the placement rules above, and NHS even notes it can help them regulate temperature and sleep cycles and can soothe them. A Moses basket is too small for two. For triplets, NHS says they can be placed next to each other in a cot while they still fit, on their backs, with their feet toward the long side of the cot. When they are older, NHS suggests separate cots close together if you have the room, so they can still comfort each other. Co-bedding, in the NHS telling, can also make it easier to keep both babies in your room for longer.

If you live in the U.S., or your pediatrician follows AAP guidance, plan for two surfaces from the start. If you are under NHS or Lullaby Trust care and considering co-bedding, read those pages in full, follow every placement rule, and do not put anything — towels, pillows, or cot dividers — between the babies. Lullaby Trust says that once any baby can roll and move about the cot, they need their own sleep space so they cannot roll into each other. NHS itself says that if one waking sets the other off, you can try separate cots side by side.

Neither body thinks an adult mattress is a solution. Lullaby Trust is explicit: do not bed-share with more than one baby at a time, and the safest place remains each baby's own space. Sofas are out of the question. See [bed-sharing](/bed-sharing-and-co-sleeping).

Prematurity is common with twins. Follow any hospital advice about monitors or feeding intervals, and use the baby's **adjusted age** when you compare them to a sleep schedule written for term babies.

## Room-sharing with two cribs

The 6-month room-share recommendation still applies. Two bassinets or a mini-crib plus a bassinet next to your bed is often more workable than trying to fit two full cribs. When they outgrow bassinets — [about 5 months or when they push up on hands and knees](/when-to-move-baby-to-crib), or sooner at the weight limit — you may need a larger room layout, not a premature move to a nursery. A shared nursery after 6 months is a family decision; see [when to move to their own room](/when-to-move-baby-to-own-room).

## Logistics: nights, feeds, and "do I pick them both up?"

NHS twins guidance is more useful here than any generic schedule:

- You can often **coordinate night feeds** so you are not starting from scratch an hour after you have finished.
- You do not always need to rush to cuddle the twin who is crying; sometimes they resettle, and automatically waking the other one makes the night longer for everyone.
- If one baby's waking routinely sets the other off, separate cots (side by side, still in your room) are the NHS next step.

A "twins schedule" is still built from the same age-based pieces as one baby — [wake windows](/wake-windows-by-age), total sleep in [how much sleep a baby needs](/how-much-sleep-does-a-baby-need), a shared [bedtime routine](/bedtime-routine-for-baby) — but the routine may run in parallel or slightly staggered. It is fine if one twin is a better napper than the other. Forcing identical naps can be more stressful than useful.

Safe surfaces still apply when you are outnumbered and exhausted: no [car-seat or swing](/baby-sleeping-in-car-seat) as a crib, no [stomach or side start](/baby-sleeping-on-stomach), no loose [blankets](/when-can-baby-sleep-with-a-blanket) in the first year.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Ask, early, whether they want each baby on a separate surface, how long to [wake for feeds](/should-you-wake-a-sleeping-baby), and whether adjusted age should guide naps. Mention if one twin is gaining poorly, if snoring or breathing differs between them, or if you have been bed-sharing because two cribs felt impossible. You should not have to wait for a crisis to have that conversation.

## Frequently asked questions

**Can twins sleep in the same crib?**  
AAP: no shared surface, including with a twin. NHS: yes, in one cot, while they are small, with specific placement and a clear, firm mattress — not a Moses basket. Follow the advice your clinician uses, and do not use an adult bed as the "same crib."

**Should twins follow the same sleep schedule?**  
Aim for a similar day, but expect differences. Coordinating feeds is more important than identical nap lengths.

**Do twins need two bedrooms?**  
No. They need safe surfaces. Those can be in your room, then later in one nursery or two, depending on space and age.

**Is it okay if one twin is a contact napper and the other is not?**  
Yes. Just stay awake for any [contact nap](/contact-naps), and do not put the second baby in an unsafe place while your hands are full.

**When should we move twins to their own room?**  
Not before 6 months, on AAP and NHS advice, unless your doctor has a specific plan. After that, see [when to move baby to their own room](/when-to-move-baby-to-own-room).

## Log two babies without guessing (Yorix)

**Yorix** can track sleep, feeds, and symptoms for more than one child, which is the main practical help at 3 a.m. when you cannot remember who ate. The app cannot tell you that a shared cot is safe, and it is not a medical device. Use the log next to your pediatrician's advice.

## Related reading

- [Siblings Sharing a Room: After the Twins and Own-Room Pages](/siblings-sharing-a-room)

- [Safe sleep for babies](/safe-sleep-for-babies)
- [Bed-sharing and co-sleeping](/bed-sharing-and-co-sleeping)
- [Newborn sleep schedule](/newborn-sleep-schedule)
- [Should you wake a sleeping baby](/should-you-wake-a-sleeping-baby)
- [When to move baby from bassinet to crib](/when-to-move-baby-to-crib)
- [When to move baby to their own room](/when-to-move-baby-to-own-room)
- [Bedtime routine for baby](/bedtime-routine-for-baby)

## Sources

1. HealthyChildren.org (AAP). "How to Keep Your Sleeping Baby Safe: AAP Policy Explained." <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/baby/sleep/Pages/A-Parents-Guide-to-Safe-Sleep.aspx>. No bed-sharing under any circumstances, including with twins; room-share at least 6 months.
2. Moon RY, et al. 2022 AAP policy, *Pediatrics*. <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35726558/>.
3. NHS. "Twins and sleep." Page last reviewed 21 April 2026. <https://www.nhs.uk/baby/newborn-twins-and-multiples/twins-and-sleep/>. Co-bedding rules; not a Moses basket; triplets note; separate cots if one wakes the other; coordinate feeds; room-share 6 months.
4. NHS. "Sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS)." <https://www.nhs.uk/baby/caring-for-a-newborn/sudden-infant-death-syndrome-sids/>. Higher risk for twins, preterm, and low-birth-weight babies; do not bed-share in those situations.
5. The Lullaby Trust. "Co-sleeping with your baby." Last reviewed 1 February 2025; updated 3 August 2026. <https://www.lullabytrust.org.uk/safer-sleep-advice/co-sleeping/>. Do not bed-share with more than one baby at a time; own space is safest.
6. The Lullaby Trust. "Twins and multiples." <https://www.lullabytrust.org.uk/baby-safety/premature-babies-and-multiples/twins-and-multiples/>. Co-bedding placement; no Moses basket; no towels, pillows, or cot dividers between babies; move to separate spaces once any baby can roll; do not bed-share with more than one baby at a time; extra caution if preterm or low birth weight.

title: When Can a Baby Sleep With a Blanket or Lovey? | Yorix
heading: When Can a Baby Sleep With a Blanket or Lovey?
description: When can babies sleep with a blanket, lovey, or stuffed animal? Why loose bedding stays out of the crib in the first year, and what changes after 12 months.
body:
# When Can a Baby Sleep With a Blanket or Lovey?

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 16, 2026 · **Updated:** November 16, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

A small blanket or a favourite stuffed toy is one of the first things many families want to add to the crib. In the first year, loose bedding and soft objects are still a suffocation and SIDS risk, which is why safe-sleep advice is so blunt: a bare crib. This page is about **when a blanket or lovey becomes a reasonable idea**, not a second article on [how to dress a baby for sleep](/how-to-dress-baby-for-sleep) or [sleep sacks](/sleep-sacks). Those remain the first-year warmth tools.

## Short answer

**Do not put a loose blanket, quilt, pillow, or stuffed toy in the sleep space for the first 12 months.** That is the AAP, KidsHealth, NHS, and Sleep Foundation position. After 12 months, the AAP's parent materials say most experts agree these objects pose little risk to **healthy** babies, while also stating that research has not shown a moment when they are 100% safe. A wearable blanket or sleep sack is not the same thing as a loose blanket and can be used earlier. A lovey or stuffed animal belongs in awake, supervised play until that first birthday, then can be introduced cautiously if you and your pediatrician are comfortable.

### Key numbers at a glance

| Question | What the sources say | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Loose blankets or stuffed toys in the crib | Keep them out until at least 12 months | AAP; KidsHealth; Sleep Foundation; NHS (clear cot) |
| After 12 months | Most experts agree little risk for healthy babies, but research has not shown a point of 100% safety | AAP patient education ("Safe Sleep and Your Baby") |
| Wearable blankets / sleep sacks | An alternative to loose blankets; still no weighted products | AAP; Sleep Foundation |
| Weighted blankets, sleepers, or swaddles | Not recommended | AAP 2022 |

## Why a first-year crib stays empty

Soft objects and loose bedding can cover a baby's face or trap them against the side of a crib or bassinet. The AAP's list is familiar: pillows, quilts, comforters, sheepskins, bumper pads, and stuffed toys. A thin receiving blanket used as a [swaddle](/how-to-swaddle-a-baby) is a separate case — and even that comes off when the baby starts to roll.

Sleep Foundation's blanket article (updated 30 September 2026) is aligned: no loose blankets under 12 months; wearable blankets are the usual substitute; after 12 months, still be cautious with heavy or very loose bedding. NHS and Lullaby Trust describe a clear cot, with any covers tucked in firmly using a [feet-to-foot](/how-to-dress-baby-for-sleep) method in UK guidance, rather than a duvet over a young baby.

A muslin "for comfort" draped over part of the mattress, a pillow "just under the head," or a quilt along the rail are still loose bedding. So is a stuffed animal left in the corner "where they cannot reach it yet." Babies move more than we expect.

## So what keeps them warm?

Use clothing and a sleep sack, not a thrown-on blanket. See [how to dress a baby for sleep](/how-to-dress-baby-for-sleep) for layers and the room-temperature disagreement between sources, and [sleep sacks](/sleep-sacks) for wearable blankets. The AAP's practical rule of thumb is about one more layer than an adult would wear in the same room, and no hats indoors.

## After 12 months: a cautious yes

Once your child is past their first birthday, a light blanket or a small soft toy is something many families add. The AAP's patient-education wording is careful: it has not been proven when it is completely safe, but most experts agree the objects pose little risk to healthy babies after 12 months. That is not a promise, and it does not apply to a child with unusual muscle tone, a breathing problem, or a sleep space that is already cluttered.

Practical cautions after 12 months, compiled from Sleep Foundation and AAP materials rather than invented as a new standard:

- Start with one small, lightweight blanket — not a heavy quilt, weighted blanket, or adult duvet.
- Skip pillows until your child is in a bed, unless your pediatrician says otherwise; a crib pillow is still a soft object near the face.
- Choose a lovey that is not large enough to cover the face, does not have loose ribbons, buttons, or batteries, and is not a weighted toy.
- Keep the crib or toddler bed otherwise clear. Adding a lovey is not a reason to add bumpers, pillows, and a quilt at the same time.

If your 13-month-old still sleeps well with only a sleep sack, you do not have to introduce a blanket.

## When a lovey is useful — and when it is not

After 12 months, a consistent comforter can become part of a [bedtime routine](/bedtime-routine-for-baby) and a [sleep association](/sleep-associations) that does not require a parent in the room. Before 12 months, practice with the lovey at playtime so it is familiar, then leave it out of the crib. Do not rely on a toy as a SIDS-prevention tool; nothing in the crib has that job except a bare, firm, flat surface and a baby on their back.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Ask before adding bedding if your child was born preterm, has a neuromuscular or breathing condition, or still has very restless or unusual sleep. If a blanket or toy is in the crib and you find your child face-down in it, remove it and mention the episode at the next visit.

## Frequently asked questions

**When can babies sleep with a blanket?**  
After 12 months, with a light blanket and a still-fairly-clear crib. Until then, use a sleep sack or extra layer of clothing.

**When can a baby have a lovey or stuffed animal at night?**  
The same 12-month line. Use it in supervised play first.

**Is a sleep sack a blanket?**  
No. It is a wearable layer. It should still be unweighted and the right size so it cannot ride up over the face.

**Can I tuck a blanket into the sides of a bassinet?**  
No. Bassinets are for younger babies, who should have no loose bedding at all.

**Are weighted blankets okay after the first birthday?**  
The AAP recommends against weighted blankets, sleepers, and swaddles. We do not treat the first birthday as a green light for a weighted product.

## Log comfort items once they are allowed (Yorix)

**Yorix** can store a short note that a lovey or blanket has become part of bedtime, which is handy if nights change after you add one. It cannot tell you that a product is safe, and it is not a medical device. Follow AAP timing, not an app.

## Related reading

- [Crib to Toddler Bed: When and How to Switch](/crib-to-toddler-bed)

- [Safe sleep for babies](/safe-sleep-for-babies)
- [How to dress a baby for sleep](/how-to-dress-baby-for-sleep)
- [Sleep sacks](/sleep-sacks)
- [How to swaddle a baby](/how-to-swaddle-a-baby)
- [Bedtime routine for baby](/bedtime-routine-for-baby)
- [Sleep associations](/sleep-associations)
- [When to move baby from bassinet to crib](/when-to-move-baby-to-crib)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026.

1. American Academy of Pediatrics. "Safe Sleep and Your Baby: How Parents Can Reduce the Risk of SIDS and Suffocation" (patient education). <https://publications.aap.org/DocumentLibrary/Solutions/PPE/peo_document088_en.pdf>. No soft objects or loose bedding in the crib; most experts agree little risk after 12 months, though research has not shown 100% safety.
2. HealthyChildren.org (AAP). "How to Keep Your Sleeping Baby Safe: AAP Policy Explained." <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/baby/sleep/Pages/A-Parents-Guide-to-Safe-Sleep.aspx>. Bare crib; no weighted blankets, sleepers, or swaddles.
3. Sleep Foundation. "When Can My Baby Sleep With a Blanket?" Updated 30 September 2026. <https://www.sleepfoundation.org/baby-sleep/when-can-my-baby-sleep-with-a-blanket>. No loose blankets under 12 months; wearable blankets okay; caution with heavy or loose bedding after 12 months.
4. Nemours KidsHealth. "Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS)." <https://kidshealth.org/en/parents/sids.html>. Nothing in the crib except the baby (and a fitted sheet).
5. NHS. "Sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS)." <https://www.nhs.uk/baby/caring-for-a-newborn/sudden-infant-death-syndrome-sids/>. Clear cot; no loose bedding; feet-to-foot if a cover is used.
6. Moon RY, et al. 2022 AAP policy, *Pediatrics*. <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35726558/>.

title: When Do Babies Sleep Through the Night? A Guide | Yorix
heading: When Do Babies Sleep Through the Night — and What Does That Phrase Mean?
description: When babies sleep through the night, what 'through the night' actually means (often 6 hours, not 12), and why many healthy babies still wake at 6 and 12 months.
body:
# When Do Babies Sleep Through the Night — and What Does That Phrase Mean?

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 16, 2026 · **Updated:** November 16, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

Few baby-sleep questions are asked with more hope, or more confusion, than **when do babies sleep through the night**. The phrase itself is slippery. Some parents mean "from 7 p.m. to 7 a.m." Research often means something much shorter. And a baby who is growing well can still wake after the age when internet charts say they "should" be done. This page is about that milestone and its definitions. For getting through the hard nights, see [baby waking at night](/survive-night-wakings-new-parents). For hourly wakings, see [baby waking every hour](/baby-waking-every-hour).

## Short answer

Many babies begin to manage a longer stretch of night sleep around **4 to 6 months**, and Sleep Foundation, citing research, says most sleep "through the night" around **6 months**. In studies, that often means **at least six uninterrupted hours**, even if the baby stirs and resettles. It does not usually mean a 12-hour, no-waking night. A 2018 *Pediatrics* study (Pennestri and colleagues) found that a large share of infants were still not meeting that six-hour definition at 6 months, and a substantial share still were not at 12 months — and those babies were not developmentally behind. Cleveland Clinic says most babies start sleeping through the night by 6 months, which lines up with the "most," not "all," wording. Newborns are not expected to do this; they need frequent feeds.

### Key numbers at a glance

| Question | What the sources say | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What "through the night" often means in research | At least 6 uninterrupted hours (sometimes an 8-hour definition is used too) | Sleep Foundation, citing Pennestri et al., *Pediatrics*, 2018 |
| When it often starts | Around 4–6 months for longer stretches; "most" around 6 months | Sleep Foundation; Cleveland Clinic; MedlinePlus via Sleep Foundation (5–8 hour stretches) |
| How many still are not there at 6 months | Sleep Foundation: about 38% of 6-month-olds in that study were not sleeping through the night | Pennestri 2018, as summarized by Sleep Foundation |
| …and at 12 months | That share dropped to less than 28% | Same |
| Newborn night sleep | Short stretches of about 1–2 hours; 14–17 hours in 24 hours is a common NSF range | Sleep Foundation; [how much sleep a baby needs](/how-much-sleep-does-a-baby-need) |
| Night feeds at 9–12 months | Sleep Foundation: most infants can sleep longer at night without a feed by 9–12 months | Sleep Foundation, "How Much Do Newborns Sleep?" |

## The definition problem

If you expect a 12-hour night and your 6-month-old sleeps from 7 p.m. to 2 a.m., you may think something is wrong. In the Pennestri study, that stretch would count. HealthyChildren.org, in a 2013 parent book extract, goes further for young babies: a "good sleeper" at that age is a child who wakes often but can get back to sleep, **not** a child who sleeps 10 hours without waking. The same page argues that frequent waking is developmentally appropriate and lets a baby rouse if they are not getting enough oxygen. "Sleeping undisturbed for prolonged periods at this age is not healthy" is their wording for early infancy — which is a very different message from "your 8-week-old should be sleeping through."

So when a friend says their baby "slept through" at 10 weeks, ask what they mean. A five-hour stretch after a late evening feed is not the same as dropping all night care.

## What the first year actually looks like

**Newborns (0–3 months).** Sleep is spread across day and night in short bursts. NHS is frank: some babies sleep much more than others, and the pattern will not line up with your need for sleep. Helping the body clock along — light and ordinary noise by day, dim and boring nights — is useful, but it does not produce a full night yet. See [newborn sleep schedule](/newborn-sleep-schedule).

**Around 4 to 6 months.** Sleep cycles lengthen, many babies start to put more sleep into the night, and a stretch of five to eight hours becomes realistic for some, according to Sleep Foundation and MedlinePlus material it cites. This is also when the [4 month sleep regression](/sleep-regression/4-months) can make nights look worse before they look better, because sleep is becoming more like an older infant's, with more brief awakenings between cycles.

**6 to 12 months.** "Most" is not "everyone." The Pennestri figures above are worth sitting with: if roughly one in three 6-month-olds in that study were not yet doing six-hour stretches, a regularly waking 6-month-old is not an outlier by default. By 9 to 12 months, Sleep Foundation says most infants can go longer at night without a feed, and many families see eight or nine hours. Separation anxiety, teething, and standing in the crib can still interrupt that progress. Our month guides from [6 months](/6-month-old-sleep-schedule) to [12 months](/12-month-old-sleep-schedule) cover those bumps without expecting a perfect night.

## What helps — and what is just a hope

Habits that have some support:

- A predictable [bedtime routine](/bedtime-routine-for-baby). Mindell's work, discussed on that page, shows routines can help children fall asleep sooner and wake less.
- A calm, dark, safe sleep space. Bed-sharing is not a shortcut to longer sleep; Sleep Foundation, citing Merck Manual, notes it may hinder sleeping through and raises SIDS risk. See [safe sleep](/safe-sleep-for-babies).
- Putting the baby down drowsy but awake, once they are past the newborn weeks, so they have practice falling asleep in the crib (HealthyChildren.org; Sleep Foundation).
- Keeping night care boring: dim light, little talk, no play, as NHS and HealthyChildren.org both suggest.

Two behavioral methods that have been studied in older infants — bedtime fading and graduated extinction (a form of check-in or interval waiting) — are summarized by Sleep Foundation and belong with a conversation about [when to start sleep training](/when-to-start-sleep-training) and [sleep training methods](/sleep-training-methods-explained). They are not for newborns.

Things that do not reliably "make" a baby sleep through the night: starting solids early (HealthyChildren.org notes that solids do not increase sleeping through the night for breastfed infants), or keeping the baby up late so they are "extra tired." An [overtired baby](/overtired-baby) often sleeps worse.

Hunger is still a real reason to wake, especially in younger babies and in babies who are not yet gaining steadily. Dropping feeds is a separate decision; see [night weaning](/night-weaning) and talk to your pediatrician before you cut night calories.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

If your baby is not gaining, has fewer wet diapers than expected, or seems unwell, nights are a feeding or health issue first. HealthyChildren.org lists steady growth, enough daytime feeds (about 8–12 breastfeeds or 5–8 bottle feeds, depending on age), at least four wet diapers, and regular stools as signs that a healthy baby often does not need to be woken for a feed — that is about waking them, not about whether they will still wake you. If snoring, long breathing pauses, very sweaty sleep, or extreme daytime sleepiness show up, ask about those too. And if you are not coping, that is a valid reason to call, even if the baby's pattern is "normal."

## Frequently asked questions

**Do newborns sleep through the night?**  
No, not in the 8- or 12-hour sense. Short stretches and night feeds are expected.

**Is a 6-hour stretch "sleeping through"?**  
In much of the research, yes. In everyday conversation, maybe not. Both uses are common, which is why the phrase causes so many arguments.

**My 12-month-old still wakes. Is that a problem?**  
Not by itself. Pennestri's study found that not meeting a 6-hour definition at 12 months was still fairly common and was not linked to poorer development in that paper. Look at total sleep, mood, and feeding, and see our [12 month old sleep schedule](/12-month-old-sleep-schedule) and [12 month sleep regression](/sleep-regression/12-months).

**Will a dream feed make my baby sleep through?**  
Sometimes it shifts the first waking later; it does not rewrite biology. See [dream feed](/dream-feed).

**Should I let my baby "cry it out" so they will sleep through?**  
That is a method choice with a right age and family fit, not a requirement for the milestone. See [when to start sleep training](/when-to-start-sleep-training) and [cry it out](/cry-it-out-method).

## See the stretch you are actually getting (Yorix)

**Yorix** logs night sleeps so you can see whether the first stretch is growing from three hours to five or six, which is easy to miss when you are exhausted. You can also log feeds to tell a hunger waking from a brief rouse. The app is a support for tired parents, not a medical device and not a diagnosis.

## Related reading

- [Baby Sleep Cycles: Why They Wake After One Cycle](/baby-sleep-cycles)
- [Preemie Sleep: Use Due Date, Not Just Birthday](/preemie-sleep)
- [Self-Soothing: A Skill That Grows, Not a Method](/self-soothing)
- [Should You Wake a Sleeping Baby?](/should-you-wake-a-sleeping-baby)

- [How much sleep does a baby need](/how-much-sleep-does-a-baby-need)
- [Night weaning](/night-weaning)
- [Baby waking at night](/survive-night-wakings-new-parents)
- [Baby waking every hour](/baby-waking-every-hour)
- [Dream feed](/dream-feed)
- [Bedtime routine for baby](/bedtime-routine-for-baby)
- [Newborn sleep schedule](/newborn-sleep-schedule)
- [6 month old sleep schedule](/6-month-old-sleep-schedule)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026.

1. Sleep Foundation. "When Do Babies Sleep Through the Night?" Updated 11 August 2026. Medically reviewed by Nilong Vyas, MD, MPH. <https://www.sleepfoundation.org/baby-sleep/when-do-babies-sleep-through-night>. Six-hour definition; "most" around 6 months; Pennestri 38% / under 28% figures; fading and graduated extinction; bed-sharing note.
2. Pennestri MH, et al. "Uninterrupted Infant Sleep, Development, and Maternal Mood." *Pediatrics*, 2018;142(6):e20174330. <https://publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article/142/6/e20174330/37494/Uninterrupted-Infant-Sleep-Development-and>.
3. Sleep Foundation. "How Much Do Newborns Sleep?" Updated 30 September 2026. <https://www.sleepfoundation.org/baby-sleep/how-much-do-newborns-sleep>. 4–6 month longer stretches of 5–8 hours; most can go longer without a feed by 9–12 months.
4. Cleveland Clinic. "Sleep in Your Baby's First Year." Last updated 15 June 2023. <https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/articles/14300-sleep-in-your-babys-first-year>. Most babies start sleeping through the night by 6 months.
5. HealthyChildren.org (AAP). "Sleeping Through the Night." Last updated 5 September 2013. <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/baby/sleep/Pages/sleeping-through-the-night.aspx>. "Good sleeper" definition; when not to wake a growing baby; drowsy signs.
6. HealthyChildren.org (AAP). "Getting Your Baby to Sleep." Last updated 4 June 2024. <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/baby/sleep/Pages/getting-your-baby-to-sleep.aspx>. Day/night contrast; drowsy but awake from about 4 months; it is normal for a 6-month-old to wake and resettle.
7. NHS. "Helping your baby to sleep." <https://www.nhs.uk/baby/caring-for-a-newborn/helping-your-baby-to-sleep/>. Wide variation; night-and-day cues.
8. MedlinePlus. "Bedtime habits for infants and children." Cited by Sleep Foundation for 5–8 hour stretches as sleep matures. <https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/002392.htm>.

title: When Do Toddlers Stop Napping? Signs and Timing | Yorix
heading: When Do Toddlers Stop Napping?
description: When do toddlers stop napping? AASM 10–13 hours at ages 3–5, signs they are ready, quiet time instead of a forced nap, and why sources disagree on exact ages.
body:
# When Do Toddlers Stop Napping?

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 16, 2026 · **Updated:** November 16, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

Giving up the last daytime nap is a preschool project, not a first-birthday one. Our [nap schedule](/baby-nap-schedule-by-age) and [2-to-1 transition](/2-to-1-nap-transition) pages cover the earlier drops. The [2-year sleep regression](/sleep-regression/2-years) covers a nap *strike* during a bump, which is not the same as outgrowing naps. This page is about **when the afternoon nap ends for good**.

## Short answer

The AASM (AAP-endorsed) range for ages 3 to 5 is **10 to 13 hours in 24 hours, which may include a nap**. When that nap disappears, those hours should move into the night — Cleveland Clinic and Sleep Foundation both say to **offer an earlier bedtime**, not to simply subtract sleep. Timing varies. Mayo Clinic: until about age 3, most children still sleep 1 to 2 hours in the afternoon; **by age 5, most have stopped**. Sleep Foundation, citing Weissbluth's 1995 study, gives a slower curve: **almost all 3-year-olds still nap**, **60% of 4-year-olds**, **fewer than 30% of 5-year-olds**, fewer than 10% at 6, and nearly all have stopped by 7. Those two pictures agree that age 5 is a common finish line; they disagree about how unusual a non-napping 3-year-old is. We show both. KidsHealth: you cannot force a child to sleep; use **quiet time** if they will not nap.

### Key numbers at a glance

| Question | What the sources say | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sleep at 3–5 years | 10–13 hours in 24 hours, which may include a nap | AASM; KidsHealth; Cleveland Clinic |
| Mayo Clinic | Most still nap until about age 3 (1–2 hours); most have stopped by age 5 | Mayo Clinic, May 2025 |
| Sleep Foundation (Weissbluth 1995) | Almost all nap at 3; 60% at 4; <30% at 5; <10% at 6; nearly all by 7 | Sleep Foundation, 23 July 2025 |
| If still napping regularly at 7 | Sleep Foundation: ask a pediatrician to rule out another sleep issue | Sleep Foundation |
| What replaces the hours | An earlier bedtime, not a shorter day of sleep | Cleveland Clinic; Sleep Foundation |

## Signs they may be ready

Sleep Foundation's list, in our own words:

- They consistently **cannot fall asleep** at nap time, but are in an even mood on days without a nap.
- The nap is making **bedtime later** or mornings earlier, and shortening the nap has not fixed it.
- On days the nap is skipped, they are **not** falling apart in the evening.
- They no longer fall asleep at all during the usual rest, and they are not fighting sleepiness — they are simply done.

**Signs they are not ready:** evenings get much worse, they are struggling to stay awake by day even after a decent night, or the "nap refusal" is really a one-week blip after [travel](/baby-sleep-and-travel), illness, or a schedule change. In that case, keep the nap and read [baby won't nap](/baby-wont-nap).

Cleveland Clinic describes the drop as often **gradual**: naps on some days and not others, or a few days of napping then a few without. That mixed pattern is expected.

## How to make the change

There is no official week-by-week medical protocol. A sourced, practical approach:

1. **Do not quit overnight** if you can help it. Sleep Foundation suggests reducing how often or how long the nap happens, rather than ending it on a Monday and hoping.
2. **Replace nap time with quiet time** (Sleep Foundation; KidsHealth). Same place, same stretch of the afternoon, with books, puzzles, or coloring — not a car ride or a show that just makes them drowsy at the wrong hour. Some days they will still fall asleep. That is fine.
3. **Move bedtime earlier** so the 10–13 hour total still happens at night. Sleep Foundation notes that, because preschoolers may need up to 13 hours, bedtime may need to be quite early depending on the morning wake. Use your child's actual wake time; we are not setting a universal 6 p.m. rule.
4. **Keep mornings consistent.** A drifting wake time makes it harder to see whether the nap is still needed.
5. **Allow occasional naps** after growth spurts, late nights, or busy days (Sleep Foundation). One nap on a weekend is not a failure of the plan.

If preschool still has a rest period, you may not control it. Protect bedtime at home anyway.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Ask if your child is still taking a long daily nap at 6 or 7, if nights are very short but they "can't" drop the nap, or if you worry about snoring, pauses, or unusual daytime sleepiness.

## Frequently asked questions

**When do toddlers stop napping?**  
Often between about 3 and 5 years, with most children finished by 5 (Mayo Clinic) and a slower curve in the Weissbluth figures Sleep Foundation cites. The birthday is not a switch.

**Should I drop the nap if bedtime is a battle at 2?**  
Usually not. First shorten or cap the nap. Two-year-olds typically still need it. See the [2-year sleep schedule](/2-year-old-sleep-schedule).

**What if they nap at daycare but not at home?**  
Common. Keep a consistent home bedtime and a quiet afternoon when you are in charge.

**Will they sleep less overall?**  
They should not have to. Move the hours to night.

**What is “quiet time” if they will not nap?**  
It is the same afternoon slot, used for rest rather than sleep: books, puzzles, or a calm room, not a new show or a late car nap (Sleep Foundation; KidsHealth; already in “How to make the change” above). Some days they will still fall asleep; that is all right. The preschool timetable, including quiet time on no-nap days, also lives on [4 year old sleep schedule](/4-year-old-sleep-schedule).

## Watch nights get longer as naps fade (Yorix)

**Yorix** can show whether an earlier bedtime is actually replacing a dropped nap in the 24-hour total. The app cannot decide that a child is done napping, and it is not a medical device.

## Related reading

- [3 Year Old Sleep Schedule: With a Nap, or Without](/3-year-old-sleep-schedule)

- [2 year old sleep schedule](/2-year-old-sleep-schedule)
- [2-to-1 nap transition](/2-to-1-nap-transition)
- [Baby won't nap](/baby-wont-nap)
- [How much sleep a baby needs](/how-much-sleep-does-a-baby-need)
- [Baby nap schedule by age](/baby-nap-schedule-by-age)
- [Bedtime routine for baby](/bedtime-routine-for-baby)
- [2 year sleep regression](/sleep-regression/2-years)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026.

1. Paruthi S, et al. AASM pediatric sleep-duration consensus, 2016. 10–13 hours at 3–5 years, including any nap.
2. Sleep Foundation. "When Should Kids Stop Taking Regular Naps?" Updated 23 July 2025. Medically reviewed by Nilong Vyas, MD, MPH. <https://www.sleepfoundation.org/children-and-sleep/when-do-kids-stop-napping>. Weissbluth 1995 percentages; readiness signs; quiet time; earlier bedtime; occasional naps; ask a doctor if still napping regularly at 7.
3. Mayo Clinic. "Baby naps: Daytime sleep tips." May 7, 2025. Most still nap 1–2 hours until about age 3; most have stopped by age 5.
4. Cleveland Clinic. "How Much Sleep Kids Need." 4 June 2024. <https://health.clevelandclinic.org/recommended-amount-of-sleep-for-children>. Gradual drop; quiet time; move bedtime earlier so hours are not lost.
5. Nemours KidsHealth. "Naps." <https://kidshealth.org/en/parents/naps.html>. Many preschoolers give up the afternoon nap; you cannot force sleep; quiet time; earlier bedtime.

title: When to Move Your Baby From Bassinet to Crib | Yorix
