description: When to move a baby out of the bassinet: CPSC's 'about 5 months or pushing up on hands and knees,' plus weight and length limits. How to make the switch.
body:
# When to Move Your Baby From Bassinet to Crib

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 16, 2026 · **Updated:** November 16, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

A bassinet is a short-term, close-at-hand sleep space. It is not meant to last until your baby has outgrown being a baby. This page is about **limits and how to move to a crib**, not about the later problem of a toddler who "won't sleep in the crib." Keep the crib in your room until you are ready to discuss a [move to their own room](/when-to-move-baby-to-own-room); that is a separate decision.

## Short answer

Follow the **manufacturer's weight and length limits**, and move sooner if your baby reaches a developmental limit. The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission, in its federal bassinet and cradle standard, states that a bassinet or cradle is **not intended to be used beyond the age of about 5 months or when a child is able to push up on his hands and knees**. Many families also move when the baby is close to the top of the sides when lying down, or when they are clearly outgrowing the space, even before the printed weight number. The next sleep space should be a safety-standard crib, mini-crib, or play yard with a firm, flat, tight-fitting mattress and no loose bedding — the same [safe-sleep](/safe-sleep-for-babies) rules, just a larger footprint.

### Key numbers at a glance

| Question | What the sources say | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CPSC intended use | Not beyond about 5 months, or when the child can push up on hands and knees | CPSC, 2013 bassinet/cradle standard announcement |
| Sleep surface angle | In a stationary position, a bassinet is intended to be no more than 10 degrees from horizontal | CPSC (same announcement); AAP (inclines over 10° are unsafe) |
| Weight or length | Follow the limit printed by the manufacturer; there is no single official pound number that applies to every model | Product manual; CPSC requires products to meet the standard |
| Room location after the move | Still in your room for at least the first 6 months | AAP 2022; NHS; Lullaby Trust |

We are not using a universal "15 lb" cutoff. That figure appears on some parent sites and for some play-yard bassinet attachments, but it is not a CPSC rule for every bassinet. Your model's label wins.

## Why bassinets have a short lifespan

Bassinets are smaller, with lower sides than a crib. That is helpful in the first weeks, when you want the baby within arm's reach for night feeds. It becomes a problem once the baby can push up, roll with more force, or — later — sit. Falls, and faces pressed against a solid or padded side, are the incidents CPSC has been concerned with.

Pushing up on hands and knees is the developmental line CPSC names. Rolling on its own is already a reason to [stop swaddling](/how-to-swaddle-a-baby). If your baby is rolling but has not yet pushed up, still check the manual: some models tell you to stop at the first signs of rolling, and you should follow the stricter of the two.

If the bassinet rocks, swings, or has an incline, use it only in the manner the manual allows, and never as a workaround for a baby who only sleeps in motion. See [car seats, swings, and loungers](/baby-sleeping-in-car-seat).

## Bedside sleepers, Moses baskets, and play yards

These are **product categories**, not a reason to skip the move this page describes. If a product is used for sleep, it still has to be a firm, flat, approved sleep space, used as the maker intended, with only a tight fitted sheet.

- **Bedside or “next-to-me” sleepers** that meet current safety standards can be a room-sharing tool, with the baby in their own surface next to your bed. Follow the weight, roll, and assembly limits; do not leave a gap that can trap. This is not a bed-share. When the baby outgrows the product, move to a crib — the point of this article.
- **Moses baskets** are a short-use bassinet-like space for a young, non-rolling baby. They have a low weight and a short lifespan. Stop when the maker says, or sooner if the baby can roll or push up. Do not put a basket on a pillow, a sofa, or a raised surface where it can fall.
- **Play yards** (pack-and-plays) can be an approved sleep space when they meet standards and are used with their own firm, flat mattress only. Do not add a second mattress, a quilt, or a travel pillow. They also show up in [baby sleep and travel](/baby-sleep-and-travel).

In-bed sleepers, nests, pods, and docks are **not** an approved infant sleep space on [safe sleep](/safe-sleep-for-babies). Do not treat a bedside sleeper as permission to bring those back in.

## How to make the switch

You do not need a long, formal program. A few practical steps, drawn from the same safe-sleep logic used on our other pages:

1. Set up the crib or play yard in **your room** if you are still in the first 6 months (and many families stay longer). The move is about the product, not about giving up room-sharing.
2. Keep the crib boring: firm mattress, fitted sheet, no [blankets, pillows, or stuffed toys](/when-can-baby-sleep-with-a-blanket) in the first year. Lower the mattress to the height the manual specifies for a mobile baby.
3. Start with **naps** in the crib for a few days if nights feel like a big leap, then move nights too. Do not run two conflicting sleep spaces for weeks unless you are mid-transition.
4. Keep the [bedtime routine](/bedtime-routine-for-baby) the same. The change is the furniture, not the whole evening.
5. If you have been using a play-yard bassinet insert, remove it when you hit the insert's own, often lower, limit. The play yard underneath may still be usable.

Some babies sleep just as well the first night. Some startle because the space feels bigger. That is usually a [sleep association](/sleep-associations) and novelty issue, not a sign you should go back to an outgrown bassinet.

## What not to do

- Do not "get a few more weeks" by stuffing blankets around a baby who is tall for the bassinet, or by adding a second mattress.
- Do not move them into your bed as a temporary fix. See [bed-sharing](/bed-sharing-and-co-sleeping).
- Do not use a secondhand crib with missing hardware, drop sides, or a recalled design. Check CPSC recall lists.
- Do not delay the move because the crib is in another room and you are not ready for that separation. Move the crib next to your bed first.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Mention the move if your baby was preterm and is at a different "adjusted" stage than the calendar age of 5 months, or if you are unsure whether what you are seeing is pushing up versus ordinary wriggling. If the baby has already fallen from a bassinet, get them checked and retire the product.

## Frequently asked questions

**When should I move my baby out of the bassinet?**  
At the manufacturer's weight or length limit, at about 5 months, or when they can push up on hands and knees — whichever comes first, unless your manual is stricter.

**Can they go back to the bassinet for naps?**  
Not once they have outgrown it. Limits apply to every sleep.

**Is a mini-crib or play yard okay instead of a full crib?**  
Yes, if it meets current safety standards and has a firm, flat, tight mattress. The AAP lists these as acceptable sleep surfaces.

**Do I have to move them to their own room at the same time?**  
No. Room-sharing can, and for the first 6 months should, continue. See [when to move baby to their own room](/when-to-move-baby-to-own-room).

**What if they sleep worse in the crib?**  
Keep the safe product, and work on the settling habit. See [sleep associations](/sleep-associations) rather than returning to an unsafe or outgrown bassinet.

## Log the date, not the product (Yorix)

**Yorix** can hold a short note of the date you moved to the crib, which helps you remember when a change started. It cannot tell you that a bassinet is still within its limit, and it is not a medical device. Check the label.

## Related reading

- [Baby Won't Sleep in the Bassinet or Crib](/baby-wont-sleep-in-crib)
- [Crib to Toddler Bed: When and How to Switch](/crib-to-toddler-bed)

- [Safe sleep for babies](/safe-sleep-for-babies)
- [When to move baby to their own room](/when-to-move-baby-to-own-room)
- [How to swaddle a baby](/how-to-swaddle-a-baby)
- [Sleep associations](/sleep-associations)
- [Bedtime routine for baby](/bedtime-routine-for-baby)
- [Newborn sleep schedule](/newborn-sleep-schedule)
- [4 month old sleep schedule](/4-month-old-sleep-schedule)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026.

1. U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission. "CPSC Approves New Federal Safety Standard for Bassinets and Cradles." 30 September 2013. <https://www.cpsc.gov/content/cpsc-approves-new-federal-safety-standard-for-bassinets-and-cradles>. Not intended beyond about 5 months or when the child can push up on hands and knees; sleep surface ≤10 degrees from horizontal.
2. HealthyChildren.org (AAP). "How to Keep Your Sleeping Baby Safe: AAP Policy Explained." <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/baby/sleep/Pages/A-Parents-Guide-to-Safe-Sleep.aspx>. Approved crib, bassinet, or play yard; firm, flat, non-inclined; room-share at least 6 months; inclines over 10° unsafe.
3. Moon RY, et al. 2022 AAP policy, *Pediatrics*. <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35726558/>. Products should meet current CPSC standards.
4. NHS. "Sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS)." <https://www.nhs.uk/baby/caring-for-a-newborn/sudden-infant-death-syndrome-sids/>. Clear, firm, flat cot or Moses basket in the parents' room for at least 6 months.
5. HealthyChildren.org (AAP). "Why Inclined Sleepers, Crib Bumpers, and Other Products Are Bad for Baby." <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/baby/sleep/Pages/Why-Crib-Bumpers-Are-Bad-News.aspx>. Cribs, bassinets, mini-cribs, convertible cribs, and play yards with a firm, flat mattress are appropriate sleep surfaces.

title: When to Move Your Baby to Their Own Room: A Guide | Yorix
heading: When to Move Your Baby to Their Own Room
description: When to move a baby to their own room: AAP room-sharing for at least 6 months, why older 'first year' wording changed, and a practical plan for the move.
body:
# When to Move Your Baby to Their Own Room

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 16, 2026 · **Updated:** November 16, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

Room-sharing — baby in your room, in their own crib or bassinet — is one of the clearer safe-sleep recommendations. Moving them to a nursery is more of a judgment call after that. This page is about **when to make that move and how to do it**. It is not a restatement of the 6-month rule alone, and it is not the same question as [moving from a bassinet to a crib](/when-to-move-baby-to-crib), which can happen in your room.

## Short answer

The AAP, NHS, and Lullaby Trust recommend that babies sleep in the **same room as you, not the same bed, for at least the first 6 months**. Older AAP material often said "ideally the first year"; the 2022 policy uses the six-month minimum. After 6 months, there is no single official week when you "must" move. Sleep Foundation notes there is no consensus on when to stop room-sharing beyond that AAP floor. Many families move sometime between 6 and 12 months, some later. Whenever you go, keep [safe-sleep](/safe-sleep-for-babies) rules in the new room, and do not treat the move as a reason to start [bed-sharing](/bed-sharing-and-co-sleeping) on the nights it feels harder.

### Key numbers at a glance

| Question | What the sources say | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Minimum room-sharing | At least the first 6 months | AAP 2022; NHS; Lullaby Trust |
| Older AAP wording | "Ideally the first year" appeared in earlier advice; 2022 uses the 6-month minimum | AAP 2022 / HealthyChildren.org |
| Room-sharing and SIDS | Can decrease risk by as much as 50% | HealthyChildren.org (AAP) |
| When to stop room-sharing after 6 months | No official consensus date | Sleep Foundation (co-sleeping article, 2025) |

## Why the first 6 months are different

Sharing a room makes night feeds and checks easier, and it is associated with a lower SIDS risk — HealthyChildren.org, summarizing the AAP, says room-sharing can decrease that risk by as much as 50%. The baby still needs their **own** firm, flat, clear surface. Room-sharing is not bed-sharing.

The 2022 wording change matters because you will still find "first year" on older pages and on some consumer sites. We are following the current policy: at least 6 months, with room-sharing still a reasonable choice after that if it is working.

## Reasons families wait, and reasons they move

Reasons to stay in your room after 6 months:

- Night feeds are still frequent (common for breastfed babies; see [night weaning](/night-weaning) before you assume they are only a habit).
- You want the safest-known arrangement for a little longer.
- The "nursery" is not actually ready as a safe sleep space (cluttered crib, a heater too close, no working monitor if you plan to use one).

Reasons families move after 6 months:

- Everyone's sleep is worse because of mutual disturbance — a real issue, and one reason the AAP did not require a full year.
- A [bassinet](/when-to-move-baby-to-crib) has been outgrown and a crib will not fit comfortably next to the adult bed.
- Another baby is on the way, or a parent's shift work makes the room unworkable.

Sleep Foundation is honest that experts do not all name the same end date. That uncertainty is not a license to move a 3-month-old to another floor of the house.

## A practical move plan

1. **Do the furniture first, in your room if needed.** If the baby is still in a bassinet, move them to a crib *in your room*, then move the crib later. Two changes at once are harder to read.
2. **Make the nursery boring and safe.** Firm mattress, fitted sheet, no loose [blankets or loveys](/when-can-baby-sleep-with-a-blanket) until after 12 months, out of reach of cords and heaters. The same rules as before, just in a different doorway.
3. **Start with naps.** A few daytime sleeps in the new room let you see how they settle without betting a whole night on it.
4. **Keep the routine identical.** Same [bedtime routine](/bedtime-routine-for-baby), same order, same [sleep associations](/sleep-associations) you are already comfortable repeating.
5. **Decide on checks in advance.** If you are going to look in, plan how you will do it so you are not inventing a new pattern at 2 a.m. A monitor can help you wait before walking in; it is not a substitute for a safe crib.
6. **Give it more than one night.** A worse first night is common. Going back and forth every other day usually confuses the experiment.

If the move collides with an [illness](/should-you-wake-a-sleeping-baby), a [vacation](/daylight-saving-baby-sleep), or a known [regression window](/sleep-regression/6-months), waiting a week or two is reasonable.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Ask at the 6-month visit what they recommend for *your* baby, especially if the baby was premature, has a breathing issue, or is still feeding very frequently at night. If you are moving earlier than 6 months because of housing or a medical need, tell them so they can help you reduce risk rather than just saying no.

## Frequently asked questions

**When can a baby sleep in their own room?**  
The official minimum in AAP, NHS, and Lullaby Trust advice is 6 months. After that, it is a family decision.

**Is 6 months too early?**  
It matches the current AAP floor. Staying longer is also consistent with the policy. Neither is "wrong" if the crib itself is safe.

**Should twins share a nursery?**  
Each baby still needs their own safe surface. Whether those cribs are in your room or in a shared nursery is discussed on [twins and sleep](/twins-and-sleep).

**What if they sleep worse after the move?**  
Keep the safe room, hold the routine, and give it several nights. If sleep falls apart for weeks, look at [associations](/sleep-associations) and [night wakings](/survive-night-wakings-new-parents) rather than pulling them into your bed.

**Can they nap in our room and sleep at night in theirs?**  
Yes, as a short transition. Try not to make it a permanent split that you then have to unwind.

## Note the move, then give it a week (Yorix)

**Yorix** can show whether nights changed after the date you moved rooms. The app cannot tell you the right week to move and is not a medical device. Use it as a log, next to AAP timing and your pediatrician's advice.

## Related reading

- [Crib to Toddler Bed: When and How to Switch](/crib-to-toddler-bed)
- [Siblings Sharing a Room: After the Twins and Own-Room Pages](/siblings-sharing-a-room)

- [Safe sleep for babies](/safe-sleep-for-babies)
- [Bed-sharing and co-sleeping](/bed-sharing-and-co-sleeping)
- [When to move baby from bassinet to crib](/when-to-move-baby-to-crib)
- [Bedtime routine for baby](/bedtime-routine-for-baby)
- [Night weaning](/night-weaning)
- [6 month old sleep schedule](/6-month-old-sleep-schedule)
- [Twins and sleep](/twins-and-sleep)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026.

1. HealthyChildren.org (AAP). "How to Keep Your Sleeping Baby Safe: AAP Policy Explained." <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/baby/sleep/Pages/A-Parents-Guide-to-Safe-Sleep.aspx>. Room-share at least the first 6 months, not the same bed; up to 50% lower SIDS risk.
2. Moon RY, et al. "Sleep-Related Infant Deaths: Updated 2022 Recommendations." *Pediatrics*, 2022. <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35726558/>. The wording change to "at least 6 months."
3. NHS. "Sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS)." <https://www.nhs.uk/baby/caring-for-a-newborn/sudden-infant-death-syndrome-sids/>. Same room for at least 6 months.
4. The Lullaby Trust. "Co-sleeping with your baby" and safer-sleep pages. <https://www.lullabytrust.org.uk/safer-sleep-advice/co-sleeping/>. Own space, in your room, for at least 6 months.
5. Sleep Foundation. "Co-Sleeping." Updated 15 July 2025. <https://www.sleepfoundation.org/baby-sleep/co-sleeping>. No consensus on when to stop room-sharing beyond the AAP minimum.

# Why Won't My Baby Sleep? Start Here, Then Follow One Link

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 16, 2026 · **Updated:** November 16, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

This is a **routing page**, not a second guide to nights, naps, or training. If your baby is fighting sleep or simply not sleeping, use the questions below and open the matching article. We will not retell [baby waking at night](/survive-night-wakings-new-parents), [overtired baby](/overtired-baby), or the schedule pages here.

## Short answer

"Won't sleep" is usually one of a few patterns, not one mystery. Name the pattern first — *when* it happens, *how old* the baby is, and *what else* is going on — then go to the page that already owns that problem. If you are worried about breathing, color, a fever, poor feeding, or a baby who is hard to wake, skip the tree and contact a clinician or emergency services.

### A one-page decision tree

Work from the top. Stop at the first row that fits.

| If this is the situation | Open this page (not a new essay here) |
| --- | --- |
| Newborn weeks: short, round-the-clock sleeps, days and nights feel swapped | [Newborn sleep schedule](/newborn-sleep-schedule), [day-night confusion](/newborn-day-night-confusion), [should you wake a sleeping baby](/should-you-wake-a-sleeping-baby) |
| A rough spell only in the early evening, first months | [Witching hour](/witching-hour). If crying is prolonged and hard to soothe, [colic](/colic) |
| You missed early sleepy signs, or they get "wired" at the crib | [Baby sleep cues](/baby-sleep-cues), then [overtired baby](/overtired-baby) and [wake windows](/wake-windows-by-age) |
| They only fall asleep in arms, at the breast or bottle, or on the move, and protest the mattress | [Baby won't sleep in the crib](/baby-wont-sleep-in-crib), [nursing to sleep](/nursing-to-sleep), [sleep associations](/sleep-associations), [contact naps](/contact-naps) |
| Nights: wakes all night, every hour, early morning, or a short first stretch | [Baby waking at night](/survive-night-wakings-new-parents), [waking every hour](/baby-waking-every-hour), [false starts](/false-starts), [early morning waking](/early-morning-waking), [split nights](/split-nights) |
| A sudden bump at a famous age | The matching regression: [3](/sleep-regression/3-months), [4](/sleep-regression/4-months), [6](/sleep-regression/6-months), [8](/sleep-regression/8-months), [12](/sleep-regression/12-months), [18](/sleep-regression/18-months), or [2 years](/sleep-regression/2-years). Overview: [sleep regression](/sleep-regression) |
| Naps will not start, or they last one cycle | [Baby won't nap](/baby-wont-nap), [short naps](/short-naps), or a transition: [3-to-2](/3-to-2-nap-transition), [2-to-1](/2-to-1-nap-transition) |
| Illness, congestion, reflux, or noisy breathing | [Sick baby sleep](/sick-baby-sleep), [reflux and baby sleep](/reflux-and-baby-sleep), [snoring and mouth breathing](/baby-snoring-and-mouth-breathing) |
| Born early | [Preemie sleep](/preemie-sleep) — use corrected age |
| Daycare, travel, or the clock change | [Daycare and baby sleep](/daycare-and-baby-sleep), [travel](/baby-sleep-and-travel), [daylight saving](/daylight-saving-baby-sleep) |
| A toddler stalls at the start of bedtime | [Toddler bedtime battles](/toddler-bedtime-battles) |
| Already in bed, then out again | [Toddler won't stay in bed](/toddler-wont-stay-in-bed) |
| Scared of the dark, or a terrified spell they will not remember | [Fear of the dark](/fear-of-the-dark) or [night terrors](/night-terrors) |
| You want a method, or you are asking about "self-soothing" | [When to start sleep training](/when-to-start-sleep-training), [self-soothing](/self-soothing), [gentle sleep training](/gentle-sleep-training), or the [methods comparison](/sleep-training-methods-explained) |

If more than one row fits, open the one that matches *this week*, not every page at once. Stacking a new method, a room change, and a dropped feed in the same night makes the picture harder to read.

## What this hub will not do

- It will not give a new sample day. Use the age schedule pages and [how much sleep a baby needs](/how-much-sleep-does-a-baby-need).
- It will not repeat safe-sleep rules. If the current workaround is a sofa, a seat, or a wedge, go to [safe sleep for babies](/safe-sleep-for-babies) first.
- It will not diagnose teething, hunger, or a medical cause. See [teething](/teething-symptoms) only as one possible thread, and call the pediatrician if you are unsure.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Call promptly for breathing trouble, color change, fever in a young infant, poor feeding, far fewer wet diapers, or a baby who is unusually sleepy or difficult to rouse. Ask at a visit if sleep has been a struggle for weeks and none of the usual patterns above seem to fit.

## Frequently asked questions

**Why is my baby fighting sleep?**  
Often they are overtired, undertired, hungry, or used to falling asleep in a different place. Use the table: cues and overtired for "wired" protests, associations and the crib page for "only in arms," and the newborn pages if they are still very young.

**Why won't my newborn sleep unless I hold them?**  
That is extremely common. Start at [newborn sleep schedule](/newborn-sleep-schedule) and [baby won't sleep in the crib](/baby-wont-sleep-in-crib), not at a formal training method.

**Is this a regression?**  
Only if the change is a time-limited bump around a typical age or skill. Use the regression hub and the age-specific page. An ongoing pattern (crib protest, short naps, night feeds) usually has its own article.

## See which pattern is actually showing up (Yorix)

**Yorix** can show whether the hard stretch is the start of the night, the first cycle, or every hour — which is the first question in the tree above. The app cannot diagnose a cause and is not a medical device.

## Related reading

- [Autism and Sleep: Common Patterns, Not a Treatment Protocol](/autism-and-sleep)
- [Baby Head Banging and Body Rocking: Usually a Rhythm, Not a Diagnosis](/baby-head-banging-and-body-rocking)
- [Cluster Feeding: Not Reverse Cycling, Not a Witching-Hour Diagnosis](/cluster-feeding)
- [Melatonin and Children's Sleep: Not a Do-It-Yourself Sleeping Pill](/melatonin-and-childrens-sleep)

- [Overtired baby](/overtired-baby)
- [Baby sleep cues](/baby-sleep-cues)
- [Baby waking at night](/survive-night-wakings-new-parents)
- [Sleep associations](/sleep-associations)
- [Baby won't sleep in the crib](/baby-wont-sleep-in-crib)
- [Baby won't nap](/baby-wont-nap)
- [Sleep regression](/sleep-regression)
- [Safe sleep for babies](/safe-sleep-for-babies)
- [When to start sleep training](/when-to-start-sleep-training)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026.

1. This page is a directory of Yorix guides, not a new evidence review. Each destination article carries its own sources. Age, safety, and illness rules are not re-derived here.
2. For "what is normal" totals and night waking by age, see the sources already cited on [how much sleep a baby needs](/how-much-sleep-does-a-baby-need) and [baby waking at night](/survive-night-wakings-new-parents) (AASM, HealthyChildren, NHS, and related pages).

title: The Witching Hour: Evening Fussiness in Babies | Yorix

description: The witching hour is a common early-evening fuss window, often not colic: typical timing, why dusk is harder, what may help, and when to use the colic page.
body:
# The Witching Hour: When Evenings Get Fussy

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 16, 2026 · **Updated:** November 16, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

"Witching hour" is a parent phrase, not a formal diagnosis. It usually means a stretch of fussiness in the **late afternoon or evening** in an otherwise well young baby. ZERO TO THREE uses the name that way: many babies cry more at the end of the day, possibly because they are tired or have had a full day of sights and sounds, and this pattern is common in the first months and usually eases with development.

This is **not** a second [colic](/colic) article. Colic already explains the clinical "rule of threes," the Period of PURPLE Crying acronym, remedies, and medical red flags. Our colic page even has a short section that mentions the witching hour. This page's job is the everyday evening window that often **does not** meet a colic definition — what it looks like, when it tends to peak, and what is reasonable to try — plus a clear pointer back to colic when the crying is more than that.

## Short answer

The American Academy of Pediatrics describes a **regular fussy period**, often between about 6 p.m. and midnight, that **peaks at about 3 hours a day around 6 weeks** and typically falls to about 1 to 2 hours a day by 3 to 4 months. Many families call that window the witching hour, even when it is shorter than a clock-hour and even when it is not colic. ZERO TO THREE notes a broader crying curve: after a quieter start, crying often rises and **peaks around 6 to 8 weeks**, when more than two hours a day can be ordinary, and eases noticeably for most families by 3 to 4 months.

If your baby has a tough spell in the early evening, settles within a few hours, and is fairly calm the rest of the day, you are likely looking at this common pattern — not a failure of your feeding or bedtime technique. If the crying is very long, very intense, and hard to soothe across the day, read [colic](/colic) and talk with the pediatrician rather than stretching this page into a diagnosis.

### Witching hour versus colic (short contrast)

| | Common evening fuss ("witching hour") | Colic (see the dedicated page) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What it is | A parent term for a late-day fussy window | A clinical label for frequent, prolonged, hard-to-soothe crying in an otherwise well baby |
| Typical timing | Late afternoon or evening, first months | Often worse in the evening too, but defined by how much and how long, not by the clock alone |
| Usual course | Rises over the first weeks, often hardest around 6 weeks, better by 3–4 months (AAP fuss-period figures; ZERO TO THREE) | Same broad age window; the colic page owns criteria, causes, and treatments |
| What this page will not do | — | Repeat the rule of threes, the PURPLE acronym essay, or the remedies list |

## Why evenings are harder

No official body has a single proven "cause of the witching hour." The explanations parents and clinicians use are everyday ones: a day's worth of stimulation catching up, an overtired baby who is then harder to settle ([overtired baby](/overtired-baby)), a cluster of feeds in the evening, or a baby whose immature nervous system simply has a fussy shift. ZERO TO THREE links evening crying to tiredness and overstimulation after the day's input. That is a plausible description, not a lab result.

Because the name is informal, app blogs sometimes give exact start weeks (for example 2 to 3 weeks). Those timelines are popular, not a diagnosis code. We stick to the sourced crying curve: worse in the first months, often peaking near 6 weeks, usually kinder by 3 to 4 months.

## What may help, without turning into a colic-remedy list

Work through needs first: hunger, a burp, a diaper, temperature, a chance to sleep. A slightly earlier bedtime can help if the baby is falling apart from tiredness, rather than pushing through to a late "normal" hour and arriving more wound up. A dimmer, quieter room in the late afternoon reduces one source of overload. Holding, walking, and the soothing sequence on [the 5 S's](/5-s-soothing-a-crying-baby) are reasonable tools for a fussy, **awake** baby, with the same limit: side or stomach only in arms, then down on the back.

Some babies feed more often in the evening. That can be normal cluster feeding; it is not automatically a problem to fix on a sleep chart. If feeds are painful, the baby is not gaining, or you suspect reflux, use [reflux and baby sleep](/reflux-and-baby-sleep) and your clinician, not a wedge in the crib.

If nothing is working and you feel yourself getting angry, put the baby on their back in the crib or bassinet and step into another room for a few minutes. ZERO TO THREE describes this as a safe break, not neglect. **Never shake a baby.** Call someone if you can. The colic page has a longer section on looking after yourself; we will not copy it here.

## When it is more than a witching hour

Use the red-flag list on [colic](/colic) and call the pediatrician or emergency services if the crying is sudden and different, the baby has a fever (100.4°F or 38°C or higher is urgent under 3 months), is vomiting, is not feeding, is hard to wake, or has trouble breathing. ZERO TO THREE also flags a sudden change in the crying, poor feeding, unusual sleepiness, dehydration, injury, or breathing trouble. If you are low, anxious, or having thoughts that scare you, that is a reason to call your own clinician — postpartum depression is common enough that ZERO TO THREE mentions it in this context, and it is not a test you have to fail before asking for help.

## Frequently asked questions

**When does the witching hour start and end?**  
There is no official start date. The AAP's regular fussy period is often in the evening, hardest around 6 weeks, and usually lighter by 3 to 4 months. ZERO TO THREE describes a similar peak at 6 to 8 weeks and improvement by 3 to 4 months.

**Is the witching hour the same as colic?**  
Not necessarily. Evening fuss can be ordinary. Colic is the more intense, prolonged end of the spectrum and has its own definition and page.

**Is PURPLE crying the same thing?**  
The Period of PURPLE Crying is an educational framework for a normal developmental crying phase, often worse in the evening. Our [colic](/colic) page already explains the acronym. This page does not repeat it.

**Will a stricter schedule stop it?**  
A slightly earlier bedtime and a calmer late afternoon can help an overtired baby. A rigid timetable will not erase a developmental fuss window, and it is not a reason to skip feeds.

## See whether the hard stretch is really only at dusk (Yorix)

**Yorix** can show whether crying clusters in the late afternoon and evening or runs through the whole day — a useful picture when you are deciding whether this is an ordinary fuss window or something to take to the pediatrician. The app cannot diagnose colic and is not a medical device.

## Related reading

- [6 Week Old Baby Sleep: The Fussy, Hungry Middle of the Early Weeks](/6-week-old-baby-sleep)
- [6 Week Sleep Regression: A Popular Name, Not a Documented Event](/6-week-sleep-regression)

- [Cluster Feeding: Not Reverse Cycling, Not a Witching-Hour Diagnosis](/cluster-feeding)

- [Colic](/colic)
- [The 5 S's for soothing a crying baby](/5-s-soothing-a-crying-baby)
- [Overtired baby](/overtired-baby)
- [Newborn sleep schedule](/newborn-sleep-schedule)
- [Reflux and baby sleep](/reflux-and-baby-sleep)
- [Bedtime routine for baby](/bedtime-routine-for-baby)
- [Safe sleep for babies](/safe-sleep-for-babies)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026.

1. ZERO TO THREE. "When Your Baby is Fussy." 11 August 2026 (page date). Crying often rises after the first days, peaks around 6–8 weeks (more than two hours a day can be common), eases by 3–4 months; evening "witching hour" linked to tiredness and overstimulation; safe break if overwhelmed; when to seek care. <https://www.zerotothree.org/resource/when-your-baby-is-fussy/>.
2. HealthyChildren.org (AAP). "Colic Relief Tips for Parents" / "Colic." Fussy periods often between 6 p.m. and midnight; length usually peaks at about 3 hours a day by 6 weeks and declines to 1 or 2 hours a day by 3 to 4 months. <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/baby/crying-colic/Pages/colic.aspx>.
3. Cleveland Clinic. "Purple Crying: Symptoms, Causes & Treatment." Accessed 15 November 2026. Period of PURPLE Crying as a developmental phase (often starting around 2 weeks and fading by 3–5 months). Used here only as context; the acronym and remedies stay on the colic page. <https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/articles/purple-crying>.
4. Karp H. Happiest Baby, "Using the 5 S's to Soothe a Crying Baby." Mentions typical late-day irritability ("witching hours") as the setting in which parents look for soothing tools. Cited as popular usage of the name, not as a clinical definition. <https://www.happiestbaby.com/blogs/baby/the-5-s-s-for-soothing-babies>.

body:
# 4 Year Old Sleep Schedule: The Preschool Day, With or Without a Nap

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 16, 2026 · **Updated:** November 16, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

This page is the **preschool timetable** at 4, and it also answers the usual 5-year questions. We will not publish a separate `/5-year-old-sleep-schedule`. The official sleep range is the same across ages 3 to 5, so the useful difference is what the afternoon looks like, and how early the morning has to be for preschool or school.

It is not [3 year old sleep schedule](/3-year-old-sleep-schedule) (the year when many families are still deciding about the nap). It is not [when do toddlers stop napping](/when-do-toddlers-stop-napping) (the process of dropping it). It is not [toddler bedtime battles](/toddler-bedtime-battles) or [toddler won't stay in bed](/toddler-wont-stay-in-bed). Use those when the fight, not the clock, is the problem.

## Short answer

The American Academy of Sleep Medicine consensus, which the AAP has endorsed and which Caring for Kids (Canadian Paediatric Society) reprints, is **10 to 13 hours in 24 hours at ages 3–5, including any nap**. KidsHealth's preschool page uses the same 10–13 hour band. There is no official AAP bedtime on the clock.

Whether a nap still happens is the part that splits families at 4 and 5. Mayo Clinic: most children still nap until about 3, and **most have stopped by 5**. Sleep Foundation, citing Weissbluth's 1995 study, gives a slower curve: almost all still nap at 3, **about 60% at 4**, **fewer than 30% at 5**, and nearly all have stopped by 7. Those two pictures agree that 5 is a common finish line; they disagree about how typical a remaining nap is at 4. We show both. We do not average them.

KidsHealth: many preschoolers already get all of their sleep at night. For those who still nap, set a regular time and a short routine; **most of those naps are about an hour**. If they will not sleep, use **quiet time**. Caring for Kids makes the same offer: after lunch, a chance to read and relax, even on days without sleep. When the nap goes, move bedtime earlier so the night can carry the total — that shift is explained on the stop-napping page, not rebuilt here.

NHS advice for young children is in the same family: a calm, predictable routine, a set bedtime, limited evening screens, and a boring response if they get up. On screens, sources do not use one number: the AAP (via HealthyChildren.org) says **at least one hour** off before bed; the NHS suggests **30 to 60 minutes**. We report both.

### Key numbers at a glance

| Topic | What the sources say |
| --- | --- |
| 24-hour total at 3, 4, and 5 | 10–13 hours, counting a nap if there is one (AASM / AAP; Caring for Kids; KidsHealth) |
| Who still naps at 4 and 5 | Mayo: most have stopped by 5. Sleep Foundation (Weissbluth 1995): about 60% at 4, under 30% at 5. Do not average |
| Length of a remaining nap | KidsHealth: most about an hour, not a requirement |
| If there is no nap | Quiet time (KidsHealth; Caring for Kids); earlier night (see [stop napping](/when-do-toddlers-stop-napping)) |
| Screens | AAP: at least 1 hour off, and out of the bedroom (KidsHealth). NHS: 30–60 minutes off |

## What a preschool weekday can look like

These are sketches, not official timetables. Anchor the morning to the real preschool or school door, then count backward so the 10–13 hour total still fits.

**Still napping.** A fairly early morning; play and a midday meal; a regular early-afternoon sleep, often around an hour; then play, supper, and a [routine](/bedtime-routine-for-baby) that is short enough that lights-out still leaves room for a long night. A late nap is what usually pushes bedtime past sense.

**No nap, or only some days.** The same kind of morning, then a protected quiet stretch after lunch (books, rest, no new show to "help them crash"). The late afternoon can get ragged. Bring the evening forward so the night, not a secret second nap at 5 p.m., holds the day's sleep. Mixed nap and no-nap days are normal in this year; the morning does better if it stays in a narrow window.

We will not add a wake-window chart for preschoolers. A steady get-up time, an honest decision about the afternoon, and an earlier night on no-nap days do more than a timer.

Caffeine has no place here (Caring for Kids: no drinks with caffeine; also watch chocolate close to bed). A comfort object and a dim [night light](/night-lights-and-baby-sleep) are reasonable if they help a child who is [afraid of the dark](/fear-of-the-dark). KidsHealth: do not start a new pattern of lying down until they fall asleep, or of falling asleep in another room, if you can help it.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Ask if the 24-hour total is regularly short of 10 hours and days are a struggle, if loud snoring or pauses worry you (see [snoring and mouth breathing](/baby-snoring-and-mouth-breathing)), or if fears or night events need sorting ([night terrors](/night-terrors) versus nightmares).

## Frequently asked questions

**How much sleep does a 5-year-old need?**  
The same official 10–13 hour band. Many 5-year-olds no longer nap; the night has to get longer. Stay on this page for the timetable, and use [when do toddlers stop napping](/when-do-toddlers-stop-napping) for the drop itself.

**What time should a 4-year-old go to bed?**  
There is no official clock. Count back from the morning you actually have, and include any nap, so the day still lands in 10–13 hours.

**Should I keep the nap for school?**  
Only if the child still sleeps, and it is not wrecking bedtime. Quiet time can replace a nap that has already gone. Forcing a nap that will not start belongs on the stop-napping and [won't nap](/baby-wont-nap) pages, not here.

## Add up the preschool day (Yorix)

**Yorix** can help you add night sleep and any remaining nap so you can see whether the day still lands in the 10–13 hour range. The app cannot set a preschool timetable and is not a medical device.

## Related reading

- [3 year old sleep schedule](/3-year-old-sleep-schedule)
- [When do toddlers stop napping](/when-do-toddlers-stop-napping)
- [How much sleep a baby needs](/how-much-sleep-does-a-baby-need)
- [Toddler bedtime battles](/toddler-bedtime-battles)
- [Toddler won't stay in bed](/toddler-wont-stay-in-bed)
- [Fear of the dark](/fear-of-the-dark)
- [Bedtime routine for baby](/bedtime-routine-for-baby)
- [Melatonin and children's sleep](/melatonin-and-childrens-sleep)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026.

1. Paruthi S, et al. American Academy of Sleep Medicine. "Recommended Amount of Sleep for Pediatric Populations: A Consensus Statement," 2016. 10–13 hours in 24 hours at 3–5 years, including any nap. Endorsed by the AAP and reprinted by Caring for Kids.
2. Nemours KidsHealth. "Sleep and Your Preschooler." Date reviewed June 2020; accessed 15 November 2026. About 10–13 hours including naps; many preschoolers already sleep only at night; remaining naps often about an hour; quiet time if they do not nap; screens off at least 1 hour; comfort object and dim night light; do not create a new every-night lie-down-until-asleep pattern. <https://kidshealth.org/en/parents/sleep-preschool.html>.
3. Canadian Paediatric Society, Caring for Kids. "Healthy sleep for your baby and child." Last updated November 2024; accessed 15 November 2026. AASM chart for 3–5 years (10–13 hours); quiet time after lunch if the nap has gone; no caffeine; screens out of the bedroom; limits at bedtime; comfort after nightmares. <https://caringforkids.cps.ca/handouts/healthy-living/healthy_sleep_for_your_baby_and_child>.
4. National Health Service (UK). "Sleep and young children." Page last reviewed 31 March 2023; accessed 15 November 2026. Predictable routine; winding down about 30 minutes before sleep; limit the bedtime visit; dim light if needed; walk-backs with little fuss; screens off for 30–60 minutes. <https://www.nhs.uk/baby/health/sleep-and-young-children/>.
5. Mayo Clinic and Sleep Foundation (Weissbluth 1995) figures for when naps stop are reported as already used on our stop-napping page: most still nap until about 3 and most have stopped by 5 (Mayo); about 60% still nap at 4 and fewer than 30% at 5 (Sleep Foundation). Do not average those two curves.

body:
# Autism and Sleep: Common Patterns, Not a Treatment Protocol

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 16, 2026 · **Updated:** November 16, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

Sleep trouble is a **common co-occurring problem** for children on the autism spectrum (HealthyChildren.org's family overview of autism names sleep problems alongside seizures, gut symptoms, and behavioral-health issues). This page is about that overlap: what families often see, what a safer night can look like, and when to involve the pediatrician. It is not a diagnosis page, not a medication or supplement protocol, and not a second [sleep training methods](/sleep-training-methods-explained) table. We will not fold ADHD, Down syndrome, or cerebral palsy into this URL.

## Short answer

There is no official AAP "autism bedtime" on the clock. What the parent-facing pages we opened do say is practical:

- A **regular sleep schedule** and a **sleep management plan** matter, for the child's rest and because caregivers who sleep are more able to stay alert (HealthyChildren.org, wandering-safety tips).
- **Predictable, visual** cues often land better than another spoken reminder. HealthyChildren.org's media advice for families of autistic children mentions visual timers and a visual daily schedule, especially for transitions off screens.
- The AAP media guidance still applies: enough time left for play, being outside, and sleep; unplugged times and spaces in the house. Screens off **at least one hour** before bed is the general AAP rule, restated on the [melatonin](/melatonin-and-childrens-sleep) page.
- Night **wandering or bolting** is a safety issue, not a "just wait it out" settling trick. The AAP, on HealthyChildren.org, advises securing doors that lead outside, considering door alarms, and talking with the pediatrician about a sleep plan if going to sleep or staying asleep is a problem. We will not invent hardware products or a monitoring protocol here.
- If someone later raises melatonin, that conversation belongs with the pediatrician, on [melatonin and children's sleep](/melatonin-and-childrens-sleep). HealthyChildren.org says melatonin **may** help some children with autism or ADHD and should be **carefully monitored**. KidsHealth is more reserved about melatonin in general. This page will not name a dose, a brand, or a start-it-tonight plan.
- HealthyChildren.org's page on complementary therapies is blunt: unproven supplements and "natural" products are not a substitute for recommended care, can interact with medicines, and are less tightly regulated than drugs. Do not add one for sleep on your own.

The usual sleep-hygiene building blocks still help, adapted to the child: a short, same-order wind-down, a dark and boring room, and a realistic 24-hour total (see [how much sleep](/how-much-sleep-does-a-baby-need) and, for preschoolers, [4 year old sleep schedule](/4-year-old-sleep-schedule)). If the fight is a general bedtime stall, use [toddler bedtime battles](/toddler-bedtime-battles). If associations or night waking are the issue, use those pages rather than inventing an autism-only method.

### What this page will not do

| Tempting next step | Why it does not live here |
| --- | --- |
| A treatment protocol or therapy list | Out of scope; the pediatrician and the child's existing care team decide |
| A melatonin or supplement dose | [Melatonin page](/melatonin-and-childrens-sleep) only, and only after a clinician conversation |
| A second methods or self-soothing rewrite | Those URLs already exist |
| Combining ADHD, Down syndrome, or CP | Different conditions; do not merge them into this slug |
| Diagnosing autism from a sleep pattern | Sleep trouble is common in many children; it is not a test |

## A safer night, in plain terms

Work with the child's actual cues, not a generic schedule that ignores sensory load (noise, light, clothing, a new house). A visual sequence for the last half hour can make "what happens next" less of a surprise. Keep the same few objects in the bed if they help, and follow [safe sleep](/safe-sleep-for-babies) for infants (back, firm, flat, clear crib). For older children who may leave the room, the AAP's wandering advice is the safety frame: locked exit doors, a plan, and enough adult rest to stay watchful. [Night lights](/night-lights-and-baby-sleep) and [fear of the dark](/fear-of-the-dark) can be part of the same conversation if fear, not wandering, is the issue.

If sleep apnea, loud snoring, or mouth breathing is in the mix, that is a medical path: [baby snoring and mouth breathing](/baby-snoring-and-mouth-breathing). Head banging or body rocking can occur in typically developing children and, sometimes, alongside other conditions (Cleveland Clinic, on those movements) — see [head banging and body rocking](/baby-head-banging-and-body-rocking), and do not treat a rhythm at sleep onset as a diagnosis.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Talk if going to sleep or staying asleep is a regular struggle, if nights are unsafe because the child leaves the home, if breathing in sleep worries you, if you are considering any supplement or medicine, or if daytime function is falling apart. The pediatrician may involve a sleep specialist or the child's existing autism-care team. We will not guess who should be on that team.

## Frequently asked questions

**Do most autistic children have sleep problems?**  
HealthyChildren.org lists sleep problems as a common co-occurring need. That is not the same as "every child," and it is not a number we will invent.

**Can I start melatonin because I have read it helps in autism?**  
No. Read [melatonin and children's sleep](/melatonin-and-childrens-sleep) and talk to the pediatrician first. This page will not write a dose.

**Is this a reason to begin cry it out?**  
Not automatically. Any settling plan should be chosen with the child's age, communication, and safety in mind, and only if a clinician agrees it is appropriate. Start with [when to start sleep training](/when-to-start-sleep-training) and [methods](/sleep-training-methods-explained) if you are even asking the question.

## See whether nights are actually getting shorter (Yorix)

**Yorix** can help you see when bedtime slips or night wakings stack up, so a clinic visit starts with a clearer picture. The app cannot diagnose autism or treat sleep and is not a medical device.

title: Baby Head Banging and Body Rocking in Sleep | Yorix
heading: Baby Head Banging and Body Rocking: Usually a Rhythm, Not a Diagnosis
description: Baby head banging and body rocking in sleep: usually a self-soothing rhythm, when it is a problem, and how this differs from twitching or night terrors.
body:
# Baby Head Banging and Body Rocking: Usually a Rhythm, Not a Diagnosis

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 16, 2026 · **Updated:** November 16, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

Head banging, body rocking, and rolling or shaking the head from side to side are **common sleep-onset rhythms** in babies and toddlers. Cleveland Clinic (last updated 26 July 2023) says they are usually a way to self-soothe, and that they are usually not harmful unless they cause injury or regularly disrupt sleep. KidsHealth (reviewed July 2018) makes the same parent-facing point: occasional head banging is often self-stimulation, self-comfort, or a way to let off frustration, and it is not, by itself, a sign of another problem.

This is one URL for both the banging and the rocking. It is not [baby twitching in sleep](/baby-twitching-in-sleep) (brief jerks, including benign neonatal sleep myoclonus). It is not [night terrors](/night-terrors). We will not diagnose rhythmic movement disorder from a blog, and we will not treat a bedtime rhythm as proof of autism or another condition.

## Short answer

Cleveland Clinic: these movements are very common in healthy babies and toddlers. **Up to 60% of babies show them by 9 months.** They occur at similar rates in boys and girls, and they can run in families. The usual theory is that the rhythm is comforting, a bit like being held or rocked. They typically settle down by **age 2 or 3**. **By age 5, only about 5% of children without an underlying condition still show them.** Adolescents and adults rarely do.

Providers use the name **rhythmic movement disorder (RMD)** only when the same kind of movement **disrupts sleep, causes injury, or makes it hard to focus on tasks**. Most children who rock or bang do **not** have a disorder, and most who do have RMD still grow out of it. In most cases, children who make these movements have no other developmental condition. They can, less often, appear alongside other diagnoses (Cleveland Clinic lists several, including autism, ADHD, and sleep apnea). Presence of a rhythm is not a diagnosis of those conditions.

KidsHealth: try not to make a big deal of it, and do not scold. Deal with whatever is upsetting the child, and protect them from injury as much as you can.

### How this differs from nearby pages

| What you are seeing | Likely page |
| --- | --- |
| Rhythmic rocking or banging as they fall asleep, or in light sleep | This page |
| Brief jerks or twitches in sleep | [Baby twitching in sleep](/baby-twitching-in-sleep) |
| Sudden scream, looking frightened, hard to wake, little memory in the morning | [Night terrors](/night-terrors) |
| Grinding or clenching the teeth | [Teeth grinding in sleep](/teeth-grinding-in-sleep) |

## Safety at home, without turning this into a clinic note

If the child is not hurting themselves, Cleveland Clinic says there is often nothing you need to "treat." Padding the usual sleep space, keeping the crib or bed away from a hard wall, and staying with ordinary [safe sleep](/safe-sleep-for-babies) rules (infants on the back, firm and flat, clear of extras) is the practical frame. If a clinician later worries about injury, Cleveland Clinic notes that they may suggest moving the mattress or, in some cases, a protective helmet during sleep. That is a **clinical** suggestion, not a product we will recommend from this page.

Do not add pillows, bumpers, or loose bedding to "soften" a crib (that fights safe-sleep rules). Do not put a helmet on an infant on your own.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

KidsHealth: see a doctor if the banging is frequent and you also have questions about developmental delay or unusual social interactions. Cleveland Clinic: make an appointment if the movements happen a lot in the **daytime**; if there are signs of infection or injury (fever, rash, bruises, scrapes); if the child is injuring themselves or you fear they might; if there is severe snoring, pauses in breathing, or consistently wrecked sleep; if the movements worsen with irritability or stress; if the child is unusually hard to wake; if eye contact or development worries you (they name poor head control, stiffness, or trouble swallowing); or if you worry the events could be seizures. A pediatrician may take a sleep history and, if needed, consider tests to rule out other problems. We will not interpret those tests here.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is head banging at bedtime a sign of autism?**  
Usually not. Cleveland Clinic: most children who do this have no other developmental condition. If you have separate developmental questions, ask the pediatrician — do not diagnose from a sleep rhythm. See also [autism and sleep](/autism-and-sleep).

**Should I stop them mid-rhythm?**  
KidsHealth: do not scold or make it a scene. If they are safe, interrupting a comforting rhythm is often unnecessary. If you are worried about injury, talk to the pediatrician rather than inventing a home restraint.

**When does it stop?**  
Cleveland Clinic: typically by 2 or 3, and only about 5% of children without another condition still show it at 5. If it is still intense after that, or it never looks like ordinary sleep-onset rocking, ask.

## Note when the rhythm actually happens (Yorix)

**Yorix** can help you mark whether the rocking or banging clusters at sleep onset or also shows up in the day. The app cannot diagnose a movement disorder and is not a medical device.

## Related reading

- [Baby twitching in sleep](/baby-twitching-in-sleep)
- [Night terrors](/night-terrors)
- [Teeth grinding in sleep](/teeth-grinding-in-sleep)
- [Autism and sleep](/autism-and-sleep)
- [Self-soothing](/self-soothing)
- [Safe sleep for babies](/safe-sleep-for-babies)
- [Baby snoring and mouth breathing](/baby-snoring-and-mouth-breathing)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026.

1. Cleveland Clinic. "Head Banging and Body Rocking" (Baby Shaking Head, Rocking & Other Rhythmic Movement Disorders). Last updated 26 July 2023; accessed 15 November 2026. Usually self-soothing and not harmful unless there is injury or sleep disruption; up to 60% of babies by 9 months; typically subsides by 2 or 3; about 5% without an underlying condition still show it at 5; RMD is the name used when the movements disrupt sleep, cause injury, or interfere with focus; most children have no other condition; when to call; helmet or mattress-move only if a clinician recommends it for injury risk. <https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/14305-head-banging-and-body-rocking>.
2. Nemours KidsHealth. "Is Head Banging Normal?" Date reviewed July 2018; accessed 15 November 2026. Often self-comfort or a release of frustration; usually not a sign of another problem; do not scold or make a big deal; protect from injury; see a doctor if banging is frequent and developmental delay or unusual social interactions are also a concern. <https://kidshealth.org/en/parents/head-banging.html>.

title: Cluster Feeding: Short Feeds, Close Together | Yorix

description: Cluster feeding is several short feeds close together, often in the early days or evenings — not reverse cycling, the witching hour, or night weaning.
body:
# Cluster Feeding: Not Reverse Cycling, Not a Witching-Hour Diagnosis

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 16, 2026 · **Updated:** November 16, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

Cluster feeding is a **feeding pattern**: several short feeds closer together than you expected. Cleveland Clinic's example is a baby who nurses about every hour instead of every three or four. It is common in the first days of life, and it can show up later in the day — often in the evening — or when a baby wants comfort. This page is about that pattern, and about when it is *not* ordinary.

It is not [reverse cycling](/reverse-cycling) (nights getting heavier because daytime intake is low, usually later on). It is not [night weaning](/night-weaning). It is not the [witching hour](/witching-hour) (an evening fuss window, which can overlap with cluster feeds but is not the same thing). It is not the popular "second night" bump, which is a short section on [newborn sleep schedule](/newborn-sleep-schedule), not a diagnosis.

## Short answer

Cleveland Clinic, last updated 19 September 2024, says cluster feeding around the clock is **normal and expected in the first few days**. A newborn's stomach is small; frequent feeds, sometimes about hourly, are how they get enough. That around-the-clock phase generally eases as the stomach grows and milk supply comes in. **By the end of the first week, a baby should not still be cluster feeding all day and all night.**

After that first week, more frequent feeds can still be normal at certain times (Cleveland Clinic names evenings) or during a growth spurt or a need for comfort. What is **not** reassuring is cluster feeding **24 hours a day, for days on end, in a baby older than one week**. That can be a sign they are not getting enough milk — a latch problem, a temporary drop in supply, or something else a pediatrician or lactation specialist should look at. Cleveland Clinic is direct: call if a baby older than a week is cluster feeding around the clock.

This article is written from a breastfeeding source. Formula-fed babies can also want closer feeds at times; the red flags about intake, wet nappies, and unusual sleepiness still belong to your pediatrician, and we will not invent a separate official "formula cluster" protocol.

Do not try to "stretch" a day-old baby to teach a schedule. The newborn page already says they are not ready for one.

### Cluster feeding versus nearby patterns

| Pattern | What it is | Where it lives |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Several short feeds close together, especially early days or evenings | Cluster feeding | This page |
| Nights heavy because days are underfed, usually later | Reverse cycling | [Reverse cycling](/reverse-cycling) |
| Evening fuss that may or may not include feeding | Witching hour | [Witching hour](/witching-hour) |
| Popular name for a very intense second night | Not a diagnosis | [Newborn sleep schedule](/newborn-sleep-schedule) |
| Choosing to drop night feeds | A later, medical conversation | [Night weaning](/night-weaning) |

## What may help, and what is a warning

Offer the breast (or a planned bottle) when the baby is asking. Skin-to-skin and a quiet room make the stretch more tolerable. Look after yourself: a partner, a snack, a place to sit. Frequent feeding is work, not a failure of routine.

See a pediatrician or a lactation specialist if, after the first week, the "every hour" pattern never lets up, if wet or dirty nappies are fewer than you were told to expect, if the baby is hard to rouse or too sleepy to feed, or if feeding is painful and milk transfer seems poor. Those are intake questions, not a reason to wait for the cluster to "finish." The newborn page's red-flag section is the same idea.

If days later become light and nights become the only long feeds, switch pages: that is [reverse cycling](/reverse-cycling), and [night weaning](/night-weaning) is the wrong first move.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Call if a baby older than one week is cluster feeding around the clock (Cleveland Clinic), if you are worried they are not getting enough, or if weight checks or nappies are off. Ask for lactation help if latch or supply is the question.

## Frequently asked questions

**How long does cluster feeding last?**  
The around-the-clock newborn phase is usually a matter of days, easing toward the end of the first week (Cleveland Clinic). Evening or occasional clusters can return later. There is no official hour at which you "graduate."

**Is evening cluster feeding the same as the witching hour?**  
They can happen in the same part of the day. Cluster feeding is a feed pattern. The witching hour is a fuss window. Use both pages if you need both.

**Should I night-wean a cluster-feeding baby?**  
No, not as a first response, and not in the newborn days. Night weaning is a later decision on its own page.

## See whether the frequent feeds are only in the evening (Yorix)

**Yorix** can help you tag when feeds actually happened, so you can see whether they bunch in the evening or run all day. The app cannot judge intake or latch and is not a medical device.

## Related reading

- [6 Week Old Baby Sleep: The Fussy, Hungry Middle of the Early Weeks](/6-week-old-baby-sleep)
- [6 Week Sleep Regression: A Popular Name, Not a Documented Event](/6-week-sleep-regression)

- [Newborn sleep schedule](/newborn-sleep-schedule)
- [Reverse cycling](/reverse-cycling)
- [Night weaning](/night-weaning)
- [Witching hour](/witching-hour)
- [Should you wake a sleeping baby](/should-you-wake-a-sleeping-baby)
- [Nursing to sleep](/nursing-to-sleep)
- [Why won't my baby sleep](/why-wont-my-baby-sleep)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026.

1. Cleveland Clinic. "Cluster Feeding." Last updated 19 September 2024; accessed 15 November 2026. Several short feeds closer than expected (for example about every hour rather than every three to four); around-the-clock clustering normal in the first days; should not still be 24/7 by the end of the first week; later evening or comfort clusters can be normal; call if a baby older than one week is cluster feeding around the clock (possible low intake, latch, or supply issue). <https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/articles/cluster-feeding>.

description: Melatonin is not a child's sleeping pill. What HealthyChildren and KidsHealth say about safety, timing, and why a pediatrician decides — not a dosing guide.
body:
# Melatonin and Children's Sleep: Not a Do-It-Yourself Sleeping Pill

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 16, 2026 · **Updated:** November 16, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

This is a **safety and decision** page: what melatonin is, what HealthyChildren.org and KidsHealth actually say, and why a pediatrician should be in the conversation before a bottle of gummies comes home. It is not a shopper's guide, not a brand review, and not a second [bedtime routine](/bedtime-routine-for-baby). If the real problem is a fight at lights-out, start with [toddler bedtime battles](/toddler-bedtime-battles) or the [why won't my baby sleep](/why-wont-my-baby-sleep) hub.

## Short answer

Melatonin is a hormone the brain releases in the dark; it helps the body get ready for sleep. The same name is sold over the counter as a **dietary supplement**. In the United States, dietary supplements are **not approved by the FDA as sleep medicines**, and KidsHealth notes that the amount in a bottle can differ from the label, or include ingredients that are not listed.

HealthyChildren.org, writing for the American Academy of Pediatrics, is clear on the order of operations: **melatonin is not a sleeping pill**. It should be used only **after a discussion with your pediatrician**, and only after you have already tried a regular bedtime routine that does not depend on a supplement. KidsHealth is even more reserved: **doctors usually do not recommend melatonin for kids and teens**, and improving sleep habits may be all that is needed. We report both tones. We do not average them into a Yorix "start age" or a default dose.

If a pediatrician does recommend a short trial, HealthyChildren.org describes a cautious approach (lowest dose first; many children respond to 0.5 mg or 1 mg, taken 30 to 90 minutes before bed; most who benefit, including many children with ADHD, do not need more than 3 to 6 mg). That is **their** wording, not a protocol you should start on your own. KidsHealth says the doctor should help you choose the form and the dose. Inhaled or room-spray products have not been studied in children and are **not recommended** (KidsHealth).

### What the sources actually say

| Question | HealthyChildren.org / AAP tone | KidsHealth tone |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Should I start it myself? | No. Talk to the pediatrician first; habits come first | No. Doctors usually do not recommend it; talk to the doctor first |
| What might it be used for? | Short-term help while you build a routine; sometimes to reset an older child's or teen's clock after a break; sometimes, with monitoring, in children with autism or ADHD | A short trial if the doctor suggests it, for example to reset a teen's schedule, or for some conditions that affect sleep |
| Official U.S. dose guideline | There is **no** specific official dosing guideline for children; the figures above are from that page, to discuss with a clinician | The doctor figures out form and dose |
| Safety cautions | Poisoning reports in children rose from 2012 to 2021 (more than 260,000 reports; most had no symptoms, some needed hospital care, two children died). Store it as you would a medicine. Some products have contained much more melatonin than the label, or serotonin or CBD | A few poisoning reports needed hospital care; products may be mislabeled; store out of reach |

HealthyChildren.org also says we **need more research** on longer use in children, including questions about growth and puberty. Common short-term side effects they list include morning sleepiness, drowsiness, and possibly more urination at night. KidsHealth lists headaches, dizziness, anxiety, and morning sleepiness. Melatonin can interact with other medicines. Neither page treats diphenhydramine (the medicine in many "PM" or allergy products) as a home sleep aid; do not add it on your own.

## Habits first — and why screens matter

A consistent wind-down, a regular bedtime, and a dark, boring room do more lasting work than a supplement (both sources). The AAP, as stated on HealthyChildren.org, recommends **avoiding screens for at least one hour before bed**. Blue light can suppress the body's own melatonin. That habit belongs on the [routine](/bedtime-routine-for-baby) page; we mention it here because it is part of why a pill is the wrong first move.

If your child is autistic, or you are considering any supplement for sleep, read [autism and sleep](/autism-and-sleep) as well — and still do not start melatonin without the pediatrician. This page will not write a treatment plan.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Talk before you buy a supplement. Talk sooner if your child is already taking one, if they are unusually sleepy by day, if they have other medicines, or if they may have swallowed some. In the United States, Poison Control is 1-800-222-1222; call 911 if a child has collapsed, is having a seizure, has trouble breathing, or cannot be woken (HealthyChildren.org).

## Frequently asked questions

**Is melatonin safe for toddlers?**  
There is no simple yes. KidsHealth: doctors usually do not recommend it. HealthyChildren.org: only after a pediatrician conversation, and not as a substitute for a routine. Long-term use in young children is not well studied.

**Can I follow a dose I saw on a blog?**  
No. There is no official pediatric dosing guideline. If a clinician recommends melatonin, use the product and the timing they name, and store it out of reach.

**Will it fix early waking or night wakings?**  
Unlikely, by itself. Early rising and night waking have their own pages: [early morning waking](/early-morning-waking), [survive night wakings](/survive-night-wakings-new-parents).

## Note the bedtime, not the bottle (Yorix)

**Yorix** can help you see whether bedtime and wake time are actually regular before anyone discusses a supplement. The app cannot recommend or dose melatonin and is not a medical device.

## Related reading

- [Bedtime routine for baby](/bedtime-routine-for-baby)
- [4 year old sleep schedule](/4-year-old-sleep-schedule)
- [Toddler bedtime battles](/toddler-bedtime-battles)
- [Autism and sleep](/autism-and-sleep)
- [How much sleep a baby needs](/how-much-sleep-does-a-baby-need)
- [Why won't my baby sleep](/why-wont-my-baby-sleep)
- [Night lights and baby sleep](/night-lights-and-baby-sleep)

## Sources

1. HealthyChildren.org (AAP). "Melatonin for Kids: What Parents Should Know About This Sleep Aid." By Anna Esparham, MD, FAAP. Last updated 22 January 2026; accessed 15 November 2026. Not a sleeping pill; pediatrician first; habits first; short-term or clock-reset uses; possible role, with monitoring, in some children with autism or ADHD; no official pediatric dose guideline; lowest-dose figures as discussed above; 2012–2021 poisoning reports; mislabeling; long-term research still needed; screens off at least 1 hour before bed. <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/healthy-living/sleep/Pages/melatonin-and-childrens-sleep.aspx>.

Doctors usually do not recommend melatonin for kids and teens; supplements are not FDA-approved as sleep medicines; amounts can differ from the label; short-term low-dose use has been studied as likely safe, with side effects; inhaled or sprayed products are not recommended for children; the doctor should advise on form and dose if a trial is used. <https://kidshealth.org/en/parents/melatonin-supplements.html>.
