description: Responsive settling: settling in arms, hands-on settling, and how help can fade as your baby grows — the AU and UK approach, not a second methods table.
body:
# Responsive Settling: Help That Can Fade, Not a Second Methods Table

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 16, 2026 · **Updated:** November 16, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

This page is the **named approach** used in Australian and UK parent guidance: you read the baby's cues, you offer comfort, and, as they grow, you gradually offer less hands-on help. Pregnancy, Birth and Baby (PBB) calls it a gentle, supportive way to help a baby go to sleep or return to sleep. Raising Children Network describes the same idea for 0–6 months and, later, for reducing help between 6 and 18 months.

It is not [sleep training methods explained](/sleep-training-methods-explained) (the side-by-side table). It is not [gentle sleep training](/gentle-sleep-training) (chair / camping out, bedtime fading, and pick up / put down in outline). It is not the [5 S's](/5-s-soothing-a-crying-baby). It is not [self-soothing](/self-soothing) (how the skill develops). Those pages stay where they are. PBB's "transition settling (camping out)" is the same *family* as the chair method already outlined on the gentle-training page — we will name it here and send you there, not copy the steps.

## Short answer

Responsive settling starts with **tired signs**, a comfortable baby (fed, dry, not overheated), and safe sleep: **on the back**, on a firm, flat surface, in a clear cot or crib (PBB; the full list is on [safe sleep](/safe-sleep-for-babies)). Then you match the help to the age and the moment.

PBB groups the practical help like this:

- **Settling in arms** — hold and gently rock until the baby is calm or asleep, then place them on their back in the cot. Most useful in the first weeks, and often up to around 3 to 6 months. If they protest in the cot, comfort them; if they become very distressed, pick them up and start again.
- **Hands-on settling** — place the baby in the cot **awake**, on their back, and stay with them. If they are calm, give them a chance. If they cry, a hand on their body, a quiet voice, gentle "shh," or rhythmic patting of the thigh, shoulder, tummy, or mattress can help. PBB says this can suit many ages, and that younger babies up to about 6 months may respond best. You can sit by the cot and pat through the rails. If you or the baby are not getting calmer, it is all right to stop and try something else.
- **Comfort settling** — generally for **about 6 months or older**: a short comfort in the cot, then you leave when they are calm. Brief fussing is common. If the cry escalates, go back. This is not "cry it out"; if it is not helping, PBB says to try again another time, or return to hands-on or in-arms help.
- **Transition settling ("camping out")** — also usually from about 6 months: you stay nearby and, over about 1 to 4 weeks, sit or lie farther away, without doing the physical work of putting them to sleep. The how-to already lives on [gentle sleep training](/gentle-sleep-training).

Raising Children Network's 6–18 month advice is the same direction in different words: wait until one way of settling is working easily before you move to a less intensive way (for example, from feeding all the way to sleep, to rocking until drowsy, to hands-on help).

There is no official AAP protocol that uses the name "responsive settling." The steps above are public-health parent guidance from AU sources, labeled as such.

### How this sits next to other Yorix pages

| If you are looking for… | Stay here? | Go here |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cue-led comfort that can fade | Yes | This page |
| Chair method / camping-out steps | Name only | [Gentle sleep training](/gentle-sleep-training) |
| The full methods table, or cry it out | No | [Methods](/sleep-training-methods-explained), [cry it out](/cry-it-out-method) |
| UK/AU "controlled comforting" as a name | A mention | The methods and CIO pages will carry the alias (a planned merge), not a third URL |
| Whether the skill can exist yet | Context only | [Self-soothing](/self-soothing) |
| Tired signs | A reminder | [Baby sleep cues](/baby-sleep-cues) |

## A few practical limits

Learn your baby's early tired signs rather than waiting for a full melt-down (PBB lists yawning, jerky movements, rubbing eyes, and, in older babies, clumsiness or extra clinginess; our cues page has the sourced list). A short pre-sleep pattern — nappy, a story, a cuddle — helps the later steps (PBB). Wrapping or a sleep bag depends on age and safe-sleep rules; see [how to swaddle](/how-to-swaddle-a-baby) and [sleep sacks](/sleep-sacks).

PBB notes a true point that also sits on [sleep associations](/sleep-associations): if a baby *always* falls asleep in the same way (nursed, rocked, held), they may look for that same condition after a night waking. Responsive settling does not require you to withdraw all comfort from a young baby. It does mean thinking, as they get older, about how much help you still want to give at the start of sleep.

## When to talk to your pediatrician or child-health nurse

Ask if your baby is not settling at all, if you are unsure they are old enough for less hands-on help, or if feeding, growth, or breathing worries you. In Australia, Pregnancy, Birth and Baby and your local child-health nurse are the usual first calls alongside your doctor.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is responsive settling the same as sleep training?**  
It is a settling approach that can, over time, reduce how much help you give. It is not a new official method in the AAP table, and it is not cry it out.

**Can I use it with a newborn?**  
Settling in arms is written for the early weeks. Hands-on settling can start when it suits, with the baby on their back in a safe cot. You cannot spoil a young baby by holding them (Caring for Kids, on a related healthy-sleep page). Newborns are not ready for a formal independent-sleep program — see [when to start sleep training](/when-to-start-sleep-training).

**What about camping out?**  
PBB lists it as a later, "transition" form of responsive settling. Our step outline is on the gentle-training page, so we do not repeat it here.

## See how long settling actually took (Yorix)

**Yorix** can help you note whether bedtime is getting shorter or a night waking is stretching. The app cannot settle a baby and is not a medical device.

## Related reading

- [Self-soothing](/self-soothing)
- [Gentle sleep training](/gentle-sleep-training)
- [Sleep training methods explained](/sleep-training-methods-explained)
- [Baby sleep cues](/baby-sleep-cues)
- [Sleep associations](/sleep-associations)
- [Safe sleep for babies](/safe-sleep-for-babies)
- [When to start sleep training](/when-to-start-sleep-training)
- [5 S's for soothing a crying baby](/5-s-soothing-a-crying-baby)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026.

1. Pregnancy, Birth and Baby (Australian Government). "Responsive settling." Last reviewed April 2025; accessed 15 November 2026. Settling in arms; hands-on settling; comfort settling from about 6 months; transition settling / camping out from about 6 months over about 1–4 weeks; tired signs; back to sleep; cue-led, consistent help. <https://www.pregnancybirthbaby.org.au/babies/sleep-and-settling/responsive-settling>.
2. Raising Children Network. "Responsive settling for babies 0–6 months" and "Responsive settling: 6–18 months." Accessed 15 November 2026. Settling in arms, hands-on settling, and verbal reassurance; later, gradually reducing help once one way is working (for example from feeding to sleep, to rocking until drowsy, to hands-on help). <https://raisingchildren.net.au/newborns/sleep/settling-routines/patting-settling> and <https://raisingchildren.net.au/babies/sleep/settling-routines/responsive-settling-at-6-18-months-reducing-settling-help>.
3. Canadian Paediatric Society, Caring for Kids. "Healthy sleep for your baby and child." November 2024. You cannot spoil a young baby by holding them; drowsy but awake is introduced later. Used here only for that early-weeks point. <https://caringforkids.cps.ca/handouts/healthy-living/healthy_sleep_for_your_baby_and_child>.

description: Sleep after a separation or in two homes: keeping a consistent bedtime when a child splits time between households — not a second bedtime-battles guide.
body:
# Sleep After Separation or Divorce: Two Homes, One Predictable Night

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 16, 2026 · **Updated:** November 16, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

When a child splits time between two households, the hard part is often not "will they ever sleep again." It is that **bedtime and the going-to-bed pattern can stop matching**. HealthyChildren.org's page on sleep problems after separation or divorce (last updated 3 July 2019) is the source this short, practical article follows. It is not legal advice, not a custody guide, and not a second [toddler bedtime battles](/toddler-bedtime-battles) or [siblings sharing a room](/siblings-sharing-a-room) page. We will not expand it to adopted or foster sleep.

## Short answer

HealthyChildren.org: it can be difficult to keep consistent bedtimes and going-to-bed routines when a child divides time between two homes. Weekend or holiday visits to the other parent are often taken in stride, like other exceptions to a basic schedule. Problems are harder when the child makes **frequent changes** — a few days in one home, the rest in the other — or when the two homes have **widely different styles** and little cooperation. Sleep trouble, bedtime refusals, and night waking are common when a child feels torn between two parents, two rooms, and two different routines.

In a stressful stretch, a child may also regress for a while: thumb sucking or bedwetting may return, or appear for the first time, in a preschooler or school-age child; night fears can make it hard to settle. An older child may withdraw, push back, or try too hard to please. Insomnia or oversleeping can show up under emotional stress (HealthyChildren.org). Those are reasons for patience, not for a brand-new sleep-training program on night one in the new room.

### What actually helps, according to that page

| Practical step | Why it is on this page |
| --- | --- |
| Keep **duplicates** of especially favorite bedtime toys, books, or music in both homes | So a forgotten object does not become the whole fight (HealthyChildren.org) |
| Aim for a **similar bedtime and a similar short routine** in both places | The fight is usually irregularity, not the color of the duvet |
| Work together more closely than may feel natural | HealthyChildren.org: it takes unusually close teamwork — perhaps even closer than when you lived under one roof |
| Give regressions time once the new pattern is stable | Sleep problems and other symptoms should gradually ease over **several weeks**. If they persist, talk to the pediatrician, who may suggest counseling or a support group |

We will not write a parenting-plan clause, a holiday calendar, or advice about who is "right." If the child is stalling, leaving the bed, or afraid of the dark in *one* settled home, use the pages written for those jobs: [toddler bedtime battles](/toddler-bedtime-battles), [toddler won't stay in bed](/toddler-wont-stay-in-bed), [fear of the dark](/fear-of-the-dark), [separation anxiety at night](/separation-anxiety-and-sleep). If a new baby has arrived in one household, [sleep regression](/sleep-regression) and the age-page already cover that bump.

A comfort object, a dim [night light](/night-lights-and-baby-sleep), and the same few books at both addresses go farther than two competing "systems." Screens off before bed still applies (the AAP's at-least-one-hour rule is on the [melatonin](/melatonin-and-childrens-sleep) and preschool-schedule pages). Do not start melatonin to "get them through the transition" without the pediatrician.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

HealthyChildren.org: once the family's situation has stabilized, these sleep problems should gradually disappear over several weeks. If they do not, talk to your pediatrician. Ask sooner if the child is unsafe at night, if bedwetting is new and persistent, if you worry about mood or withdrawal, or if nights are a battleground in both homes.

## Frequently asked questions

**Should both homes use the exact same bedtime?**  
As close as real life allows. The source's point is consistency and cooperation, not a legal standard.

**What if one home has no routine?**  
This page cannot referee. You can still keep your house predictable, duplicate the comfort objects, and ask the pediatrician for help if sleep does not recover after several weeks of a more stable pattern.

**Is this the same as night-time separation anxiety?**  
It can look similar. The difference is the two-home, two-routine stress. Use [separation anxiety at night](/separation-anxiety-and-sleep) when the fear is being apart from you in a settled house.

## See whether both houses are running late (Yorix)

**Yorix** can help you see whether bedtime and night wakings look different on days in each home. The app cannot write a parenting plan and is not a medical device.

## Related reading

- [Toddler bedtime battles](/toddler-bedtime-battles)
- [Toddler won't stay in bed](/toddler-wont-stay-in-bed)
- [Separation anxiety at night](/separation-anxiety-and-sleep)
- [Fear of the dark](/fear-of-the-dark)
- [Siblings sharing a room](/siblings-sharing-a-room)
- [Sleep regression](/sleep-regression)
- [4 year old sleep schedule](/4-year-old-sleep-schedule)
- [Bedtime routine for baby](/bedtime-routine-for-baby)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026.

1. HealthyChildren.org (AAP). "Sleep Problems After Separation or Divorce." Last updated 3 July 2019; accessed 15 November 2026. Consistent bedtimes are harder when a child splits time between two homes; frequent changes and uncooperative, mismatched styles make sleep trouble more likely; duplicate favorite bedtime objects; close teamwork; regressions (including thumb sucking, bedwetting, night fears, insomnia or oversleeping) can appear for a while; once the situation is stable, symptoms should ease over several weeks; if they persist, talk to the pediatrician, who may suggest counseling or a support group. This article is not legal advice. <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/healthy-living/sleep/Pages/Sleep-Problems-After-Separation-or-Divorce.aspx>.

description: Toddler teeth grinding in sleep (bruxism): why it is common, when to see a dentist, and how it differs from ordinary teething pain.
body:
# Teeth Grinding in Sleep: Toddler Bruxism, Not a Second Teething Page

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 16, 2026 · **Updated:** November 16, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

The grating sound from a crib or toddler bed is often **bruxism**: clenching or grinding the teeth, usually during sleep (including naps). HealthyChildren.org (last updated 17 April 2026) says it is common in toddlers and preschoolers and can even start before a child's first birthday. This page is about that habit. It is not a second [teething and sleep](/teething-symptoms) article, even though teething pain is one possible trigger.

## Short answer

Many children grind or clench and never know they are doing it. Family members hear it first. Most outgrow it without lasting damage (KidsHealth, reviewed January 2021). The two parent pages we opened do not use the same "when it stops" line, and we will not average them: HealthyChildren.org says **in most cases it disappears by age 6**; KidsHealth says **most kids outgrow bruxism when they lose their baby teeth**. Until then, routine dental visits are the way to catch wear early.

Research has not pinned down one cause (HealthyChildren.org). Contributors that dentists and pediatricians often discuss include stress (school, family, friendships, even an argument at home), teeth that do not line up, irritation in the mouth, pain from teething or an earache, allergies that affect breathing in sleep, some sleep disorders, some health conditions, and some stimulant or antipsychotic medicines, including some ADHD medicines. HealthyChildren.org also notes research linking **secondhand smoke** (tobacco or cannabis) with bruxism.

KidsHealth lists similar everyday triggers (alignment, pain, stress) and, less often, medical reasons such as hyperactivity, cerebral palsy, or some medicines. By itself, bruxism is **not** a sign of a serious mental-health problem (HealthyChildren.org), even when stress is part of the picture.

### Signs, and when it is more than a sound

| What you may notice | What sources say to do |
| --- | --- |
| Grinding noises in sleep | Common; often more bothersome to the household than to the child (KidsHealth) |
| Morning face, ear, or jaw soreness; pain with chewing; sensitive teeth | Mention it to the dentist and, if it is regular, the pediatrician |
| Chipped, cracked, or worn teeth | A dental visit; permanent teeth need protection if an older child is grinding (HealthyChildren.org) |
| Loud grinding plus a child who does not seem to get enough rest | HealthyChildren.org: a sleep study may be the next conversation — the clinician decides, not this page |

HealthyChildren.org also flags jaw soreness in older children, because grinding that continues into the teen or adult years can be linked with temporomandibular joint (TMJ) and muscle problems.

## What may help — without inventing a treatment

A calm bedtime wind-down is the first practical step both pages name: a warm bath or shower, quiet music, a book, or (on HealthyChildren.org) simple breathing; teens may want to design their own version. Screens off **at least one hour** before bed helps at every age (HealthyChildren.org). If stress is the likely fuel, KidsHealth: ask what is upsetting them and help with that, rather than only treating the sound.

Do not invent dental treatment at home. If teeth are sore or damaged, the dentist may recommend a **custom night guard** made from a mold of the child's teeth (both pages). HealthyChildren.org: over-the-counter guards exist, but a custom guard is usually more comfortable and more effective, and this is typically a conversation for **older** children when a dentist or orthodontist sees worrisome damage. We will not name a brand or a start-at-home age.

Medication changes, if a medicine is a suspected trigger, are a **pediatrician** decision (HealthyChildren.org). Sleep-related breathing problems belong on [baby snoring and mouth breathing](/baby-snoring-and-mouth-breathing), not here.

## When to talk to the dentist or pediatrician

See the dentist if you hear regular grinding, if there is morning pain, or if teeth look worn or chipped. See the pediatrician as well if sleep seems poor, breathing in sleep worries you, a medicine might be involved, or you have questions about stress or another condition. In rare cases, KidsHealth says, everyday stress relief is not enough; if the child cannot sleep or is acting unlike themselves, work with the dentist or doctor on a plan.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is this just teething?**  
Teething pain can be a trigger, but bruxism is its own habit and can last after a tooth has come through. Use [teething and sleep](/teething-symptoms) for the eruption itself.

**Will they damage their adult teeth?**  
Most young children outgrow grinding before that is a long-term problem. HealthyChildren.org: take chipped, cracked, or worn teeth in an older child seriously, so permanent teeth can be protected.

**Can I buy a guard at the pharmacy tonight?**  
Ask the dentist first. Both pages point to a custom guard if one is needed, not to a casual over-the-counter fix.

## Note how often you hear the grinding (Yorix)

**Yorix** can help you mark nights when the grinding is loud or the morning is sore, so a dental visit has a clearer history. The app cannot examine teeth and is not a medical device.

## Related reading

- [Teething and sleep](/teething-symptoms)
- [Baby snoring and mouth breathing](/baby-snoring-and-mouth-breathing)
- [Bedtime routine for baby](/bedtime-routine-for-baby)
- [Baby head banging and body rocking](/baby-head-banging-and-body-rocking)
- [Night terrors](/night-terrors)
- [Toddler bedtime battles](/toddler-bedtime-battles)
- [Melatonin and children's sleep](/melatonin-and-childrens-sleep)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026.

1. HealthyChildren.org (AAP). "Teeth Grinding in Children: What to Know About Bruxism." Last updated 17 April 2026; accessed 15 November 2026. Common in toddlers and preschoolers and can start before the first birthday; most cases disappear by age 6; possible contributors including stress, alignment, teething or earache, allergies, some medicines, some conditions, and secondhand smoke; when to involve the dentist or doctor; bedtime routine and screens off at least 1 hour; custom night guard for older children with worrisome damage, rather than a casual over-the-counter guard. <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/healthy-living/oral-health/Pages/Teeth-Grinding-in-Children.aspx>.
2. Nemours KidsHealth. "Bruxism (Teeth Grinding or Clenching)." Medically reviewed January 2021; accessed 15 November 2026. Many kids have it and most outgrow it when they lose their baby teeth; causes, possible problems (headaches, worn enamel, soreness); dentist diagnosis; custom night guard if teeth are damaged or the jaw is sore; a relaxing bedtime; ask about stress; see a clinician if everyday steps are not enough. <https://kidshealth.org/en/parents/bruxism.html>.

description: 12 week old baby sleep: the 14–17 hour band, 5–6 hour night stretches for some, early bedtime false starts, and how this differs from a 3-month schedule.
body:
# 12 Week Old Baby Sleep: Longer Nights for Some, Still Not a Timetable

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 16, 2026 · **Updated:** November 16, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

This is the **week 12 snapshot**. It is not [3 month old sleep schedule](/3-month-old-sleep-schedule) (the month timetable — 12 weeks is three months) and not [3 month sleep regression](/sleep-regression/3-months) (the place for "is this the 4-month change starting early?"). If bedtime falls apart 30–45 minutes in, use [12 week old false starts](/12-week-old-false-starts).

## Short answer

You are still in the **0–3 month** sleep band: **14–17 hours** in 24 hours (NSF via KidsHealth), with the same wider published ranges as earlier week pages. The AASM's official duration recommendations **have not started yet**; they begin at 4 months. We will not give you a unique official "week 12 total."

What may be new is a **longer night stretch**. KidsHealth: at 1–3 months, "sleeping through the night" often means **about 5 or 6 hours**, not a 12-hour, no-wake night. Newcastle Hospitals NHS and Derbyshire NHS, already used on the 3-month page, describe around **5 hours** as a possible longest stretch by about 3 months for some babies. Others still wake much more often. Both can be normal in a baby who is feeding and growing.

Days can look slightly more predictable, and a slightly earlier bedtime starts to be a reasonable experiment. Formal sleep training is still usually early (Sleep Foundation: often 4–6 months). If sleep has suddenly gone backwards after a better spell, read the 3-month regression page before you name a new event.

### Key numbers at a glance

| Topic | What sources say | Who |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 24-hour total | 14–17 hours at 0–3 months; AASM not yet in force | NSF / KidsHealth; AASM |
| A longer night stretch | About 5–6 hours is the usual "through the night" meaning at 1–3 months; some NHS pages mention around 5 hours by about 3 months | KidsHealth; Newcastle / Derbyshire NHS |
| Naps | Many babies at 1–3 months take 2–3 daytime naps — still a wide range | KidsHealth |
| Awake time | Cleveland Clinic: about 1–2 hours at 1–3 months | Cleveland Clinic |
| Training | Generally later, around 4–6 months | Sleep Foundation |

## What is usually going on this week

The body clock has had a few weeks to practise (Sleep Foundation's 8–9 week landmark is behind you). Morning light and a boring night are more worth protecting. Three-month well visits and, in many places, **immunizations** also land around now — extra fuss or sleepiness can follow; do not over-bundle (see [sick baby sleep](/sick-baby-sleep)).

Rolling may be starting for a few babies and is still in the future for many. If they are trying to roll, stop swaddling with arms in — [how to swaddle](/how-to-swaddle-a-baby).

## What parents often struggle with at 12 weeks

From recurring community threads, in our words:

- Wanting a "real schedule" because a friend already has a 7 p.m. bedtime. Some 12-week-olds can handle an earlier night; some still do better a bit later. There is no official AAP clock.
- A first **false start**: down after the routine, up 30–45 minutes later. That is this week's specialist page, not a reason to jump into a full training method.
- One 5-hour stretch that does not repeat the next night, and a fear that you "broke" it by feeding.
- Short naps that have not lengthened just because the calendar said 3 months.

## A slightly earlier evening (example only)

This is not the 7:00 a.m. / 7:30 p.m. grid on the 3-month page.

Try a *sketch* in which the last nap is done early enough that the baby is clearly tired, but not screaming, around 8:00 p.m. A short bath or wash, a feed, a song, down in the crib or bassinet **awake or nearly so**. If they are up at 8:35, treat it as a [false start](/12-week-old-false-starts), not as morning. Night feeds still happen. If an 8:00 lights-out produces a worse evening, you have learned something; you have not failed week 12.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Ask if the 24-hour total looks far outside the band and days are a struggle, if you are considering dropping night feeds, if snoring or pauses worry you, or if a sudden change came with illness. Fever under 12 weeks (or 3 months, follow your local rule) is always a call.

## Frequently asked questions

**What is a good bedtime for a 12 week old?**  
There is no official time. Count backward from a morning that works for your house, include naps, and stay inside a realistic 14–17 hour day. Earlier is a trial, not a law.

**How long should a 12 week old nap?**  
There is no official nap length. Many naps are still one cycle. See [short naps](/short-naps) for later months, and do not force that plan this week.

**Is this the 12 week sleep regression?**  
Use [3 month sleep regression](/sleep-regression/3-months).

## See whether the long stretch actually repeats (Yorix)

body:
# 12 Week Old False Starts: Up Again Before the Night Has Begun

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 16, 2026 · **Updated:** November 16, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

A **false start** is a full waking within about the first hour after bedtime, often at **30–45 minutes**, around the end of the first sleep cycle. That definition already lives on [false starts](/false-starts). This page is only about what that looks like at **12 weeks**, when nights are just starting to organise and a formal "move the last wake window by 15 minutes" plan is usually still early. It is not [12 week old baby sleep](/12-week-old-baby-sleep), not [3 month sleep regression](/sleep-regression/3-months), and not [short naps](/short-naps) (a short *daytime* cycle).

## Short answer

At 12 weeks, a 30–45 minute post-bedtime wake is common enough that parent communities treat it as a stage, not a rare glitch. The general false-starts page (which notes that "false start" is a coach term, not a medical one) lists typical causes: undertired, overtired, needing the same help you used to fall asleep, hunger, or discomfort.

Those causes can all be true at 12 weeks, with a different emphasis:

- Bedtime may have been moved **earlier** than the baby can yet handle, so 7:00 p.m. looks like a late nap, not the night.
- The evening fussy stretch may not be finished (PURPLE Crying often eases by 3–4 months, not on a switch at week 12).
- A 5–6 hour "through the night" stretch (KidsHealth's usual meaning at 1–3 months) has not started, and the first cycle simply ends with a feed.
- The baby falls asleep in arms and protests the crib 20 minutes later — a [sleep association](/sleep-associations) starting to show, not a reason to begin cry-it-out tonight.

Sleep Foundation generally discusses formal sleep training around **4–6 months**. Use this page to **triage**, then visit the general false-starts article when a gentle 15-minute adjustment is actually age-appropriate. Do not paste that 5-step plan here.

### 12 weeks vs the general false-starts page

| Question | At 12 weeks | Later |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Is this a false start? | Yes, if they fully wake within about an hour of bedtime | Same definition — [false starts](/false-starts) |
| First move | Check whether bedtime was ambitious, whether they are hungry, whether the evening fuss is still running | A measured change to the last wake window is often the main lever |
| Formal training | Usually still early | When readiness fits, see [when to start sleep training](/when-to-start-sleep-training) |
| One good 5-hour stretch last night | Does not guarantee tonight will match | Nights may be more stable, but regressions can still appear |

## What parents often describe

Recurring community situations, in our words: "down at 7:00, up at 7:30"; the baby would have stayed asleep in arms; it only happens at bedtime, not after later night feeds; pushing bedtime later seemed to help more than a darker room. Those are clues, not a study.

## What to try tonight (a light triage)

1. Treat 7:30 p.m. as **still evening**, not morning: dim, boring, no play.
2. Offer a feed if it has been a long gap, then put them back down on the back in a clear, firm space.
3. If this only started when you jumped bedtime earlier by an hour, try a slightly later wind-down for a few nights before you invent a training method.
4. If they are inconsolable and this is new with a fever or poor feeds, stop troubleshooting and call the pediatrician.

The deeper "overtired vs undertired" check and the 15-minute plan stay on the general page for when the baby is older.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Ask if every night starts with an hour of distress, if you worry they are in pain, if breathing is noisy, or if you are not coping. A few false starts in an otherwise feeding, growing 12-week-old are a common early-night pattern, not an emergency.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is a 12 week false start the 12 week regression?**  
Not automatically. If the whole 24 hours has gone backwards, read [3 month sleep regression](/sleep-regression/3-months). If it is only the first cycle after lights-out, stay here.

**Should I just hold them until they are deeply asleep?**  
You can get through tonight that way. It may also be the association you later change. See [sleep associations](/sleep-associations) and do not force a week-12 extinction plan.

**When can I use the full false-starts plan?**  
When the baby is closer to the usual training-readiness window, or when your pediatrician agrees a gentle schedule tweak is appropriate. The plan lives on [false starts](/false-starts).

## See whether the first stretch always dies (Yorix)

**Yorix** can help you see if the first wake is always at 30–45 minutes, or only on early-bedtime nights. The app cannot run a false-start plan and is not a medical device.

## Related reading

- [12 week old baby sleep](/12-week-old-baby-sleep)
- [3 month sleep regression](/sleep-regression/3-months)
- [3 month old sleep schedule](/3-month-old-sleep-schedule)

- [Witching hour](/witching-hour)

3. Sleep Foundation. Formal sleep-training readiness generally discussed around 4–6 months. Accessed 15 November 2026.
4. National Center on Shaken Baby Syndrome, Period of PURPLE Crying. The fussy pattern often eases by 3–4 months, so late-evening fuss can still be in the picture at 12 weeks. <https://www.dontshake.org/purple-crying>. Accessed 15 November 2026.

body:
# 2 Week Old Baby Sleep: Pieces, Feeds, and 'Sleeping All Day'

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 16, 2026 · **Updated:** November 16, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

This is a **week 2 snapshot**, not a timetable and not [newborn sleep schedule](/newborn-sleep-schedule) (the first-weeks overview). It is also not [1 month old sleep schedule](/1-month-old-sleep-schedule). If you are asking whether long sleep can be unsafe, use [can a newborn sleep too much](/can-a-newborn-sleep-too-much) as well.

## Short answer

There is still **no official clock schedule** at 14 days. Hunger, not daylight, mostly runs the day. For the 0–3 month band, the National Sleep Foundation figure quoted by KidsHealth is **14–17 hours in 24 hours**, in pieces. Other ranges are wider: Sleep Foundation and Pregnancy, Birth and Baby give **11–19 hours**; NHS pages describe anything from about **8 to 18 hours** as possible in the newborn months. HealthyChildren.org describes **about 16–17 hours**, often only **1–2 hours at a time**. We report those bands. We do not invent a special "week 2 total," and we do not average the ranges.

Feeds are still frequent. KidsHealth: in the first weeks, wake a newborn who is sleeping a long stretch **about every 3–4 hours to feed** until weight gain is going well — often through the first couple of weeks — then ask your pediatrician whether a longer night stretch is all right. HealthyChildren.org's formula-feeding Q&A: in the first month, wake a formula-fed baby who sleeps **more than 4–5 hours**. Those two clocks do not match perfectly. Your baby's doctor, not this page, sets the alarm.

Parents often describe week 2 as "they sleep all day" or "they suddenly did a 5-hour stretch — did I do something wrong?" Those are the worries of this week. They are not a "2 week sleep regression". A baby who is **hard to wake**, feeding poorly, or jaundiced needs a clinical call, not a wait-and-see schedule.

### Key numbers at a glance

| Topic | What sources say | Who |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 24-hour total at 0–3 months | 14–17 hours (other ranges 11–19, or NHS about 8–18). No official week-2 figure | NSF / KidsHealth; Sleep Foundation; PBB; NHS |
| Length of a single stretch | Often 1–2 hours; rarely more than 3 hours in the early weeks | HealthyChildren.org; Newcastle Hospitals NHS (on the newborn page) |
| Wake to feed | KidsHealth: about every 3–4 hours until weight gain is good. HC formula Q&A: wake in the first month if more than 4–5 hours | KidsHealth; HealthyChildren.org |
| Wet diapers after days 4–5 | At least 5–6 a day | HealthyChildren.org |

## What week 2 is usually about

The first nights are already behind you. Feeding still drives almost every waking. Breastfed babies often feed about every 2–3 hours; bottle-fed babies about every 3–4 hours (KidsHealth). A slightly longer stretch can appear and then disappear the next night. That is ordinary, not a new skill you must protect at all costs.

Day and night may still look backwards: long, sleepy stretches in the light, more stirring after dark. The body clock is not in charge yet. Pregnancy, Birth and Baby places the *start* of that clock later, around 4–6 weeks. Do not try to "fix" week 2 with a 7 p.m. bedtime.

Safe sleep does not change because they are 14 days old: **on the back**, firm and flat, clear space, in your room — see [safe sleep](/safe-sleep-for-babies). If you find them on their side, roll them onto the back again; that question lives on [baby sleeping on the stomach](/baby-sleeping-on-stomach).

## What parents often ask at 2 weeks

These situations come up again and again in parent communities. We describe them in our own words. They are not statistics, and they are not a diagnosis.

- **Sleeping "all day."** Newborns can look almost always asleep and still be in a normal range. The useful checks are on the too-much-sleep page: they wake to feed or can be woken, they have enough wet diapers, they have some alert moments, and they are not floppy or hard to rouse.
- **A first 4- or 5-hour stretch.** Ask whether your pediatrician still wants night feeds at set gaps. If yes, wake them. If weight gain is already good and you were told a longer stretch is all right, keep the room dark and do not start a noisy "morning."
- **Hard to wake for a feed.** Try unwrapping, a diaper change, skin-to-skin. If they will not rouse, feed poorly, or look yellow or unwell, that is a same-day clinical question, especially in the first two weeks.

## A stretch of an afternoon (example only)

We are not publishing a 7 a.m. timetable this week — that shape already lives on the month pages and would fake a routine you do not have yet. Think in **loops**.

One afternoon might go: a feed at about 2:00, a brief diaper and a look at your face, asleep in the bassinet by 2:25, a short waking around 3:10 that settles with a hold, a proper waking and feed at 4:00, then another messy 40-minute nap on your chest because the bassinet did not work. Tomorrow the same hours will not match. The newborn page already shows a morning loop; this is only to show how scrappy a week-2 afternoon can look and still be ordinary.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Call if you cannot wake them for feeds, if wet diapers are fewer than you were told to expect, if they seem jaundiced or floppy, if breathing worries you, or if you were given a jaundice or weight-gain plan and cannot stick to it. The fuller red-flag list is on the newborn page. In the U.S., 911 or emergency care for a baby who cannot be woken, is struggling to breathe, or is a colour you do not recognise.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is there a 2 week sleep regression?**  
No official one. Early-days cluster feeding and very broken nights are common. See [cluster feeding](/cluster-feeding) and the "second night" note on the newborn page. Do not start a training plan.

**Can a 2 week old sleep too much?**  
Sometimes long sleep is normal, and sometimes it is a reason to wake them or to call. Use [can a newborn sleep too much](/can-a-newborn-sleep-too-much).

**Should I start a bedtime routine now?**  
A short, dim, boring wind-down is harmless. A clock bedtime that you defend is not a week-2 job.

## Log the stretches, not a timetable (Yorix)

**Yorix** can help you see how long stretches actually lasted, and when feeds happened, so a weight-check visit is not a blur. The app cannot tell you whether to wake a baby and is not a medical device.

## Related reading

- [Newborn sleep schedule](/newborn-sleep-schedule)
- [Can a newborn sleep too much?](/can-a-newborn-sleep-too-much)
- [Should you wake a sleeping baby](/should-you-wake-a-sleeping-baby)
- [Cluster feeding](/cluster-feeding)
- [Newborn day-night confusion](/newborn-day-night-confusion)
- [Safe sleep for babies](/safe-sleep-for-babies)
- [6 week old baby sleep](/6-week-old-baby-sleep)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026.

1. National Sleep Foundation panel (Hirshkowitz et al., 2015), as quoted by Nemours KidsHealth. 14–17 hours in 24 hours for 0–3 months. Accessed 15 November 2026.
2. Sleep Foundation and Pregnancy, Birth and Baby newborn ranges (11–19 hours) and NHS newborn ranges (about 8 to 18 hours), as already reported on our newborn-sleep-schedule page. No official week-2 total. Accessed 15 November 2026.
3. HealthyChildren.org (AAP). Newborn sleep often about 16–17 hours, frequently in 1–2 hour stretches; wet diapers at least 5–6 a day after days 4–5. Formula-feeding Q&A: in the first month, wake a formula-fed baby who sleeps more than 4–5 hours. Accessed 15 November 2026.
4. Nemours KidsHealth. Wake a newborn about every 3–4 hours to feed until weight gain is going well, often the first couple of weeks; breastfed babies often feed every 2–3 hours, bottle-fed every 3–4 hours. Accessed 15 November 2026.
5. Pregnancy, Birth and Baby. Circadian rhythm begins to develop around 4–6 weeks (so it is not in charge at week 2). Accessed 15 November 2026.

body:
# 6 Week Old Baby Sleep: The Fussy, Hungry Middle of the Early Weeks

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 16, 2026 · **Updated:** November 16, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

This is the **week 6 snapshot**. It is not [1 month old sleep schedule](/1-month-old-sleep-schedule) (weeks 4–7 as a month view) and not [6 week sleep regression](/6-week-sleep-regression) (the popular name for this rough patch). If evenings are the whole problem, also use [witching hour](/witching-hour) and [cluster feeding](/cluster-feeding) rather than copying those pages here.

## Short answer

The official 24-hour band has **not** changed: for 0–3 months, KidsHealth quotes the National Sleep Foundation **14–17 hours**. Wider ranges still apply (11–19; NHS about 8–18). There is no separate AAP or NSF "week 6 quota."

What *has* often changed is the texture of the day. Pregnancy, Birth and Baby: the body clock **starts to develop around 4–6 weeks**, so light and dark begin to matter a little more — not as a finished timetable. Many families also hit a harder evening: more fuss, more frequent feeds, shorter daytime naps. Parent communities often call this a "6 week regression" or a "growth spurt." There is **no official sleep-regression event** at 6 weeks (see the regression page). The Period of PURPLE Crying, a well-described fussy period, often **peaks around 6–8 weeks** and then eases by 3–4 months (National Center on Shaken Baby Syndrome and clinical explainers). That is a crying pattern, not a sleep-hour chart.

Do not start formal sleep training this week. Sleep Foundation generally places readiness later, around 4–6 months.

### Key numbers at a glance

| Topic | What sources say | Who |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 24-hour total | Still the 0–3 month band: 14–17 hours (other ranges as above). No week-6 official total | NSF / KidsHealth |
| Body clock | Begins to develop around 4–6 weeks | Pregnancy, Birth and Baby |
| Fussy period | Period of PURPLE Crying often begins ~2 weeks, peaks ~6–8 weeks, eases by 3–4 months | NCSBS / clinical explainers |
| "Sleeping through" at 1–3 months | A stretch of about 5–6 hours, not 12 hours — and not required at 6 weeks | KidsHealth |

## What is usually going on this week

Babies are often a little more awake and interested, which is lovely at 10 a.m. and miserable at 6 p.m. Feeds may pack together in the late afternoon and evening — that is [cluster feeding](/cluster-feeding), and after the first week it should not be *around the clock* without a feeding check. A short, same-order wind-down (dim light, feed, a song) can start to mean "night," because the clock is just beginning to listen. It will not switch off an evening peak by itself.

Social smiling is often appearing around this stretch; the usual pediatric milestone language is a social smile **by 2 months**. Do not treat a missed smile at exactly 42 days as a sleep problem. If development worries you, ask the pediatrician, not a schedule.

## What parents often struggle with at 6 weeks

Paraphrased from recurring community threads, not from a survey:

- A loose daytime pattern seemed to start last week, and this week it fell apart.
- From late afternoon, the baby will not settle in the bassinet and wants to feed again and again.
- Naps in the crib are 20–40 minutes; longer sleep happens only in arms.
- Nights that had one slightly longer stretch go back to hourly waking for a while.

None of that, by itself, means you caused a "bad habit." It also does not mean you should run a cry-it-out plan. Get through the evening with help if you can, keep nights boring, and use the regression page if you want the popular name unpacked.

## A late-day sketch (example only)

This is not the 7:00 a.m. table on the 1-month page. It is one **evening**, labelled as a sketch.

From about 5:00 p.m. the baby is tired and wired: a short feed, a brief doze on your chest, then another feed. Between 6:30 and 8:30 there may be almost no bassinet success — walking, a carrier, or a partner taking a shift is the work, not a failed routine. Sometime after 9:00, a proper feed and a dim room may finally start a longer stretch. Night feeds still come. If tomorrow's evening is quieter, that does not mean you "fixed" week 6 with a trick.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Ask if the baby is not waking to feed, has too few wet diapers, seems in pain, is hard to rouse, or if you are not coping. Evening fuss that you can soothe at least some of the time is common; a cry you cannot make sense of with poor feeding or a fever is not a "wait for week 8" problem. If you feel angry or unsafe with a crying baby, put them down in a safe crib and take a break — the PURPLE Crying materials exist in part for that moment.

## Frequently asked questions

**How much should a 6 week old sleep in 24 hours?**  
The 0–3 month band, usually quoted as 14–17 hours. There is no official week-6 total.

**How long should a 6 week old sleep at night without eating?**  
That is a [wake-to-feed](/should-you-wake-a-sleeping-baby) question, and it depends on weight gain and what your pediatrician already told you — not on a new 6-week rule.

**Is this a sleep regression?**  
It is a popular name. Read [6 week sleep regression](/6-week-sleep-regression) rather than starting a training book.

## See whether evenings are the only hard part (Yorix)

**Yorix** can help you tag whether the rough stretch is clustered in the evening or runs all day. The app cannot diagnose a 'regression' and is not a medical device.

## Related reading

- [6 week sleep regression](/6-week-sleep-regression)
- [1 month old sleep schedule](/1-month-old-sleep-schedule)
- [Cluster feeding](/cluster-feeding)
- [Witching hour](/witching-hour)
- [Should you wake a sleeping baby](/should-you-wake-a-sleeping-baby)
- [8 week old baby sleep](/8-week-old-baby-sleep)
- [Newborn day-night confusion](/newborn-day-night-confusion)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026.

1. National Sleep Foundation panel (Hirshkowitz et al., 2015), as quoted by Nemours KidsHealth. 14–17 hours in 24 hours at 0–3 months. Accessed 15 November 2026.
2. Pregnancy, Birth and Baby. The circadian rhythm starts to develop around 4–6 weeks. Accessed 15 November 2026.
3. Nemours KidsHealth. At 1–3 months, "sleeping through the night" often means a stretch of about 5–6 hours. Accessed 15 November 2026.
4. National Center on Shaken Baby Syndrome, Period of PURPLE Crying, and clinical explainers (including UNC Health Talk; Gold Coast Health). The pattern often begins around 2 weeks, peaks around 6–8 weeks, and eases by 3–4 months. This is a description of crying, not an official sleep-hour total. <https://www.dontshake.org/purple-crying>. Accessed 15 November 2026.
5. Sleep Foundation. Formal sleep-training readiness is generally discussed around 4–6 months, not at 6 weeks. Accessed 15 November 2026.

body:
# 6 Week Sleep Regression: A Popular Name, Not a Documented Event

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 16, 2026 · **Updated:** November 16, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

Parents search **6 week sleep regression** — and **8 week sleep regression** — when a baby who had a slightly easier stretch suddenly wants to feed all evening, naps go to pieces, or nights get shorter again. This page is for that popular name. It is not [sleep regression](/sleep-regression) (the ages hub), not [3 month sleep regression](/sleep-regression/3-months), and not a second [6 week old baby sleep](/6-week-old-baby-sleep) timetable.

## Short answer

There is **no official 6-week or 8-week sleep regression** in the clinical sources we use. Our regression hub already says sleep in the first 8 weeks is irregular from the start, not a "regression" from a stable baseline. Cleveland Clinic and Sleep Foundation describe regressions as popular names for rough patches, not clockwork events every baby must have.

What *is* often going on in this stretch, with sources:

- The body clock is only **starting** to develop around 4–6 weeks (Pregnancy, Birth and Baby). Days can feel more organized for a few days and then look messy again. That is not a skill being lost.
- Evening [cluster feeding](/cluster-feeding) and [witching hour](/witching-hour) fuss are common. After the first week, cluster feeding should not be *all day, every day* without a feeding check (Cleveland Clinic, on the cluster page).
- The Period of PURPLE Crying, a well-described pattern of fussiness, often **peaks around 6–8 weeks** and eases by 3–4 months (National Center on Shaken Baby Syndrome and clinical explainers). That is about crying, not a sleep-hour quota.
- Parent and health-visitor language sometimes calls this a "growth spurt." There is no official AAP calendar of spurts we will treat as law.

So the honest label is: a hard 6–8 week patch with a popular name. Formal sleep training is still usually too early (Sleep Foundation: often 4–6 months).

### What this is — and is not

| Popular worry | Better frame | Where to go |
| --- | --- | --- |
| "6 week regression" | A popular name for a fussy, hungry, short-nap stretch | This page + [6 week old baby sleep](/6-week-old-baby-sleep) |
| "8 week regression" | Usually the same 6–8 week patch, not a second event | This page |
| "12 week regression" | Often the early edge of the 3–4 month sleep-architecture change | [3 month sleep regression](/sleep-regression/3-months) |
| "2 week regression" | Early-days cluster / very broken nights, not a documented regression | [2 week old baby sleep](/2-week-old-baby-sleep), [newborn sleep schedule](/newborn-sleep-schedule) |

## What actually helps this week

Keep the rules you already have: feed when the baby is asking (unless your clinician has given a different plan), put them down on the back in a clear, firm space, use morning light and a boring night, and accept that some naps will be in arms. A short, same-order evening cue is enough "routine."

Do not start melatonin, diphenhydramine, or a crib-training program because a forum thread used the word regression. If you want a later methods overview, use [when to start sleep training](/when-to-start-sleep-training) and wait.

If you feel yourself getting angry with a crying baby, put them in a safe crib and take a break. The PURPLE Crying materials exist in part for that moment.

## How long does it last?

There is **no official duration**. Clinical pages on PURPLE Crying describe a pattern that often eases by 3–4 months, with a peak around 6–8 weeks — that is the crying curve, not a promise that sleep will "return to normal" on day 10. Parent communities often talk about a stretch of days to a couple of weeks. We will not turn those anecdotes into a number.

If the rough patch came with a fever, poor feeding, or a baby who is hard to rouse, do not wait for a calendar.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Call if feeding or wet diapers are off, if the baby is unusually hard to wake, if breathing or colour worries you, or if you are not coping. A noisy evening in an otherwise growing, dirty-diapered baby is a common story. A quiet, floppy, or painfully inconsolable baby is not "just week 6."

## Frequently asked questions

**Is the 6 week sleep regression real?**  
The *name* is popular. A documented, clockwork sleep-regression event at 6 weeks is not what the clinical sources describe.

**Is the 8 week sleep regression different?**  
Usually no. Use this page, plus [8 week old baby sleep](/8-week-old-baby-sleep) for the week snapshot.

**Should I sleep-train to get through it?**  
Usually not at this age. See the readiness page.

## See when the evenings actually got hard (Yorix)

**Yorix** can help you see whether nights shortened for a few days or for weeks. The app cannot diagnose a regression and is not a medical device.

body:
# 8 Week Old Baby Sleep: When the Clock Stirs and Naps Stay Short

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 16, 2026 · **Updated:** November 16, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

This is the **week 8 snapshot**. It is not [2 month old sleep schedule](/2-month-old-sleep-schedule) (the month view — week 8 is two months). If the only question is 30-minute crib naps, go to [8 week old short naps](/8-week-old-short-naps). If someone has called this a regression, use [6 week sleep regression](/6-week-sleep-regression).

## Short answer

The 24-hour band is still the 0–3 month one: **14–17 hours** (NSF via KidsHealth), with the same wider ranges already listed on the week-2 and week-6 pages. We will not invent an "8 week official total."

The landmark that *does* belong to this stretch is the body clock. Sleep Foundation: **melatonin and cortisol start following a daily rhythm at about 8–9 weeks**, which is when sleep may begin to look a little more predictable. Pregnancy, Birth and Baby: some babies begin sleeping for longer periods around **8 weeks**. Day-night confusion often eases here; it may not vanish on the 56th day.

Naps, meanwhile, are still allowed to be messy. A bassinet nap that ends at about half an hour, while a contact or carrier nap lasts longer, is the classic week-8 complaint. That is usually one short sleep cycle, not a failed 2-month "schedule." The lengthening plan on [short naps](/short-naps) is written for later months. Do not run it as a program this week.

### Key numbers at a glance

| Topic | What sources say | Who |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 24-hour total | 14–17 hours at 0–3 months; no official week-8 figure | NSF / KidsHealth |
| Body clock | Melatonin and cortisol start a daily rhythm at about 8–9 weeks | Sleep Foundation |
| Longer periods of sleep | Some babies, around 8 weeks | Pregnancy, Birth and Baby |
| "Through the night" at 1–3 months | A 5–6 hour stretch is the usual meaning, not a guarantee | KidsHealth |
| Fussy peak | Period of PURPLE Crying often still near its peak at 6–8 weeks | NCSBS |

## What is usually going on this week

Mornings may start to look more like mornings: a feed, a bit of light, a first nap that is the "best" one of the day. Evenings can still be the hard end of the PURPLE / witching stretch. In the U.S., **2-month immunizations** often fall around this week; in the UK, **8-week vaccinations** do. Extra sleepiness or fuss after vaccines is common enough that [sick baby sleep](/sick-baby-sleep) already has a short after-vaccine note: dress for the room, do not add extra wraps, and call if you are worried.

A social smile is expected **by 2 months** in usual milestone language. Celebrate it; do not use it as a sleep-training checkpoint.

## What parents often struggle with at 8 weeks

From recurring community threads, in our words:

- The bassinet nap ends at 29–30 minutes, sometimes with a cry, while the same baby will sleep longer on a chest or in a carrier.
- Nights are "actually all right," and days feel impossible — or the opposite, after vaccines.
- Someone has gone back to work or started daycare early, and crib naps there are even shorter than at home. That is an early two-environment problem ([daycare and baby sleep](/daycare-and-baby-sleep)), not proof that you missed a nap-training window.
- Eat–play–sleep graphics make the day feel like a failure because every nap still starts with a feed. At 8 weeks that loop is still allowed to be loose.

## A mixed-nap day (example only)

This is not the 7:00 / Nap 1 / Nap 2 table on the 2-month page.

Imagine a 7:30 a.m. waking and feed, a decent first nap in the bassinet that dies at 35 minutes, a late-morning contact nap that actually lasts, a short afternoon doze in the stroller, and a 4:30 p.m. "nap" that is really a fidget. Bedtime might still be after 8:30. We are not moving you to a 7 p.m. lights-out this week just because an app suggested it. If a late bedtime is wrecking *you*, a slightly earlier wind-down is a comfort experiment, not a rule.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Same backbone as the earlier week pages: poor feeding, too few wet diapers, a baby who is hard to rouse, breathing worries, or a reaction after vaccines that does not sit right with you. Ask before you drop a night feed just because one 6-hour stretch happened.

## Frequently asked questions

**How many hours should an 8 week old sleep?**  
The 0–3 month band, usually quoted as 14–17 hours in 24 hours, including naps. No official week-8 total.

**Is a 30-minute nap enough?**  
Often, at this age, that *is* a nap. Read [8 week old short naps](/8-week-old-short-naps).

**Should I start sleep training this week?**  
Usually no. See [when to start sleep training](/when-to-start-sleep-training).

## See which naps were short, and where (Yorix)

**Yorix** can help you mark bassinet naps against contact naps so you can see the pattern without guessing. The app cannot lengthen a nap and is not a medical device.

1. National Sleep Foundation panel (Hirshkowitz et al., 2015), as quoted by Nemours KidsHealth. 14–17 hours in 24 hours at 0–3 months. Accessed 15 November 2026.
2. Sleep Foundation. Melatonin and cortisol start following a daily rhythm at about 8–9 weeks. Formal sleep-training readiness is generally discussed around 4–6 months. Accessed 15 November 2026.
3. Pregnancy, Birth and Baby. Some babies begin sleeping for longer periods around 8 weeks. Accessed 15 November 2026.
4. Nemours KidsHealth. At 1–3 months, "sleeping through the night" often means about 5–6 hours. Accessed 15 November 2026.

description: 8 week old 30-minute naps are often one sleep cycle, not a failed schedule. Why the usual 'lengthen the nap' plan is too early.
body:
# 8 Week Old Short Naps: Thirty Minutes Can Still Be a Nap

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 16, 2026 · **Updated:** November 16, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

At 8 weeks, a nap that ends at about **30 minutes** — sometimes almost on the minute — is one of the most common complaints in parent communities. This page is for that moment. It is not [short naps](/short-naps) (the general "why naps end after one cycle," with a lengthening plan aimed at later months). It is not [8 week old baby sleep](/8-week-old-baby-sleep) (the full week snapshot). It is not [contact naps](/contact-naps) or [baby won't nap](/baby-wont-nap), though both are close neighbours.

## Short answer

A 30-minute nap at 8 weeks is often **one short sleep cycle**, after which a young baby surfaces fully instead of drifting into the next cycle. Cleveland Clinic, as already cited on the short-naps page, describes infant cycles as short (about 30 minutes in newborns, lengthening later). The short-naps page also notes that app guides often call 30–45 minute "catnaps" common from about **3 to 7 months**, with many babies linking cycles later, around **5–6 months**. If catnaps are still considered ordinary *after* 8 weeks in those guides, they are not a crisis *at* 8 weeks.

The practical difference is the plan. The general short-naps article includes steps for lengthening naps (pause, dark room, practising crib fall-asleep). At 8 weeks, that program is usually **too early**. Sleep Foundation discusses formal training around **4–6 months**. This week, the job is to get enough total rest — sometimes by mixing bassinet attempts with a contact, carrier, or stroller nap — without deciding that a 30-minute crib nap means you failed.

Is a 30-minute nap "enough"? As a single nap, it may leave the baby tired sooner. As part of a 24-hour total still in the **14–17 hour** 0–3 month band (NSF via KidsHealth), several short naps plus night sleep can still add up. Watch mood and the evening stack, not one nap's stopwatch.

### Why this is not the general short-naps page

| At 8 weeks | Later (see [short naps](/short-naps)) |
| --- | --- |
| 30-minute bassinet naps are often ordinary | Still common at 3–7 months, but you may start gentle lengthening once training age is appropriate |
| Contact or carrier sleep is a valid way to catch up rest | You may be ready to practise more crib sleep, if you want to |
| Do not run a formal nap-training plan | The step-by-step plan lives there, not here |
| Daycare at 8 weeks is an early edge case | Two-environment naps are on [daycare and baby sleep](/daycare-and-baby-sleep) |

## What parents often see

Recurring community situations, in our words: the crib or bassinet nap ends at 29–30 minutes with a protest, even in a dark room; the same baby will sleep longer on a chest; nights may be the easier part of the day; an early return to work or daycare makes the already-short crib nap even shorter. None of that is a clinical statistic. It is why this page exists.

A "rescue" — finishing a short nap in arms — is a survival tool, not a moral failing. If you never put them down, you will be exhausted; if you only ever practice the bassinet and they are a wreck by late afternoon, the day is no better. A mix is allowed.

## What to try — without turning this into training

- Offer the first nap of the day in the bassinet if that is the one that sometimes lasts; use a carrier or a hold when you need a longer stretch later.
- Watch for early tired signs rather than stretching wake time to "build pressure" the way later guides suggest. At 8 weeks, an extra 20 minutes awake can simply make the evening worse.
- Keep [safe sleep](/safe-sleep-for-babies) for any unsupervised nap: back, firm, flat, clear. A chest nap is a **supervised** hold, not a bed.
- Do not add inclined products, swings, or a nest of pillows to "make the nap last."

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Ask if the baby is not getting enough total rest to feed and settle at all, if they are hard to rouse or unusually floppy between short naps, or if breathing in sleep worries you. Short naps alone, in a growing, dirty-diapered, sometimes-cheerful baby, are usually a stage.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is a 30-minute nap enough for an 8 week old?**  
It can be a complete cycle. Judge the whole day, not one nap. If evenings are a constant scream and the total looks far off the 14–17 hour band, talk to the pediatrician rather than only chasing one longer nap.

**Will this last until 6 months?**  
Some babies take longer crib naps sooner; many do not link nap cycles until later in the first year (the short-naps page's app-example timing). We will not promise a week.

**Should I stop contact naps so they learn?**  
Not as a week-8 rule. See [contact naps](/contact-naps).

## See how often the nap died at half an hour (Yorix)

**Yorix** can help you mark 30-minute crib naps against longer held naps without doing the maths in your head. The app cannot train a nap and is not a medical device.

## Related reading

- [8 week old baby sleep](/8-week-old-baby-sleep)
- [Short naps](/short-naps)
- [Contact naps](/contact-naps)
- [Baby won't nap](/baby-wont-nap)
- [Daycare and baby sleep](/daycare-and-baby-sleep)
- [Safe sleep for babies](/safe-sleep-for-babies)
- [6 week old baby sleep](/6-week-old-baby-sleep)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026.

1. Cleveland Clinic, as already cited on our short-naps page: infant sleep cycles are short (about 30 minutes in newborns, lengthening later). Accessed 15 November 2026.
2. The short-naps page already reports app-example language (Huckleberry) that 30–45 minute catnaps are common from about 3–7 months, with many babies linking cycles around 5–6 months. That is not clinical law, and it supports treating 8-week short naps as ordinary rather than a failed program. Accessed 15 November 2026.
3. National Sleep Foundation panel (Hirshkowitz et al., 2015), as quoted by Nemours KidsHealth. 14–17 hours in 24 hours at 0–3 months, naps included. Accessed 15 November 2026.
4. Sleep Foundation. Formal sleep-training readiness generally discussed around 4–6 months. Accessed 15 November 2026.

description: Can a 2 week old sleep too much? Long sleep can be normal. When to wake for feeds, and red flags such as a baby who is hard to rouse.
body:
# Can a Newborn Sleep Too Much? Long Sleep vs Hard to Wake

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 16, 2026 · **Updated:** November 16, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

Newborns can look as if they do little except sleep, and still be well. This page answers the fear behind **can a 2 week old sleep too much** and **can a newborn sleep too much**. It is not [should you wake a sleeping baby](/should-you-wake-a-sleeping-baby) (the feeding-clock rules) and not [2 week old baby sleep](/2-week-old-baby-sleep) (the week snapshot), though you will need both. If sleep has *suddenly* increased in an older young baby, also see [why is my baby suddenly sleeping more](/why-is-my-baby-suddenly-sleeping-more).

## Short answer

**Yes, a newborn can sleep a lot and be fine — and yes, sometimes "too much" is a warning.** The useful test is not a stopwatch total by itself. Healthy newborns often sit in a **wide** 24-hour range: KidsHealth quotes the National Sleep Foundation **14–17 hours** for 0–3 months; Sleep Foundation and Pregnancy, Birth and Baby give **11–19**; NHS pages include totals from about **8 to 18**. HealthyChildren.org describes **about 16–17 hours**, often in short pieces. A baby who seems to "sleep all day" can still be inside those bands.

What matters more:

- They **wake to feed**, or you can wake them for the feeds your pediatrician still wants (KidsHealth: often every 3–4 hours in the first weeks until weight gain is good; HealthyChildren.org formula Q&A: wake in the first month if a formula-fed baby sleeps more than 4–5 hours).
- Wet diapers are in the range you were given (HealthyChildren.org: at least 5–6 a day after days 4–5).
- When they are awake, they have some alert, responsive moments.
- They are not **hard to rouse**, floppy, poorly feeding, or jaundiced in a way that worries you.

If the last line is true, this is not a "lucky good sleeper" story. It is a same-day call.

### A simple triage

| What you are seeing | What it often is | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sleeps many hours, but wakes or can be woken to feed, has enough wet diapers, has some alert time | Often ordinary newborn sleep | Follow your wake-to-feed plan; see the week or newborn page |
| A one-off 5-hour stretch at 2 weeks | Can be normal; may still need a planned wake | [Should you wake a sleeping baby](/should-you-wake-a-sleeping-baby) |
| You cannot wake them, they go limp at the breast or bottle, fewer wet diapers, yellow skin, or very weak cry | A clinical warning, not a schedule tweak | Call the pediatrician now; emergency care if you cannot rouse them or breathing is wrong |

## What parents often mean by "too much"

In What to Expect and Reddit threads, the same picture repeats: a 2-week-old who seems to sleep 18–22 hours, or "all the time," and a parent who is scared to enjoy it. We will not treat those hour counts as data. The questions those parents actually use as a test are the ones in the table above — wake, feed, diapers, alertness — not a forum total.

Day-night confusion can add to the illusion: long daytime sleeps and a wide-awake evening look like "they slept too much today." That pattern has its own page: [newborn day-night confusion](/newborn-day-night-confusion).

Jaundice deserves a special mention in the first two weeks. Sleepy, hard-to-feed babies with yellow skin need the plan their clinician already gave, or a call if they have not been seen. This page will not diagnose jaundice.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Call if you cannot wake them for a feed, if they are feeding poorly, if wet diapers drop, if they look yellow, grey, or blue, if they are floppy, or if something feels wrong even if you cannot name it. In the U.S., 911 if a baby cannot be woken or is struggling to breathe. Do not wait for the next scheduled visit to ask about a baby you cannot rouse.

## Frequently asked questions

**Can a 2 month old sleep too much during the day?**  
The same triage applies, with a slightly more mature baby. Long day sleep that wrecks nights is a timing issue ([should you wake](/should-you-wake-a-sleeping-baby) has a nap section). Hard to rouse is still a call.

**Is 22 hours of sleep normal?**  
There is no official 22-hour target. Some newborns sleep a very large share of the day and are well. The ranges above already disagree with each other, which is why behaviour, feeding, and diapers matter more than beating a number.

**Should I keep waking them at night after the first two weeks?**  
Only if your pediatrician still wants that. The rules live on the wake-to-feed page.

## Log feeds and stretches for the visit (Yorix)

**Yorix** can help you show when feeds and long stretches actually happened. The app cannot decide if a baby is too sleepy and is not a medical device.

## Related reading

- [Should you wake a sleeping baby](/should-you-wake-a-sleeping-baby)
- [2 week old baby sleep](/2-week-old-baby-sleep)
- [Newborn sleep schedule](/newborn-sleep-schedule)
- [Why is my baby suddenly sleeping more?](/why-is-my-baby-suddenly-sleeping-more)
- [Newborn day-night confusion](/newborn-day-night-confusion)
- [Newborn grunting in sleep](/newborn-grunting-in-sleep)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026.

1. National Sleep Foundation panel (Hirshkowitz et al., 2015), as quoted by Nemours KidsHealth. 14–17 hours in 24 hours at 0–3 months. Accessed 15 November 2026.
2. Sleep Foundation and Pregnancy, Birth and Baby (11–19 hours) and NHS newborn ranges (about 8 to 18 hours), as already reported on our newborn-sleep-schedule page. Accessed 15 November 2026.
3. HealthyChildren.org (AAP). About 16–17 hours in short stretches; at least 5–6 wet diapers a day after days 4–5; formula-feeding Q&A: wake in the first month if a formula-fed baby sleeps more than 4–5 hours. Accessed 15 November 2026.
4. Nemours KidsHealth. Wake a newborn about every 3–4 hours to feed until weight gain is going well, often the first couple of weeks. Accessed 15 November 2026.

title: Why Does My Baby Wake Up at 4am? | Yorix
heading: Why Does My Baby Wake Up at 4am? Still Night, Not Morning
description: Why does my baby wake up at 4am? This is often still night, not the start of the day. How it differs from 5am early rising and from a split night.
body:
# Why Does My Baby Wake Up at 4am? Still Night, Not Morning

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 16, 2026 · **Updated:** November 16, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

**4 a.m.** is an awkward clock time. It can feel like the night has failed, and it can also *become* the start of the day if the lights go on and a big feed plus play begin. This page is for that exact hour. It is not [early morning waking](/early-morning-waking) (built around **5 a.m.** and waking **before about 6 a.m.** as a too-early start to the day). It is not [split nights](/split-nights) (a long, wide-awake stretch in the middle of the night). You may need those pages after you decide which pattern you actually have.

## Short answer

A 4 a.m. waking is often **still night**. Sleep pressure is low by the small hours, and sleep is lighter (the same physiology the early-waking page already explains for pre-dawn hours). What you do in the next 15 minutes matters. A brief, boring feed or a diaper in the dark may let the baby go back to sleep until a more reasonable morning. A bright room, a chat, and a "breakfast" can teach 4 a.m. as wake time.

That is why this is not a second 5 a.m. article. At 5 or 5:30, many families are negotiating whether the day has begun. At 4:00, the goal is usually **to keep it night**.

Common reasons, none of them official diagnoses:

- **A feed is still needed** — especially in younger babies, or after a long first stretch. KidsHealth's "through the night" at 1–3 months is often only 5–6 hours; a 10 p.m. start can land a waking near 4.
- **A night feed was just dropped**, and 4 a.m. is now a hungry habit or a genuine gap. Do not drop feeds against medical advice.
- **The start of a split night** — if they then stay up for an hour or more, switch to [split nights](/split-nights).
- **Early rising in disguise** — if they will not go back, and 4 a.m. becomes their regular get-up, use [early morning waking](/early-morning-waking), but still try to keep 4 a.m. dark for a week before you surrender the morning.
- Light, noise, a wet diaper, or a room that is too warm or too cold — the usual environment checks.

### Which page should I stay on?

| What happens after 4 a.m. | Use |
| --- | --- |
| A short feed or cuddle, then back to sleep until 6 or 7 | This page — you protected the night |
| They stay cheerfully or crankily awake for 1–2 hours, then sleep again | [Split nights](/split-nights) |
| They are up for the day at 4–5 a.m. and will not sleep again | [Early morning waking](/early-morning-waking) |
| This is a 12-week-old who just went down at 10 p.m. | Also [12 week old baby sleep](/12-week-old-baby-sleep) |

## What parents often describe

Recurring community situations, in our words: a 4 a.m. "party" that started after someone turned on a lamp and offered a large feed; a waking that appeared when a 3 a.m. feed was removed; an older baby who is in a split night, not an early morning; a hope that a later bedtime will fix 4 a.m., which sometimes helps and sometimes makes them more overtired. Those are patterns to test, not rules.

## What to try (keep it boring)

- Treat 4 a.m. like a night waking: lowest light, little talk, no play.
- If they are hungry, feed, then put them back on the back in their own firm, flat space.
- Hold the "day" until your target morning (often around 6 a.m. — the early-waking page's usual threshold). A 4 a.m. diaper and a 4:10 a.m. breakfast out of the room is how the hour becomes a habit.
- Check the room: dark enough, comfortable on the chest, no exciting noise. A fan is not a SIDS device; cords stay out of reach.
- Give a change several nights. One lucky morning is not a new schedule.

Do not start melatonin for a 4 a.m. waking. See [melatonin and children's sleep](/melatonin-and-childrens-sleep) if that question has come up for an older child, and talk to the pediatrician first.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Ask if the baby is distressed every night at the same hour, if you are unsure whether a night feed is still needed, if snoring or pauses come with the waking, or if you are exhausted to the point of not coping. A regular, calm 4 a.m. feed in a growing infant is often a timing problem, not an emergency.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is 4am the same as early morning waking?**  
It can turn into that. At the moment it happens, try to keep it as night. If the day has truly started, use the 5 a.m. page.

**Will a later bedtime fix it?**  
Sometimes a slightly later bedtime helps; sometimes it produces a more overtired 4 a.m. Test one small change at a time.

**Should I just start the day at 4?**  
You can, but you will usually regret it by afternoon. Protect a realistic morning if you can.

## See whether 4 a.m. is a blip or the new morning (Yorix)

**Yorix** can help you see whether the baby went back to sleep after 4 a.m., or whether the day began there. The app cannot reset a body clock and is not a medical device.

## Related reading

- [Early morning waking](/early-morning-waking)
- [Split nights](/split-nights)
